questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which one of the following ion is released by the ryanodine receptor (RyR) leading to malignant hyperthermia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ca2+

Ryanodine receptors are Ca²⁺ release channels on the sarcoplasmic reticulum of skeletal muscle. In malignant hyperthermia, defective RyR causes uncontrolled Ca²⁺ release into the cytosol. Excess intracellular Ca²⁺ leads to sustained muscle contraction and hypermetabolism. Thus Ca²⁺ is the ion responsible.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents with fever, headache, photophobia, and neck rigidity for the last 2 days. He had undergone a heart transplant one year back and is on immunomodulatory drugs. A lumbar puncture was taken in view of meningitis which showed reduced glucose, increased protein, and increased leukocytes with predominant neutrophils. On microscopy, differential motility was seen, non-motile at 37 degrees and tumbling motility at 25 degrees. What is the most likely organism causing this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Listeria

The clinical scenario and LP findings are suggestive of meningitis. Differential motility with risk factors of immunosuppression suggests a Listeria infection.

Risk factors for Listeria meningitis include:

* Age>50

* Diabetes

* Chronic illness

* Malignancy

* Immunosuppressive therapy

Listeria monocytogenes shows slow tumbling motility when grown at 25 °C.

But at 37°C, it is non-motile because the peritrichous flagella are produced by the bacillus optimally between 20°C and 30°C. This is known as differential motility as motility pattern changes with a change in temperature.

Listeria moves from cell-to-cell using host cell actin framework.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which one of the following statements regarding fetal well-being is not correct?
options: Daily fetal movement count is a simple reliable method of fetal well-being.
Modified biophysical profile includes non-stress test and fetal breathing.
Healthy fetus should have minimum of 10 movements in 12 hours period.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Modified biophysical profile includes non-stress test and fetal breathing.

• The Modified Biophysical Profile (Modified BPP) consists of Non-Stress Test (NST) + Amniotic Fluid Index (AFI) (or deepest vertical pocket)
• It does not include fetal breathing movements. Fetal breathing is assessed only in the Complete Biophysical Profile (BPP).

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• A. Daily fetal movement count is a simple reliable method of fetal well-being. Correct.
• B. Modified biophysical profile includes non-stress test and fetal breathing. Incorrect. It includes NST + AFI, not fetal breathing.
• C. Mothers perceive 88% of fetal movements. Correct.
• D. Healthy fetus should have a minimum of 10 movements in 12 hours. Correct (Cardiff “Count-to-10” method).

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Identify the finding that is seen in antemortem drowning?
questions.explanation: The image shows a hand tightly clutching grass/weeds, which is a classic sign of cadaveric spasm. This occurs at the moment of death, where muscles undergo instantaneous stiffening without relaxation. It is a strong indicator of antemortem drowning, as the victim grasps surrounding objects (like aquatic plants) during the struggle. Why this is important : Cadaveric spasm suggests the person was alive at the time of entering water, making it a key forensic sign of antemortem drowning. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Pugilistic attitude: Seen in burn victims due to heat-induced muscle contraction, not drowning. (C) Washerwoman hand: Skin wrinkling due to prolonged immersion; occurs both ante- and postmortem, so not specific. (D) Emphysema aquosum: Refers to overdistended lungs in drowning, but it is not depicted in this image. The gripping of objects clearly indicates cadaveric spasm, confirming antemortem drowning
questions.learning: The image shows a hand tightly clutching grass/weeds, which is a classic sign of cadaveric spasm. This occurs at the moment of death, where muscles undergo instantaneous stiffening without relaxation.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A male patient diagnosed with tuberculosis took complete treatment. Sputum examination was done after the completion of the intensive and the continuation phases. It was found to be negative. What is the status of the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cured

The negative sputum examination at the end of the treatment implies the status of the patient is cured.

Tuberculosis (TB) is a communicable disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The disease mainly affects the lungs and causes pulmonary tuberculosis.

A bacteriologically confirmed TB case is one in which the biological specimen tests positive on smear microscopy and culture. A clinically diagnosed TB case is one that is diagnosed as an active TB case by a clinician, who has decided to give the patient a full course of TB treatment.

There are two phases in the treatment of TB. The intensive phase lasts for 2 months and four drugs are used. They are isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. The continuation phase lasts for 4 months, where isoniazid is given along with rifampicin and Ethambutol.

After the completion of anti-tubercular treatment, the sputum/culture is tested and one of the outcomes given below is assigned to the patient:

• Cured - A TB patient whose smear or culture turned negative in the last month of treatment and on at least one previous occasion
• Treatment completed - A TB patient who completed treatment without any failure, but has no record to show that sputum smear or culture results in the last month of treatment and on at least one previous occasion were negative; it may be either because tests were not done or because results are unavailable
• Treatment failed - A TB patient whose sputum smear or culture is still positive after treatment for 5 months or more
• Lost to follow-up - A TB patient who did not start treatment or whose treatment was interrupted for 2 consecutive months or more
• Died - A TB patient who dies before starting or during the course of treatment for any reason
• Not evaluated - A TB patient for whom no treatment outcome is assigned; this includes cases "transferred out" to another treatment unit and cases for whom the treatment outcome is unknown to the reporting unit whose treatment I interrupted
questions.learning: Cured — The negative sputum examination at the end of the treatment implies the status of the patient is cured. Tuberculosis (TB) is a communicable disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presented with diarrhea, dermatitis, and dementia. Which of the following vitamin deficiencies would you suspect in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vitamin B3 deficiency

The given clinical scenario of a patient with diarrhea, dermatitis, and dementia is suggestive of niacin/vitamin B3 deficiency.

Niacin deficiency causes pellagra, found mostly among people eating corn/maize-based diets, which are low in niacin and tryptophan. Excess leucine in jowar and maize disrupts the conversion of tryptophan to niacin.

Niacin can be synthesized in the body from tryptophan. Two compounds, nicotinic acid and nicotinamide, have the biological activity of niacin. The nicotinamide ring of the coenzymes nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP) participate in oxidation/reduction reactions.

The initial symptoms of pellagra include loss of appetite, generalized weakness, irritability, abdominal pain, and vomiting. This is followed by bright red glossitis and a characteristic pigmented, scaly skin rash in sun-exposed areas. This rash is known as Casal’s necklace when it forms a ring around the neck.

The 4Ds of pellagra:

• Diarrhea
• Dermatitis
• Dementia, leading to
• Death

It is diagnosed by measuring urinary levels of 2-methyl nicotinamide and 2-pyridone.

It is treated by oral supplementation of 100–200 mg of nicotinamide or nicotinic acid three times daily for 5 days.

Casal’s necklace finding in niacin deficiency:

Other options:

Option B: Vitamin B1/Thiamine deficiency can manifest as wet beriberi (CVS features like heart failure and edema) or Shoshin beriberi, an acute and fulminant form of wet beriberi, dry beriberi (peripheral neuritis), or as Wernicke encephalopathy with Korsakoff psychosis (in alcoholics). Dietary deficiency of thiamine inhibits pyruvate dehydrogenase. Chronic alcoholics may develop potentially fatal pyruvic and lactic acidosis.

Option C: Vitamin B6/Pyridoxine deficiency is rare but has been observed in alcoholics, newborns, formulas low in vitamin B6, and women taking oral contraceptives. Isoniazid, an anti-TB drug, leads to pyridoxine deficiency resulting in peripheral neuropathy. Hence pyridoxine supplementation is included in ATT regimens.

Option D: Vitamin B12/Cobalamin deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia, dementia, spinal cord degeneration, homocysteinemia, etc.
questions.learning: Vitamin B3 deficiency — The given clinical scenario of a patient with diarrhea, dermatitis, and dementia is suggestive of niacin/vitamin B3 deficiency. Niacin deficiency causes pellagra, found mostly among people eating corn/maize-based diets, which are…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young lady presents with recent-onset palpitations and dizziness. Her ECG shows absent P waves and an irregularly irregular RR interval. Her pulse rate is 140 bpm and BP is 80/60 mmHg. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Synchronized cardioversion

In the given clinical scenario, the patient presenting with recent-onset palpitations and dizziness with ECG showing irregularly irregular rhythm with absent p waves, is suggestive of atrial fibrillation. Since the patient is hemodynamically compromised (hypotension), synchronized cardioversion is the most appropriate management.

Urgent electrical cardioversion is indicated if a patient with AF has shock or severe hypotension, pulmonary edema or ongoing myocardial infarction. Although there is a risk of potential thromboembolism if the patient has not been put on anticoagulation before, the need for rate control outweighs this risk. In these patients, heart rate control is achieved using IV β-blockers or calcium channel blockers like verapamil (Option B) or diltiazem. Additionally, they are also given subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin as soon as possible.

In hemodynamically stable patients with AF of >48 hours duration or unknown duration, there is a high risk of formation of a thrombus in the left atrium. If the patients are cardioverted at this stage, this thrombus can embolize into the systemic circulation, leading to end organ damage, such as stroke. Therefore, for these patients, any of the following two management strategies can be followed:

* Give anticoagulation for 3 weeks → cardioversion (pharmacological or electrical) → continue anticoagulation for 4 more weeks

* Start anticoagulation and do transesophageal echocardiography → if thrombus is absent, do cardioversion (pharmacological or electrical) → continue anticoagulation for 4 more weeks. If a thrombus is present, then cardioversion is delayed by 3 weeks.

Direct-acting oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are preferred over warfarin for anticoagulation. However, warfarin is the preferred drug if the patient has a mechanical prosthetic valve, advanced CKD or moderate-severe mitral stenosis.

Apart from anticoagulation, the most important aspect of the treatment of chronic AF is rate control. The drugs used for this are β blockers (such as metoprolol) and calcium channel blockers (such as diltiazem and verapamil). Reversion to sinus rhythm can be done electrically or using medications. Pharmacological cardioversion can be done using ibutilide, dofetilide and amiodarone (class III antiarryhthmics- Option A) or flecainide and propafenone (class Ic drugs).

Atrial fibrillation rhythm is irregularly irregular. P waves are absent, these irregular waves are known as fibrillation waves, characteristic of atrial fibrillation.

Other options:

Option C: Adenosine is the first-line drug for Supraventricular tachycardia. It blocks conduction across the AV node and terminates the SVT. It is given as a 6-18 mg bolus
questions.learning: Synchronized cardioversion — In the given clinical scenario, the patient presenting with recent-onset palpitations and dizziness with ECG showing irregularly irregular rhythm with absent p waves, is suggestive of atrial fibrillation.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Identify the marked structure in the eye.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Canal of Petit

The marked structure represents the Canal of Petit.

In front of the anterior hyaloid membrane and behind the ciliary body and zonule is the capsulohyaloid sinus (or space), or Petit's canal. This is one of the sites of retrolental hemorrhages. This is also the route along which blood sometimes enters the lens, through some rupture in the posterior lens capsule.

Other options-

Option A: Posterior capsule of lens has circular adhesions with anterior hyaloid surface called as the hyaloideocapsular ligaments of Weiger or retrolental ligament. The circular attachment is known as Egger's line. The potential space between the anterior hyaloid face and the posterior lense capsule with the circular attachment is referred to as the Berger's space.

Option B: Lens capsule is a thin, transparent, hyaline membrane surrounding the lens which is thicker over the anterior than the posterior surface

Option C: The canal of Hannover lies between orbiculo-anterocapsular and orbiculo-posterocapsular parts of zonular fibers.
questions.learning: Canal of Petit — The marked structure represents the Canal of Petit. In front of the anterior hyaloid membrane and behind the ciliary body and zonule is the capsulohyaloid sinus (or space), or Petit's canal.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: According to law, an act is not considered an offense if it is committed by a person of unsound mind who is incapable of understanding the nature of the act or that it is wrong. Which legal rule of insanity applies in this situation?
questions.explanation: The legal principle described is the Mc Naughton's (M'Naghten) rule, which serves as the foundational standard for the insanity defense in many jurisdictions, including India (Section 84 of the IPC). It states that a person is not criminally responsible if, at the time of the act, they suffered from a "defect of reason" from a disease of the mind such that they were unaware of the nature and quality of the act, or that the act was wrong or contrary to the law. Durham's rule (Option A) is a broader standard stating an act is not an offense if it was the "product" of a mental disease. Curren's rule (Option C) relates to the substantial capacity to conform conduct to the law. The Irresistible impulse rule (Option D) focuses on a person's inability to control their actions even if they knew they were wrong. Mc Naughton's remains the most widely used legal test for criminal responsibility in forensic psychiatry
questions.learning: The legal principle described is the Mc Naughton's (M'Naghten) rule, which serves as the foundational standard for the insanity defense in many jurisdictions, including India (Section 84 of the IPC).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is the disorder associated with hexanucleotide repeat?
questions.explanation: While many neurodegenerative disorders are caused by trinucleotide repeat expansions, Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) and Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) are uniquely associated with a hexanucleotide repeat expansion (GGGGCC) in the C9orf72 gene. This is the most common genetic cause of both familial FTD and familial ALS. In contrast, Fragile X syndrome (Option A) results from a CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene. Huntington disease (Option B) is caused by a CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the HTT gene. Myotonic dystrophy (Option C) is associated with a CTG trinucleotide repeat expansion. The pathogenic C9orf72 hexanucleotide expansion leads to the formation of toxic RNA foci and dipeptide repeat proteins, which accumulate within neurons and cause neuronal dysfunction and death. Clinically, FTD is characterized by early changes in personality, behavior, executive function, and language, typically presenting between 45 and 65 years of age, earlier than Alzheimer disease. Recognizing this specific hexanucleotide repeat expansion is crucial for accurate diagnosis, prognostication, and genetic counseling in patients with FTD–ALS spectrum disorders
questions.learning: While many neurodegenerative disorders are caused by trinucleotide repeat expansions, Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) and Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) are uniquely associated with a hexanucleotide repeat expansion (GGGGCC) in the C9orf72 gene.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A postmenopausal woman with a long-standing history of uterine fibroids presents with lower abdominal pain for the past four months. Radiological evaluation shows characteristic degenerative changes within the fibroids. Based on these findings, which type of degeneration is most likely present?
questions.explanation: Uterine leiomyomas (fibroids) can undergo several types of degeneration depending on changes in blood supply or the patient’s physiological state. "Calcific degeneration" is the most common form of degeneration seen in postmenopausal women. As the fibroid becomes ischemic due to postmenopausal circulatory changes, calcium carbonate and phosphate are deposited within the tumor tissue. On radiological imaging, this appears as characteristic "popcorn calcifications" within the pelvis, as seen in the provided X-ray. Hyaline degeneration (Option B) is the most common type overall but typically occurs during the reproductive years. Fatty degeneration (Option A) and cystic degeneration (Option D) are less common and present with different radiographic textures. Calcific degeneration is usually asymptomatic, although it can occasionally cause localized pain if the fibroid is large or if there is torsion. Identifying these distinct calcification patterns on imaging allows for the correct diagnosis of fibroids in the postmenopausal period, avoiding confusion with other pelvic masses or malignancies
questions.learning: Uterine leiomyomas (fibroids) can undergo several types of degeneration depending on changes in blood supply or the patient’s physiological state. "Calcific degeneration" is the most common form of degeneration seen in postmenopausal women.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: NAPQI is the metabolite of which of the following drug toxicity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Paracetamol

N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI) is a metabolite of paracetamol drug toxicity.

Paracetamol is an analgesic and antipyretic with weak anti-inflammatory action. It is mainly metabolized in the liver by conjugation with glucuronic acid and sulfate and is excreted in the urine.

At toxic doses, the glucuronide and sulfate conjugation pathway becomes saturated. The metabolites of paracetamol get converted into NAPQI. NAPQI is highly reactive and causes enzymatic dysfunction in the liver. Normally, minor amounts of NAPQI produced in our body are rapidly eliminated by conjugation with reduced glutathione(GSH) and then excreted into the urine.

Therefore, paracetamol toxicity is treated with N-acetyl cysteine(NAC), which replenishes GSH. NAC thereby helps in the excretion of NAPQI from the body. N-acetyl cysteine is an anti-oxidant and functions by detoxifying NAPQI.

Paracetamol poisoning is the most common cause of liver failure necessitating transplantation.

The maximum dose of acetaminophen that can be given is 4 g/day.
questions.learning: Paracetamol N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI) is a metabolite of paracetamol drug toxicity. Paracetamol is an analgesic and antipyretic with weak anti-inflammatory action.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A diabetic patient develops whitish plaques in the oral cavity. A KOH mount reveals the presence of budding yeast containing pseudohyphae. Which of the following is the most suitable culture medium for the isolation of this microorganism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sabouraud's dextrose agar

The most likely diagnosis for the given clinical scenario is oral candidiasis, with Sabouraud's dextrose agar (SDA) being the most suitable culture medium for Candida albicans.

Candida albicans is an opportunistic pathogen that causes candidiasis. It is a yeast when part of the normal flora of mucous membranes but forms pseudohyphae and hyphae when it invades tissue. They are not dimorphic. It forms germ tubes when incubated at 37 degrees Celsius. It is gram-positive and forms colonies of yeasts on Sabouraud's dextrose agar.

Oral candidiasis, or oral thrush, is a patchy, pseudomembranous lesion that can be scraped off, and it develops over the tongue, lips, gums, or palate. It is composed of epithelial cells, yeasts, and pseudohyphae.

It occurs in almost all individuals with AIDS. Other risk factors include high levels of glucose, cellular immunodeficiency, and corticosteroids or antibiotics. It is treated with topical nystatin, oral ketoconazole, or fluconazole.

Other options:

Option A: Chocolate agar: When blood agar is heated to 80-90°C for 15-20 minutes, the V factor is released from within the erythrocytes.

Option C: Thayer-Martin medium is a selective media used to isolate Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Neisseria meningitides.

Option D: Loeffler's serum slope is a medium for the growth of Corynebacterium diphtheriae.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Correctly matched antidote with toxicity
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Benzodiazepene-Flumazenil

Benzodiazepine-Flumazenil is the correct match of toxicity with its antidote.

Flumazenil is a competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine binding site of the GABA A receptor. It antagonizes both the agonist (benzodiazepines) and inverse-agonist (beta-carbolines) of this receptor.

The duration of clinical effects usually is only 30–60 min. It is absorbed rapidly after oral administration, less than a quarter of the drug reaches the systemic circulation. This is due to the extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism. Flumazenil is eliminated almost entirely by hepatic metabolism to inactive products with a t1/2 of about 1 hour.

It is primarily indicated for the management of benzodiazepine overdose and the reversal of benzodiazepine anaesthesia. Flumazenil is only available for intravenous administration. It reliably reverses the sedation, respiratory depression, and amnesia caused by benzodiazepines.

Other options:

Option A: In organophosphate poisoning (insecticide) with both muscarinic and nicotinic manifestations, antidotes administered are atropine and pralidoxime. Atropine is effective against muscarinic receptors. Pralidoxime (2-PAM) is a cholinesterase-reactivating agent. Hence, both drugs must be co-administered to treat both muscarinic and nicotinic symptoms.

Option B: Treatment of atropine toxicity includes administration of a short-acting barbiturate or diazepam to control convulsions. Physostigmine is used as an antidote to atropine poisoning to treat delirium and coma. Other measures for symptomatic management are respiratory support and control of hyperthermia.

Option D: In Arsenic toxicity, the antidote preferred is freshly prepared hydrated ferric oxide, which converts toxic arsenic to non-toxic ferric arsenite. DMSA (Succimer), British anti-Lewisite (BAL), and penicillamine can also be used.
questions.learning: Benzodiazepene-Flumazenil Benzodiazepine-Flumazenil is the correct match of toxicity with its antidote. Flumazenil is a competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine binding site of the GABA A receptor.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a contraindication to the procedure shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Primigravida

The procedure shown in the image is the external cephalic version (ECV). Being a primigravida (first pregnancy) is not a contraindication to ECV. The procedure can be performed in both primigravida and multigravida patients as long as other contraindications are not present.

ECV is recommended to manage transverse lie when the membranes are intact.

Prerequisites for ECV - Women who have reached 370/7 weeks of gestation. Multiparity, unengaged presenting part, nonanterior placenta, nonobese patient, and abundant amnionic fluid improve the chances of ECV.

Absolute contraindications - When vaginal delivery is contraindicated, e.g. placenta previa

Relative contraindications - Early labor, oligohydramnios or ruptured membranes, known nuchal cord, structural uterine abnormalities, fetal growth restriction, multifetal gestation, and prior abruption of the placenta
questions.learning: Primigravida — The procedure shown in the image is the external cephalic version (ECV). Being a primigravida (first pregnancy) is not a contraindication to ECV.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: If a tumor compresses the structures passing through the opening marked in the given image, which of the following sensations would be affected?
options: Sensation in the anterior scalp and dorsum of the nose
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sensation in the anterior scalp and dorsum of the nose

The marked foramen is the superior orbital fissure. If a tumour compresses the structures passing through this foramen, it would impair sensation in the anterior scalp and dorsum of the nose, as this would affect the frontal nerve and nasociliary nerve.

The superior orbital fissure is an important anatomical opening in the skull that allows several critical structures to pass through. Among these structures, the frontal nerve and nasociliary nerve are branches of the ophthalmic nerve, the first division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V1), which is responsible for sensory innervation to parts of the face.

The frontal nerve provides sensation to the forehead, the anterior scalp, and the dorsum of the nose, while the nasociliary nerve supplies sensation to parts of the nasal cavity. Therefore, if a tumour or lesion compresses the structures passing through the superior orbital fissure, it would likely affect the sensation in the anterior scalp and dorsum of the nose because these areas are innervated by the branches of the trigeminal nerve that pass through this fissure.

Other options:

Option A: Sensation of the nasopharynx is innervated by other branches of the trigeminal and glossopharyngeal nerve, not by structures passing through the superior orbital fissure.

Option B: While some sensation from the nasal cavity comes from the trigeminal nerve, the specific branches affected by a lesion in the superior orbital fissure are more focused on the anterior areas of the face.

Option D: Sensation of the chin is primarily innervated by the mandibular branch (CN V3) of the trigeminal nerve, which passes through the foramen ovale, not the superior orbital fissure.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: During a caloric test, what type of nystagmus is expected after irrigation of the ear with cold water?
options: Horizontal nystagmus towards the same side
Horizontal nystagmus towards the opposite side
Vertical nystagmus towards the same side
Vertical nystagmus towards the opposite side
questions.explanation: The caloric test is a standard diagnostic tool used to evaluate the function of the horizontal semicircular canals and the vestibular system. The direction of the resulting nystagmus (specifically the fast phase) is easily remembered by the mnemonic COWS: Cold Opposite, Warm Same. Following cold water irrigation of one ear, the normal physiological response is horizontal nystagmus with the fast phase directed towards the opposite side of the irrigated ear. Conversely, warm water irrigation would produce nystagmus towards the same side (Option A). Caloric stimulation does not typically produce primary vertical nystagmus (Options C and D), which instead suggests central nervous system or brainstem pathology. A normal response indicates a healthy vestibular apparatus. An absent or significantly reduced response (canal paresis) indicates peripheral vestibular dysfunction, commonly seen in conditions like Meniere's disease or vestibular neuronitis. The caloric test is essential for the comprehensive assessment of patients complaining of dizziness and vertigo
questions.learning: The caloric test is a standard diagnostic tool used to evaluate the function of the horizontal semicircular canals and the vestibular system. The direction of the resulting nystagmus (specifically the fast phase) is easily remembered by the mnemonic COWS:…

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 14-year-old male presented with a mushroom-like tumor in the distal femur for the past 2 years. Which of the following features will help the clinician to identify a malignant transformation?
options: Initially growth of the tumor was away from the joint, now the growth of tumor is towards the joint.
Tumor does not have malignant transformation potential.
Tumor is in continuation with bone marrow cavity of the normal bone.
Hyaline cap thickness on MRI is 2cms.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hyaline cap thickness on MRI is 2cms.

The given X-ray shows a well-defined exostosis pointing to the diagnosis of osteochondroma. 2cms thickness of hyaline cap thickness on MRI is suggestive of malignant transformation.

Osteochondroma can turn into low-grade chondrosarcoma but the malignant transformation is extremely rare(Option B). It should be suspected in the following cases:

1. Growth after skeletal maturity
2. Lucency in the bone
3. Additional scintigraphic activity
4. Cortical destruction
5. Pain after puberty
6. Soft tissue mass
7. Thickened cartilage cap >2 cm

Osteochondromas are common benign bone tumors mostly arising from the metaphysis of long bones. The cortical and medullary continuity of the tumor with the underlying bone is a pathognomonic feature that establishes the diagnosis. (Option C). The lesions consist of a bony mass, often in the form of a stalk, produced by endochondral ossification of a growing cartilaginous cap. Most of these lesions are asymptomatic and are discovered incidentally.

These are of two types: Pedunculated and sessile, pedunculated types are more common. The definite stalk is directed away from the physis(Option A). The lesions are usually covered with a cartilaginous cap which cannot be seen radiologically and hence the lesions are larger clinically than what their X-Ray appearance suggests. The important feature is that the host bone flares from the cortex into the osteochondroma.

Most patients are asymptomatic and never seek medical attention. However, symptomatic people may undergo resection.
questions.learning: Hyaline cap thickness on MRI is 2cms. The given X-ray shows a well-defined exostosis pointing to the diagnosis of osteochondroma.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents with multiple painful vesicular lesions on an erythematous base arranged along a dermatomal distribution over the trunk, as shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The presentation of multiple painful blisters (vesicles) on an erythematous base, strictly aligned along a single dermatome, is the hallmark clinical finding of Herpes Zoster (shingles). This condition is caused by the reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus (VZV) that has remained latent in the sensory dorsal root ganglia since a primary chickenpox infection. Herpes simplex (Option A) typically presents with localized clusters of vesicles on the lips or genitals and does not follow a dermatomal pattern. Molluscum contagiosum (Option C) is characterized by painless, firm, umbilicated pearly papules rather than painful vesicles. Chicken pox (Option D) involves a widespread, pleomorphic rash (vesicles in different stages) across the entire body, rather than a localized dermatomal eruption. Diagnosis of Herpes Zoster is usually clinical, although Tzanck smear showing multinucleated giant cells can support it. Management involves antiviral therapy like acyclovir to reduce the duration of the rash and the risk of post-herpetic neuralgia, which is the most common chronic complication
questions.learning: The presentation of multiple painful blisters (vesicles) on an erythematous base, strictly aligned along a single dermatome, is the hallmark clinical finding of Herpes Zoster (shingles).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following method is employed to measure the viral load?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Real time PCR

Viral load can be measured by the real time-PCR technique.

Real time-PCR assays are commonly used for viral load quantification of HIV, hepatitis C virus, hepatitis B virus, and CMV.

Other options:

• Western blotting is used for the detection of protein.
• ELISA is an immunosorbent assay used to detect antigens of infectious agents present in clinical specimens.
• Immuno electrophoresis includes electrophoretic separation of antigens followed by an antigen-antibody reaction.
questions.learning: Real time PCR Viral load can be measured by the real time-PCR technique. Real time-PCR assays are commonly used for viral load quantification of HIV, hepatitis C virus, hepatitis B virus, and CMV.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The number of live births occurring in a year per 1,000 women of reproductive age refers to which demographic indicator?
questions.explanation: The General Fertility Rate (GFR) is a refined measure of fertility that relates the number of live births in a year to the population of women who are biologically capable of bearing children (typically ages 15-44 or 15-49). It is expressed as live births per 1,000 women in the reproductive age group. Gross Reproduction Rate (Option A) measures the number of daughters a woman would have. Total Fertility Rate (Option B) represents the average number of children a woman would have if she completed her reproductive years at current rates. Net Reproduction Rate (Option C) adjusts for maternal mortality. GFR is a more accurate indicator of fertility than the Crude Birth Rate because it uses the specific sub-population at risk of childbearing as the denominator. This makes it a useful tool for comparing fertility levels across different regions or time periods with varying demographic structures
questions.learning: The General Fertility Rate (GFR) is a refined measure of fertility that relates the number of live births in a year to the population of women who are biologically capable of bearing children (typically ages 15-44 or 15-49).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: How does the affinity of carbon monoxide for hemoglobin compare with that of oxygen?
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin is the primary protein in red blood cells responsible for transporting gases throughout the body. While it is designed to bind oxygen, it has a remarkably higher affinity for carbon monoxide (CO). Physiologically, the affinity of carbon monoxide for hemoglobin is approximately 210 to 250 times greater than that of oxygen. This extremely high affinity means that even at low concentrations, carbon monoxide can displace oxygen from hemoglobin binding sites to form carboxyhemoglobin, significantly reducing the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity. Options A (100), B (400), and D (150) are incorrect based on standard physiological measurements. This preferential binding is the underlying mechanism of carbon monoxide poisoning, as the molecule not only blocks oxygen binding but also shifts the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve to the left, further impeding the release of oxygen to the tissues. Consequently, 250 is the most accurate representative value for this increased affinity
questions.learning: Hemoglobin is the primary protein in red blood cells responsible for transporting gases throughout the body. While it is designed to bind oxygen, it has a remarkably higher affinity for carbon monoxide (CO).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old man undergoes semen analysis as part of an infertility evaluation. According to the WHO 2021 (6th edition) reference values, what is the lower reference limit for total sperm motility (progressive + non-progressive)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 42%

According to the WHO Laboratory Manual for the Examination and Processing of Human Semen (6th edition, 2021), the lower reference limit for total sperm motility (progressive + non-progressive) is 42%, while progressive motility alone should be ≥30%.

Why not the other options?

• A. 42%: Correct. Current WHO 2021 lower reference limit for total motility.
• B. 40%: WHO 2010 (5th edition) lower reference limit; no longer current.
• C. 30%: Refers to progressive motility, not total motility.
• D. 50%: WHO 1999 (4th edition) lower reference limit; outdated.

High-Yield WHO 2021 Semen Reference Values

| Parameter | Lower Reference Limit

| --------- | ---------------------

| Semen volume | 1.4 mL

| Sperm concentration | 16 million/mL

| Total sperm number | 39 million/ejaculate

| Total motility | 42%

| Progressive motility | 30%

| Vitality (live sperm) | 54%

| Normal morphology | 4%
questions.learning: 42% According to the WHO Laboratory Manual for the Examination and Processing of Human Semen (6th edition, 2021), the lower reference limit for total sperm motility (progressive + non-progressive) is 42%, while progressive motility alone should be ≥30%.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the minimum per capita space required for each worker according to the Factory Act?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 500 cu ft

The minimum per capita space required for each worker according to the Factory Act is 500 cu ft.

The Factories Act, 1948 states the following in the matters of Safety and Welfare measures:

* > 1000 Workers in a factory – the appointment of 'Safety Officers'

* > 500 Workers – there should be a Welfare Officer

* > 250 Workers – a canteen shall be provided

* > 30 female workers- Crèche

According to the Indian Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017: Effective as of the 1st of July 2017, mandatory crèche (daycare) facilities for every establishment employing 50 or more employees (inclusive of males and females). As this act is more recent, it supersedes the Factory Act, 1948 with regards to the requirement for a crèche.

Maximum hours of work per week including overtime work hours is 60 hours.

Pearl PF1016: The Factories act, 1948 and The Maternity Act, 2017

The Factories act,1948

* The act defines factory as an establishment employing 10 or more workers where power is used, and 20 or more workers where power is not used.

* Age of employment –  prohibition children of < 14 years from working.

* Adolescents between 15 – 18 years

* Can be employed  only in certain industries and  work between 6 AM – 7 PM

* They should not be made to work for more than four and a half hours

* They are allowed to take leave once in every 15 days and have an accumulated leave of up to 40 days

* Hours of work for adults: maximum hours of work for an industrial worker should be not more than 48 hours per week, not exceeding 9 hours a day, if working overtime then it should be no more than 60 hrs per week

* Per capita space availability: For factories established after 1948 – min 500cuft / person

* Safety and Welfare measures:

* > 1000 Workers – Safety officer

* > 500 Workers – Welfare officer

* > 250 Workers – Canteen

* > 50 Workers- Crèche*

The Maternity Act, 2017 is a landmark law which has enhanced the duration of paid maternity leave:

* Working mothers- 12 weeks to 26 weeks

* Working mothers, already with 2 surviving children - 12 weeks

* Adopting mother and commissioning mothers- 12 weeks from the date on which the child is being handed over to the mother.

*for fifty women worker after the 1976 amendment.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A normally developing infant can sit briefly while leaning forward on her hands, reach for and grasp a cube, and transfer it from one hand to the other. She babbles, but cannot wave bye- bye and does not yet use a pincer grasp. What is her most likely age?
questions.explanation: This question tests the chronological mastery of developmental milestones. At 7 months, a typical infant can sit with support (leaning forward on hands), can "transfer objects from hand to hand," and begins "polysyllabic babbling". The inability to wave "bye-bye" is consistent, as that social milestone typically appears at 9–10 months. Furthermore, the lack of a "pincer grasp" (thumb and finger) is consistent, as that matures around 9 months; a 7-month-old uses a "radial-palmar" grasp to hold a cube. A 4-month-old (Option A) cannot yet sit or transfer objects. A 10-month-old (Option C) would have a pincer grasp and could wave bye-bye. A 14-month-old (Option D) would be walking and speaking single words. Therefore, the specific combination of sitting with support and hand-to-hand transfer precisely localizes the child's development to the 7-month mark
questions.learning: This question tests the chronological mastery of developmental milestones. At 7 months, a typical infant can sit with support (leaning forward on hands), can "transfer objects from hand to hand," and begins "polysyllabic babbling".

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following comes under ASA grade 1?
questions.explanation: The ASA (American Society of Anesthesiologists) physical status classification is used to assess a patient’s preoperative physical condition and predict perioperative risk. ASA Grade 1 refers to a completely healthy patient with no systemic disease and no functional limitations. Such individuals are physically fit, have no underlying medical conditions, and are considered to have the lowest anesthetic risk. Examples include a young adult undergoing elective surgery like hernia repair or a child scheduled for tonsillectomy without any comorbidities. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Mild disease: This corresponds to ASA Grade 2, which includes patients with mild systemic illness such as controlled hypertension or diabetes without complications. (C) Moderate disease: This falls under ASA Grade 3, where there is significant systemic disease causing functional limitation, such as poorly controlled hypertension or stable angina. (D) Morbid patient: This corresponds to ASA Grade 4 or 5, indicating severe systemic disease that is life-threatening or a moribund state. Thus, ASA Grade 1 clearly represents a healthy patient
questions.learning: The ASA (American Society of Anesthesiologists) physical status classification is used to assess a patient’s preoperative physical condition and predict perioperative risk.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 27-year-old pregnant woman in her first trimester presents for a routine antenatal checkup. In her case, ABO incompatibility does not occur due to the presence of which antibody?
questions.explanation: In most pregnancies where the mother is Type O and the fetus is Type A or B, ABO incompatibility can occur because the mother produces anti-A and anti-B antibodies of the IgG class (Option B), which can cross the placenta. However, in mothers with other blood types (like Type A or B), the anti-A or anti-B antibodies they produce are predominantly of the IgM class. IgM antibodies are large pentamers that CANNOT cross the placenta. Therefore, ABO incompatibility does not occur (or is extremely rare) in these cases because the maternal IgM antibodies are physically blocked from reaching the fetal circulation. IgA (Option A) and IgD (Option C) are not involved in these hemolytic interactions. This biological barrier is why ABO incompatibility is much less common and generally much milder than Rh incompatibility, where the IgG anti-D antibodies easily cross the placenta and cause severe hemolysis. Understanding antibody transport across the placental membrane is a fundamental concept in neonatal hematology and fetal medicine
questions.learning: In most pregnancies where the mother is Type O and the fetus is Type A or B, ABO incompatibility can occur because the mother produces anti-A and anti-B antibodies of the IgG class (Option B), which can cross the placenta.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: With regard to Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy, match List I with List II and select the correct answer using the code given below the lists:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A-1, B-3, C-2

• β-myosin heavy chain (MYH7) mutation → Marked hypertrophy

• A common cause of familial hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
• Often produces marked LV hypertrophy, sometimes with LV outflow tract obstruction.

• Troponin mutations → Myocardial disarray with minimal hypertrophy

• Mutations involving cardiac troponin T/I can produce extensive myocyte/fiber disarray despite relatively mild ventricular hypertrophy.
• These patients may have an increased risk of sudden cardiac death.

• Myosin-binding protein-C (MYBPC3) mutation → Hypertrophy with later/variable expression

• Often produces a delayed or variable phenotype, with hypertrophy developing later in life.
• Arrhythmias can occur as part of the HCM phenotype.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.topic: General Pharmacology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Match the incorrect pair of drugs and enzyme/reaction they inhibit:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 5FU: Dihydrofolate reductase

5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) inhibits thymidylate synthase, not dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR). It forms a stable ternary complex with thymidylate synthase and reduced folate, blocking dTMP synthesis and thereby inhibiting DNA synthesis. DHFR inhibition is the mechanism of methotrexate, not 5-FU.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Azathioprine : PRPP synthetase — Azathioprine (→6-MP) inhibits de novo purine synthesis via PRPP-dependent steps; this pairing is acceptable in exam context.

B. Mycophenolate : IMP → AMP conversion — Mycophenolate inhibits IMP dehydrogenase, blocking guanine nucleotide synthesis.

C. Leflunomide : Carbamoyl phosphate → orotic acid — Leflunomide inhibits dihydroorotate dehydrogenase in pyrimidine synthesis.
questions.learning: 5FU: Dihydrofolate reductase 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) inhibits thymidylate synthase, not dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR). It forms a stable ternary complex with thymidylate synthase and reduced folate, blocking dTMP synthesis and thereby inhibiting DNA synthesis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true about disulfiram?
options: When used with alcohol, the patients feels drowsy, with chest discomfort and respiratory depression
It can be initiated even in minimally motivated person
Its action persists up to 2-3 days after stopping the drug
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. When used with alcohol, the patients feels drowsy, with chest discomfort and respiratory depression

Disulfiram is used in behavioural modification technique for alcohol de-addiction. The principle of action is aversive conditioning.

Disulfiram is an irreversible inhibitor of both cytosolic and mitochondrial forms of aldehyde dehydrogenase. Ethanol consumption during disulfiram therapy can lead to increased concentrations of acetaldehyde. Increased acetaldehyde levels can cause flushing, pulsating headache, throbbing pain in head and neck, nausea, vomiting, rashes, respiratory difficulties, chest pain, autonomic manifestations and other aversive reactions.

Disulfiram can only be given to highly motivated individuals. Disulfiram should not be administered until the person has abstained from alcohol for at least 12 hours. The disulfiram-alcohol reaction may occur as long as 14 days after the last dose of disulfiram.

Disulfiram like reaction with alcohol ingestion is also seen with the following drugs:

• Metronidazole
• Sulfonylureas like chlorpropamide
• Cephalosporins like cefoperazone, cefamandole

Other modalities of treatment:

• Pharmacotherapy: Typically 5-10 days, treatment for detoxification: Benzodiazepine and chlordiazepoxide are the drugs of choice.
• Rehabilitation programs: Typically 28-day programs, learn about relapse prevention and identification of triggers.
• Maintenance phase: Baclofen, Acamprosate, Naltrexone, Topiramate, SSRI, Ondansetron
• Psychotherapy: Group therapy such as Alcoholics Anonymous
questions.learning: When used with alcohol, the patients feels drowsy, with chest discomfort and respiratory depression Disulfiram is used in behavioural modification technique for alcohol de-addiction.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text:
Match the following:

1. Color vision
a. Applanation tonometer

2. Intraocular pressure
b. Ishihara chart

3. Peripheral vision
c. Tangent screen test

4. Central vision
d. Perimetry
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1-b, 2-a, 3-d, 4-c

The correct option is Option C: 1-b, 2-a, 3-d, 4-c.

Color vision is tested with Ishihara plates, which is a pseudoisochromatic chart. There are patterns of colored and grey dots that reveal one pattern to persons with normal color vision and another to those with the color deficiency.

The below image shows Ishihara chart.

An applanation tonometer is used to measure the intraocular pressure. It is based on the Imbert-Fick law, which states that the pressure inside a sphere(P) is equal to the force (W) required to flatten its surface divided by the area of flattening (A).

P = W/A

The following is an image of the applanation tonometer:

Perimetry is the procedure of estimating the extent of the visual fields. There are 2 types of perimetry: kinetic and static perimetry.

In kinetic perimetry, a target of given luminance is moved from a non-seeing area in the periphery towards the center, where it is perceived. In the static method, the location of a stimulus remains fixed, with the intensity increased until it is seen by the subject (threshold is reached) or decreased until it is no longer detected.

The tangent screen perimetry evaluates the central 30 degrees field at 1 m, thereby testing the central vision.
questions.learning: 1-b, 2-a, 3-d, 4-c The correct option is Option C: 1-b, 2-a, 3-d, 4-c. Color vision is tested with Ishihara plates, which is a pseudoisochromatic chart.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 35-year-man presents with nosebleeds, bleeding gums and multiple ecchymoses. Lab investigations show Hb: 8.5, Platelet count: 12, 000 and Total leucocyte count: 52,000 with 83% blasts as seen below. The blasts are CD33+. The most likely diagnosis is ______
options: Chronic Lymphocytic leukemia / Small Lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acute myeloid leukemia (AML)

The morphology of blasts with abundant cytoplasm, fine azurophilic granules and Auer rods, delicate nuclear chromatin with 1-4 prominent nucleoli on peripheral smear and CD33 positivity suggest a diagnosis of acute myeloid leukemia (AML).

The 2016 WHO classification of acute myeloid leukemia (AML):

* AML with recurrent genetic abnormalities

* AML with myelodysplasia-related changes

* Therapy-related myeloid neoplasms

* AML, not otherwise specified

* Myeloid sarcoma

* Myeloid proliferations of Down syndrome

AML is a tumor of hematopoietic progenitors caused by acquired oncogenic mutations that impede differentiation, leading to the accumulation of immature myeloid blasts in the marrow. It occurs at all ages, but the incidence rises throughout life, peaking after 60 years of age. Occasionally, blasts are entirely absent from the blood (aleukemic leukemia). Bone marrow examination is essential to exclude acute leukemia in pancytopenic patients

Pearl PF1317: WHO classification of Acute Myeloid Leukemia

The WHO system divides acute myeloid leukemia (AML) into several groups:

AML with certain genetic abnormalities (gene or chromosome changes)

* AML with a translocation between chromosomes 8 and 21 [t(8;21)]

* AML with a translocation or inversion in chromosome 16 [t(16;16) or inv(16)]

* APL with the PML-RARA fusion gene

* AML with a translocation between chromosomes 9 and 11 [t(9;11)]

* AML with a translocation between chromosomes 6 and 9 [t(6:9)]

* AML with a translocation or inversion in chromosome 3 [t(3;3) or inv(3)]

* AML (megakaryoblastic) with a translocation between chromosomes 1 and 22 [t(1:22)]

* AML with the BCR-ABL1 (BCR-ABL) fusion gene*

* AML with mutated NPM1 gene

* AML with biallelic mutations of the CEBPA gene (that is, mutations in both copies of the gene)

* AML with mutated RUNX1 gene*

*This is still a "provisional entity," meaning it is not yet clear if there's enough evidence that it is a unique group.

AML with myelodysplasia-related changes

AML related to previous chemotherapy or radiation

AML not otherwise specified (This includes cases of AML that do not fall into one of the above groups and is similar to the FAB classification.)

* AML with minimal differentiation (FAB M0)

* AML without maturation (FAB M1)

* AML with maturation (FAB M2)

* Acute myelomonocytic leukemia (FAB M4)

* Acute monoblastic/monocytic leukemia (FAB M5)

* Pure erythroid leukemia (FAB M6)

* Acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (FAB M7)

* Acute basophilic leukemia

* Acute panmyelosis with fibrosis

Myeloid sarcoma (also known as granulocytic sarcoma or chloroma)

Myeloid proliferations related to Down syndrome

Undifferentiated and biphenotypic acute leukemias are not strictly AML, but are leukemias that have both lymphocytic and myeloid features. They are sometimes called mixed phenotype acute leukemias (MPALs).

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A deceased male was brought to the morgue for a post-mortem examination. His relatives reported that he had a tattoo over his skin, which was not found on examination. Which of the following structures would you examine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lymph nodes

The lymph nodes should be examined in this case.

Some amount of material or dye used for creating tattoo marks is transported through lymph to the regional lymph nodes. Hence, in cases where a tattoo mark has disappeared naturally or has been removed, the lymph nodes must be examined.
questions.learning: Lymph nodes — The lymph nodes should be examined in this case. Some amount of material or dye used for creating tattoo marks is transported through lymph to the regional lymph nodes.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the arrow-marked chamber?
questions.explanation: This is an axial CT scan of the thorax. On axial imaging, anatomical orientation is such that the anterior structures are at the top of the image, and the right side of the patient appears on the left side of the image. The arrow points to a chamber located anteriorly and somewhat toward the patient’s right side, which corresponds to the right ventricle (RV). The right ventricle forms the most anterior part of the heart and lies just behind the sternum, making it the chamber most commonly seen in the anterior position on CT. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Right atrium: Located more right-sided and slightly posterior, not the most anterior chamber. (B) Left atrium: Lies posteriorly, forming the base of the heart. (D) Left ventricle: Located more posterior and left-sided, forming the apex but not the most anterior structure. Thus, the arrow-marked chamber is the right ventricle
questions.learning: This is an axial CT scan of the thorax. On axial imaging, anatomical orientation is such that the anterior structures are at the top of the image, and the right side of the patient appears on the left side of the image.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 58-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of flushing and diarrhea. Further evaluation reveals a mass in the distal small intestine, and laboratory testing shows elevated urinary levels of 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA). Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of a small intestinal mass, cutaneous flushing, and secretory diarrhea is the classic clinical presentation of Carcinoid Syndrome. This syndrome occurs when a carcinoid tumor (a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor) metastasizes to the liver or arises outside the portal drainage, allowing bioactive amines like serotonin to enter the systemic circulation. The definitive diagnostic hallmark is the elevation of urinary 5-HIAA, which is the primary metabolite of serotonin. Neuroblastoma (Option B) is a common pediatric tumor that secretes catecholamines. Leiomyoma (Option C) is a benign smooth muscle tumor without endocrine activity. Chromaffinoma (Option D), or pheochromocytoma, secretes catecholamines and presents with hypertension and palpitations rather than intestinal masses and serotonin-related flushing. Therefore, the intestinal location and high 5-HIAA levels confirm that a carcinoid tumor is the underlying cause of the patient’s symptoms

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: During a forensic examination, the police presented a skull bone for analysis, and the cephalic index was determined to be 85. Which race does the skull likely belong to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mongoloids

A skull bone with a cephalic index of 85 belongs to the Mongoloid race.

Cephalic Index is used to determine the race of the individual.

Cranial index = Maximum skull breadth x 100 / Maximum skull length.

There are three main racial groups: Caucasian, Mongoloid and Negroid. All the skulls cannot be accurately differentiated into the 3 broad categories because of the racial mixing.

The skull offers the best evidence of racial origins.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text:
A female presents to you with 6 weeks of amenorrhea complaining of bleeding per vagina and slight abdominal pain. The urine pregnancy test is positive and hCG level is 2800 IU/L. A mass is seen on the left adnexa measuring 3 × 2.5 cm. She is hemodynamically stable. How will you manage this patient?

hCG- Human chorionic gonadotropin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Single-dose methotrexate injection

The clinical scenario of a patient with 6 weeks of amenorrhea, abdominal pain, and vaginal bleeding with beta-hCG levels of 2800 mIU/mL and a gestational sac in the left adnexa measuring 3 × 2.5 cm points to the diagnosis of unruptured ectopic pregnancy. The most appropriate management for this patient is a single dose of methotrexate injection.

Symptoms and signs of ectopic pregnancy are often subtle or absent in unruptured ectopic pregnancy. The classic triad includes amenorrhea, which is followed by pain and vaginal bleeding. Lower abdominal and pelvic pain is usually seen with tubal rupture. The pain is severe and frequently described as sharp, stabbing, or tearing.

Management of ectopic pregnancy:

1. Medical management is preferred in the following cases:

• Low initial serum beta-hCG level (Less than 5,000 IU/L)
• Small ectopic pregnancy size (Less than 3.5 cm)
• Absent fetal cardiac activity
• Hemodynamically stable

The most popular method of treating ectopic pregnancies is intramuscular methotrexate injection, which can be done in single-dose or multidose protocols. The dose for single-dose therapy is 50 mg/m2 body surface area (BSA).

Single-dose therapy is preferred over the multidose protocol as the former offers simplicity, lower costs, and less involved post-therapy monitoring.

2. Expectant management: A low initial serum hCG concentration, a considerable reduction in levels over 48 hours, and a sonographic inhomogeneous mass instead of a tubal halo or other gestational features are predictive variables for success.

3. Surgical management with salpingectomy or salpingostomy is done when:

• Criteria for expectant and medical management are not met
• Gestational sac >3.5 cm
• Fetal cardiac activity present
• Beta-hCG >5000 mIU/mL
• Significant pain and hemoperitoneum
• Failure of expectant or medical management
• Clinical status of the patient warrants urgent intervention
• Doubtful compliance with medical management

Other options:

Option A: Oral methotrexate is not the preferred route for treating ectopic pregnancy, as it may lead to variable absorption and unreliable dosing. Intramuscular injection is the preferred route of administration for methotrexate in the management of ectopic pregnancy.

Option C: Serial methotrexate with leucovorin rescue is a multidose protocol that can be used to treat ectopic pregnancy. However, the single-dose methotrexate injection is preferred in this case due to its simplicity, lower costs, and less involved post-therapy monitoring.

Option D: Salpingectomy, the surgical removal of the affected fallopian tube, is reserved for patients who do not meet the criteria for medical management or expectant management, have significant pain and hemoperitoneum, or have failed medical management. This patient does not fulfill the criteria for surgical management.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In the following table, the end results of planning are qualified by brief characteristics. How many of the pairs given below are correctly matched?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Only one of the pairs

In health planning and management, goals, objectives, and targets are distinct terms with different characteristics.

Why is only Pair 2 correct?

• 1. Goal – Always constrained by time ✗

• A goal is a broad, general statement of the desired end result.
• It is not necessarily time-bound and allows varying degrees of achievement.

• 2. Objective – Precise; either achieved or not achieved ✓

• An objective is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound (SMART).
• It is a precise statement with a definite endpoint and is considered either achieved or not achieved.

• 3. Target – Permits the concept of degree of achievement ✗

• A target is a quantified, time-bound level of achievement (e.g., 90% immunization by 2025).
• It is also precise and is generally regarded as achieved or not achieved, rather than permitting broad degrees of achievement.
• The concept of “degree of achievement” is more applicable to goals.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A man is using nasal drops continuously for long period of time. What can be the possible adverse effect from its use?
questions.explanation: Rhinitis Medicamentosa is a condition of rebound nasal congestion specifically caused by the prolonged and continuous use of topical decongestants (such as oxymetazoline or xylometazoline). These drops work by causing intense vasoconstriction. With overuse (typically more than 5–7 days), the nasal mucosa loses its sensitivity and develops secondary hyperemia and edema once the drug wears off, leading to a vicious cycle of dependency. Mulberry turbinate (Option A) describes the pitted appearance of the inferior turbinate in chronic hypertrophic rhinitis. Allergic rhinitis (Option B) is an IgE-mediated response to allergens. Vasomotor rhinitis (Option C) is a non-allergic condition triggered by physical factors like temperature or odors. Rhinitis medicamentosa is characterized by a "red, beefy" appearance of the mucosa on examination. Management involves immediate cessation of the decongestant drops, often supplemented with topical nasal corticosteroids or a short course of oral steroids to manage the rebound swelling during withdrawal
questions.learning: Rhinitis Medicamentosa is a condition of rebound nasal congestion specifically caused by the prolonged and continuous use of topical decongestants (such as oxymetazoline or xylometazoline).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with symptoms of eye strain. An image demonstrates that light rays are focused at different points along different meridians of the eye. Which refractive error best explains this finding?
questions.explanation: The provided image illustrates Sturm's conoid, a diagnostic optical phenomenon characteristic of astigmatism. In astigmatism, parallel light rays do not converge at a single focal point due to unequal refractive power in different meridians of the cornea or lens. Instead, they form two distinct focal lines at different planes. The area between these lines is the Sturm's conoid, and the point of relatively clear vision is the "circle of least confusion". This error leads to blurred vision and eye strain (asthenopia). Amblyopia (Option A) is a developmental reduction in vision unrelated to acute focusing errors. Hypermetropia (Option B) involves light focusing at a single point behind the retina. Presbyopia (Option D) is an age-related loss of accommodation affecting near vision but does not create multiple focal lines. Thus, the presence of two focal planes confirms astigmatism

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 50-year-old male presented with diarrhoea for a few weeks. His family members report observing abnormal behaviour that they had not noticed earlier. Recently, he has developed a rash around his neck, as shown below. This rash flares up when exposed to sunlight. Which of the following supplements is most likely to benefit the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Nicotinamide

The above clinical scenario of a patient with diarrhoea, abnormal behaviour (probably dementia) and rash around his neck (casal's neck) points to a diagnosis of pellagra which is secondary to nicotinamide/ niacin/ vitamin B3 deficiency. Hence this patient will benefit from nicotinamide supplements.

Niacin deficiency is mostly seen among people eating corn/maize-based diets, which are low in niacin and tryptophan. Excess leucine in jowar and maize disrupts the conversion of tryptophan to niacin.

Niacin can be synthesized in the body from tryptophan. Two compounds, nicotinic acid and nicotinamide, have the biological activity of niacin. The nicotinamide ring of the coenzymes nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP) participate in oxidation/reduction reactions.

The initial symptoms of pellagra include loss of appetite, generalized weakness, irritability, abdominal pain, and vomiting. This is followed by bright red glossitis (beefy tongue) and a characteristic pigmented, scaly skin rash in sun-exposed areas. This rash is known as Casal’s necklace when it forms a ring around the neck.

The 4 D's of pellagra are Diarrhea, Dermatitis, Dementia, and if untreated, Death.

It is diagnosed by measuring urinary levels of 2-methyl nicotinamide and 2-pyridone. It is treated by oral supplementation of 100–200 mg of nicotinamide or nicotinic acid three times daily for 5 days.

questions.text: The following table gives BP values before and after administration of drug ‘X’. What would be the probable mechanism of action of drug ‘X’?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. β1 agonist and β2 agonist

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 34-year-old woman presents with migratory arthritis and a continuous heart murmur, and echocardiography reveals mitral regurgitation. Biopsy findings, as shown in the image, indicate a characteristic pathological change. What is the most likely abnormality suggested by these findings?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of migratory arthritis followed by evidence of carditis (mitral regurgitation) is the classic manifestation of Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF). The pathognomonic histological finding in ARF is the Aschoff body. Aschoff bodies are focal areas of inflammation (granulomas) found within the heart muscle (myocardium). They consist of a central area of fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by lymphocytes, plasma cells, and large, activated macrophages known as Anitschkow cells (which have "caterpillar nuclei"). Epithelioid granuloma (Option B) is characteristic of tuberculosis. Granulomatous vasculitis (Option C) is seen in Wegener's or Giant Cell Arteritis. Granuloma inguinale (Option D) is a sexually transmitted infection showing Donovan bodies. Finding Aschoff bodies confirms that the cardiac damage is part of the autoimmune response to a previous Group A Streptococcal infection. Management centers on treating the underlying streptococcal infection and using anti-inflammatory agents to reduce cardiac and joint damage, followed by long-term penicillin prophylaxis to prevent recurrent attacks
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of migratory arthritis followed by evidence of carditis (mitral regurgitation) is the classic manifestation of Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 65-year-old patient presents with right-sided nasal obstruction and occasional blood-stained nasal discharge. His CT and endoscopy findings are shown in the below image. What could be the underlying cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Inverted papilloma

In an elderly patient, unilateral nasal obstruction, epistaxis, and pale polypoidal mass arising from the lateral wall of the nose are suggestive of inverted papilloma (Ringertz tumor).

Inverted papilloma (transitional cell papilloma) is a tumor originating from the nonolfactory mucosa of the nose (Schneiderian membrane) and paranasal sinuses. The most common site of origin is the lateral wall of the nose in the middle meatus.The unilateral growth of hyperplastic papillomatous tissue into the stroma characterizes this condition. Human papillomavirus (HPV) is believed to be the cause.

It primarily affects men aged 40-70 and presents unilaterally with symptoms such as nasal obstruction, nasal discharge, and epistaxis. Invasive growth into the sinuses or orbit can lead to proptosis, diplopia, and lacrimation.

On nasal endoscopy, it appears as a pale polypoidal mass resembling a nasal polyp. Computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are used to determine the location and extent of the lesion. MRI can also help differentiate between associated sinus secretions and the tumor mass. Biopsy is essential for diagnosis, as it is important to differentiate it from simple nasal polyps, which may be associated with or mistaken for the tumor.

The treatment of choice is medial maxillectomy, which can be performed through lateral rhinotomy, sublabial degloving approach, or preferably, an endoscopic approach. In 10%-15% of cases, the tumor is associated with malignancy. Recurrence is possible, and radiotherapy is generally not recommended due to the potential risk of inducing malignancy.

Other options:

Option B: Carcinoma maxilla arises from the lining of the maxillary sinus and its early features include additional symptoms like facial paraesthesias, pain, or epiphora and depending on the direction of spread of the growth, would cause additional symptoms.

Option C: Esthesioneuroblastoma (olfactory neuroblastoma) arises from the olfactory epithelium in the upper third of the nose. It has bimodal peaks of incidence at 10–20 years and 50–60 years. Unilateral nasal obstruction and epistaxis are the most common symptoms. The tumour also invades the orbit and the surrounding structures, which results in other symptoms like proptosis, headache, epiphora, diplopia, and blurred vision.

Option D: Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is seen almost exclusively in males in the age group of 10–20 years and is very rarely seen in older people and females. Profuse, recurrent, and spontaneous epistaxis is the most common presentation.
questions.learning: Inverted papilloma — In an elderly patient, unilateral nasal obstruction, epistaxis, and pale polypoidal mass arising from the lateral wall of the nose are suggestive of inverted papilloma (Ringertz tumor).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 9-month-old infant is able to roll over, babble ‘mama’ and ‘dada,’ and exhibits stranger anxiety but is unable to sit without support. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Reassurance

Developmental milestones can show normal variation, and a single mildly delayed milestone in the presence of otherwise appropriate development does not necessarily indicate pathology.

• At 9 months, expected milestones include babbling (“mama/dada”), stranger anxiety, and rolling over, all of which are present in this child
• Sitting without support typically develops around 8–9 months, but slight delay can still fall within normal variation
• Absence of red flag signs (loss of milestones, global delay, abnormal tone) supports reassurance

Clinical approach:

• If development is normal in other domains (social, language, fine motor), isolated borderline delay can be observed
• Regular follow-up is important to ensure progression
questions.learning: Reassurance Developmental milestones can show normal variation, and a single mildly delayed milestone in the presence of otherwise appropriate development does not necessarily indicate pathology. • At 9 months, expected milestones include babbling…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In an experimental model of acute kidney injury, renal perfusion is transiently reduced, leading to sublethal ischemic injury of tubular epithelial cells. Renal function is later restored after reperfusion. Which of the following is the earliest cellular change that occurs in renal tubular epithelial cells during the ischemic phase?
options: Activation of apoptotic pathways with caspase activation
Disruption of the tubular basement membrane
Loss of epithelial cell polarity with redistribution of membrane proteins
Necrosis and sloughing of tubular epithelial cells into the lumen
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Loss of epithelial cell polarity with redistribution of membrane proteins

In ischemic acute tubular injury, the earliest cellular event is loss of epithelial cell polarity, characterized by redistribution of membrane proteins such as Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase from the basolateral to the apical surface. This disrupts vectorial transport of sodium, leading to impaired tubular reabsorption and early functional decline, even before structural damage occurs. Importantly, this stage represents reversible injury, and timely reperfusion can restore normal function.

As ischemia persists, injury progresses in a predictable sequence: cytoskeletal disruption → apoptosis → necrosis and sloughing of epithelial cells → tubular obstruction and back-leak → basement membrane damage (late and severe).

Why not other options?

A. Activation of cytoplasmic caspases (Apoptosis) → Occurs after initial reversible injury; represents progression to programmed cell death, not the earliest event

B. Damage to tubular basement membrane → Late finding, seen in severe or prolonged ischemia; associated with poor recovery

D. Necrosis and sloughing of epithelial cells → Occurs after loss of polarity and cytoskeletal damage; leads to tubular obstruction and is not an early change
questions.learning: Loss of epithelial cell polarity with redistribution of membrane proteins In ischemic acute tubular injury, the earliest cellular event is loss of epithelial cell polarity, characterized by redistribution of membrane proteins such as Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase from the…
