questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Not seen in decompression sickness
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hemodilution

Hemodilution is not seen in decompression sickness. Instead, hemoconcentration is seen in decompression sickness.

Hemodilution refers to the dilution of blood, usually due to excessive fluid intake or other medical conditions, but it is not a feature of decompression sickness.

Decompression sickness (DCS) is a condition that occurs when a person ascends too quickly after being exposed to high-pressure environments (such as deep-sea diving), causing nitrogen bubbles to form in the bloodstream and tissues.

Other options

Option A: Vision changes or loss can occur in DCS due to gas bubbles affecting the optic nerve or retinal circulation, leading to temporary or permanent vision impairment.

Option B: Gas bubbles in DCS can also affect the auditory system, leading to hearing loss or tinnitus, a common feature of the condition.

Option D: Decompression sickness can lead to coagulopathy, which refers to abnormal blood clotting due to the formation of nitrogen bubbles that disrupt the vascular system, potentially causing bleeding or clotting disorders.
questions.learning: Hemodilution Hemodilution is not seen in decompression sickness. Instead, hemoconcentration is seen in decompression sickness.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What hormonal mechanism is responsible for lactational amenorrhea, the temporary absence of menstruation during the postpartum period in breastfeeding women?
questions.explanation: Lactational amenorrhea is a physiological state of infertility that occurs after childbirth while a woman is breastfeeding. The primary driver is "increased prolactin secretion" from the anterior pituitary in response to the infant's suckling stimulus. High levels of circulating prolactin exert a negative feedback effect on the hypothalamus, leading to the suppression of pulsatile Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH) secretion. In turn, this results in low levels of LH and FSH, preventing the development of ovarian follicles and ovulation. Increased GnRH (Option B) would lead to menstruation. Decreased prolactin (Option C) occurs when breastfeeding stops, leading to the return of menses. Increased progesterone (Option A) is characteristic of pregnancy or the luteal phase, not the lactational period. This mechanism is the basis for the Lactational Amenorrhea Method (LAM) of contraception. However, its effectiveness as a contraceptive depends on exclusive breastfeeding and the absence of any menstrual bleeding since delivery
questions.learning: Lactational amenorrhea is a physiological state of infertility that occurs after childbirth while a woman is breastfeeding. The primary driver is "increased prolactin secretion" from the anterior pituitary in response to the infant's suckling stimulus.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 50-year-old male was diagnosed with a submandibular gland tumour and underwent removal of the tumour following which lingual nerve was found to be damaged. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Taste sensation of posterior one-third of tongue is lost.
Taste sensation of anterior two-thirds of tongue is lost.
General sensation of posterior one-third of tongue is lost.
General sensation of anterior two-thirds of tongue is lost.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. General sensation of anterior two-thirds of tongue is lost.

General sensation from the anterior 2/3rd of the tongue is carried by the lingual nerve, which is injured in this case.

In the anterior two-thirds of the tongue,

* General sensation is carried by the lingual nerve.

* Taste sensation is carried by chorda tympani branch of the facial nerve.

In the posterior one-third of the tongue,

* Both general and taste sensations are carried by the glossopharyngeal nerve.

Valleculae is supplied by the internal laryngeal branch of the vagus nerve.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: GnRH deficiency with hyposmia is typically seen in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Kallmann syndrome

Kallmann syndrome is a congenital form of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism caused by failure of migration of GnRH-producing neurons and olfactory neurons during embryogenesis. It is characterized by GnRH deficiency with hyposmia/anosmia, resulting in delayed puberty, infertility, and low LH, FSH, and sex steroid levels.

Why not the other options?

• B. Bardet-Biedl syndrome: Characterized by obesity, retinal dystrophy, polydactyly, renal abnormalities, and hypogonadism, but hyposmia is not a typical feature.
• C. Prader-Willi syndrome: Presents with hypotonia, hyperphagia, obesity, intellectual disability, and hypogonadism, not hyposmia.
• D. Wallenberg syndrome: A lateral medullary stroke causing dysphagia, hoarseness, ataxia, and sensory deficits; not associated with GnRH deficiency.
questions.learning: Kallmann syndrome Kallmann syndrome is a congenital form of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism caused by failure of migration of GnRH-producing neurons and olfactory neurons during embryogenesis.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Identify the mask in the image used for patients with COVID-19 infection.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Non-rebreathing mask

The mask in the image is a non-rebreathing mask (NRBM). It can be used for patients with COVID-19 infection.

A NRBM has a reservoir bag attached to the mask in order to provide additional reservoir volume. In addition, there is a valve attached, which provides a unidirectional flow of gases. Flutter valves on the side ports prevent room air entrainment, while a valve incorporated between the mask and the reservoir bag prevents the entry of the exhaled gases.

NRBM can provide the highest FiO2 of 0.9 to 1.0. without intubation at the fresh gas flow of 12-15 L/min. They are used for preoxygenation before intubation and post-extubation in covid patients.

Other options:

Option A: The venturi mask is a high-flow, fixed-performance device that delivers a specific oxygen concentration to the patient. It is a color-coded device that connects to the oxygen tubing distally and has a nozzle connecting to a mask proximally. Oxygen flows through a central constriction inside the device. Room air enters through surrounding apertures which dilutes the oxygen to the required concentration. The venturi mask is based on Bernoulli's principle.

Option B: Hudson mask is a simple face mask that delivers oxygen without forming a tight seal against the patient's face. There are holes on either side of Hudson's mask. This provides air entrainment, meeting the peak inspiratory flow and venting out the expired gases.

Option C: A nebulizer is used to deliver drugs to the breathing system. It generates an aerosol, producing droplets of varying sizes. It is shown below.
questions.learning: Non-rebreathing mask — The mask in the image is a non-rebreathing mask (NRBM). It can be used for patients with COVID-19 infection.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A man sufferred trauma to the eye from a punch while fighting with another person. What is the most common site of fracture in the orbit?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Floor

The most common site of an orbital fracture due to blunt trauma is the floor of the orbit as it is relatively weak.

The floor consists of three bones: the zygomatic, maxillary, and palatine bones. The posteromedial portion of the maxillary bone is relatively weak and may be involved in a "blowout" fracture.

Isolated fracture of the orbital floor when a large blunt object strikes the globe is called blowout fracture. The orbital contents herniate through the antrum.

Clinical signs: periocular swelling (early stage), enophthalmos, ecchymosis and subconjunctival hemorrhage (later stages).

Investigations:

* X-Ray (Water's view) shows a teardrop opacity

* CT scan is used for confirmation of the diagnosis

Treatment:

Initial treatment consists of observation, oral antibiotics, ice packs, and nasal decongestants. Subsequent treatment is aimed at the prevention of vertical diplopia and cosmetically unacceptable enophthalmos.

Indications of surgery:

* Enophthalmos greater than 2 mm

* Persistent and progressive diplopia in the primary position

* Entrapment of orbital contents

* Fractures involving more than half of the orbital floor with or without herniation will develop enophthalmos if not corrected
questions.learning: Floor — The most common site of an orbital fracture due to blunt trauma is the floor of the orbit as it is relatively weak. The floor consists of three bones: the zygomatic, maxillary, and palatine bones.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 6-year-old boy is diagnosed with cryptorchidism, and the condition has not resolved spontaneously after a period of observation. Which medication is appropriate for the medical management of this condition?
questions.explanation: Cryptorchidism (undescended testis) requires management to prevent infertility and reduce the risk of malignancy. While surgery is the primary treatment, hormonal therapy can be considered for cases where the testis is palpable and low in the inguinal canal. Pulsatile administration of Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH) (Option A) mimics the natural physiological rhythm, stimulating the pituitary to release LH and FSH, which in turn causes the Leydig cells in the testis to produce testosterone. This localized rise in testosterone can facilitate the descent of the testis into the scrotum. Non-pulsatile GnRH (Option B) actually suppresses the pituitary-gonadal axis and is used to treat precocious puberty. Direct testosterone (Option C) or estrogen (Option D) are not appropriate for inducing testicular descent. Hormonal therapy success is generally limited to about 15-20% of cases. If no descent occurs by age 1 or after a hormonal trial, surgical orchidopexy is mandatory to secure the testis in the scrotum
questions.learning: Cryptorchidism (undescended testis) requires management to prevent infertility and reduce the risk of malignancy. While surgery is the primary treatment, hormonal therapy can be considered for cases where the testis is palpable and low in the inguinal canal.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The normal rate of dilatation of the cervix in a primigravida in the active phase of labor is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1 cm/hour

During the active phase of labor, the expected rate of cervical dilatation in a primigravida is approximately 1 cm/hour. This is an important parameter used to assess the progress of labor.

Why not the other options?

• A. 0.25 cm/hour: Too slow; suggests abnormal labor.
• B. 0.5 cm/hour: Below the expected rate for normal active labor.
• C. 0.75 cm/hour: Less than the accepted normal rate.
questions.learning: 1 cm/hour During the active phase of labor, the expected rate of cervical dilatation in a primigravida is approximately 1 cm/hour. This is an important parameter used to assess the progress of labor.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the correct method for measurement of nasogastric tube?
options: Tip of nose to ear lobule to xiphisternum
Angle of mouth to tragus to xiphisternum
Ala of nose to angle of mandible to xiphisternum
Angle of mouth to ear lobule to umbilicus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tip of nose to ear lobule to xiphisternum

The correct method for measuring a nasogastric tube (Ryle's tube) is from the tip of the nose to the ear lobule to the xiphisternum.

Nasogastric (NG) tubes play a role in treating intestinal obstruction and can also be used to provide nutritional support. The commonly used method to determine the length of a nasogastric tube (NG tube) is the NEX method, which involves measuring from the tip of the nose to ear to xiphisternum. The approximate length to be inserted is 55cms.

Ideally, Ryle's tube is inserted in the sitting position with the neck slightly flexed. Confirmation of the correct position is done by the following:

• Auscultation in the epigastric area while injecting a bolus of air
• An abdominal radiograph is the best way to confirm the location of the tube

An NG tube placed for suction should ideally be located within the stomach to avoid potential damage to the duodenum. For decreased risk of aspiration, the ideal location for an NG tube is postpyloric (55-60cm).

Indications for NG tube :

Drainage purposes:

• Conservative management of bowel obstruction and postop paralytic ileus
• Gastric decompression prior to emergency surgery
• Aspiration of gastric fluid

Feeding purposes:

• Nutritional support in patients in motor neuron disease, stroke, and following upper aerodigestive tract procedures
• Administration of medication

Contraindications:

Absolute:

• Severe midface trauma
• Recent nasal surgery

Relative:

• Coagulation abnormality
• Esophageal varices
• Recent banding of esophageal varices
• Anastomoses in the stomach and esophagus

Instruments tray used for nasogastric tube insertion:
questions.learning: Tip of nose to ear lobule to xiphisternum — The correct method for measuring a nasogastric tube (Ryle's tube) is from the tip of the nose to the ear lobule to the xiphisternum.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following has the highest risk of causing invasive pulmonary aspergillosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Febrile neutropenia

Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (IPA) is a highly aggressive, angioinvasive fungal infection caused by Aspergillus fumigatus (most common).

Key Pathophysiology

• Neutrophils = primary defense against Aspergillus

• In neutropenia (<500/µL):

• No phagocytosis of hyphae
• Unchecked fungal proliferation
• Angioinvasion → thrombosis → hemorrhagic infarction

Pulmonary infarction → cavitation

Halo sign/ Air crescent sign

Key Findings:

• Halo sign (early) → Ground-glass opacity around nodule (hemorrhage)
• Air crescent sign (late) → Cavitation with air pocket

| Risk Factor | Mechanism | Risk Level

| ----------- | --------- | ----------

| Febrile neutropenia | Loss of neutrophil defense | Highest

| Hematologic malignancy | Immunosuppression | +++

| Bone marrow transplant | Severe immune compromise | +++

| Prolonged steroids | Impaired macrophage function | ++

| Advanced AIDS | T-cell deficiency (less role here) | +

| COPD (severe) | Structural lung disease | +

| Feature | ABPA | Invasive Aspergillosis

| ------- | ---- | ----------------------

| Host | Asthma / CF | Immunocompromised

| Mechanism | Hypersensitivity | Tissue invasion

| Eosinophilia | Present | Absent

| IgE | ↑↑ | Normal

| Hyphae | In mucus | In tissue + vessels

| Severity | Chronic | Life-threatening
questions.learning: Febrile neutropenia Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (IPA) is a highly aggressive, angioinvasive fungal infection caused by Aspergillus fumigatus (most common).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Every pregnant woman receives a free antenatal check-up on the 9th of each month, along with free medicines and delivery services, including cesarean sections, under the JSSK program. What does JSSK stand for?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram

JSSK stands for Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram. It is an initiative by the Indian government aimed at reducing maternal and infant mortality.

The provisions of JSSK include:

• Free transport
• Free treatment
• Free drugs and consumables
• Free diagnostics and diet
• Free and cashless delivery
• Free C-Section
• Free provision of blood

Note: Previously under JSSK, the free entitlements were provided only for sick newborns till 30 days after birth. Now it is expanded to cover infants also.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A female presented a few weeks ago to the OPD with an itchy skin rash. She was prescribed a topical ointment that relieved the itching. However, after a few days of stopping the ointment application, she presented to the OPD again with the same complaints. The lesions are shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tinea incognito

In this case, the patient presented with an itchy skin rash and was most likely given topical corticosteroids. The image shows atypical lesions of tinea, which is a fungal infection. Although steroids could have provided initial relief, it is not the appropriate treatment for this condition. Therefore, the skin rash reappeared when the patient stopped using the ointment. This scenario is suggestive of tinea incognito.

Tinea corporis/ ringworm infection is caused by the dermatophyte Trichophyton rubrum. It results from the invasion and proliferation of the causal fungi in the stratum corneum with lesions on the trunk and limbs.

Characteristic lesions are circular, usually sharply marginated with a raised edge with central resolution. Scaling is a common but not a constant finding. The diagnosis is mostly clinical. In case of doubt, skin scrapings from site of lesion examined under a microscope may show fungal mycelium.

Steroids suppress inflammation without eliminating the fungus; so the typical raised margin is diminished, scaling is lost, and inflammation is reduced. Hence, diagnosis becomes difficult. Once steroid dosage is decreased or stopped, scaling reappears and shows fungal mycelium.

Pharmacological treatment of fungal Tinea infection is :

Localised disease, recent onset

* Topical terbinafine twice daily for 2 weeks

* Topical azole once or twice daily for 2–4 weeks

Widespread disease

* First-line:
Oral terbinafine 250 mg/day 2–3 weeks
Oral Itraconazole 100 mg/day 2–4 weeks

* Second line:
Oral Griseofulvin 1 g/day for 4 weeks
questions.learning: Tinea incognito — In this case, the patient presented with an itchy skin rash and was most likely given topical corticosteroids. The image shows atypical lesions of tinea, which is a fungal infection.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which labeling is not correctly matched in the below image?
questions.explanation: The axillary artery is divided into three parts by the pectoralis minor muscle, and each part gives off specific branches. Label A identifies the superior thoracic artery, which arises from the first part. Label B identifies the thoracoacromial artery, a major branch of the second part. Label D identifies the posterior circumflex humeral artery, which arises from the third part and passes through the quadrangular space. Label C is incorrectly matched if it fails to show the subscapular artery arising from the third part and dividing into the circumflex scapular and thoracodorsal arteries. The subscapular artery is the largest branch of the axillary artery and is vital for the collateral circulation around the scapula. Surgeons must accurately identify these vessels during axillary dissections for breast cancer or shoulder surgery to avoid hemorrhage. Mislabeling these branches complicates the understanding of the vascular supply to the upper limb and thoracic wall

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old male underwent surgery for an ileal perforation. Due to heavy contamination, only the sheath was closed, and the wound was left open. Daily wound washing was performed, and the wound was closed on postoperative day 5. By which mechanism does wound healing occur in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tertiary intention

Wound healing occurs by tertiary intention in this case. The wound is cleaned and left open for a few days. This allows soft tissues to drain and also ensures no infection is present before surgical closure can be done.

Wound closure is categorized into primary, secondary, or tertiary:

Primary closure is done for clean wounds with minimal tissue loss that are amenable to approximation of wound edges. Healing occurs by primary intention. Primary closure is ideally performed within 6 to 8 hrs of trauma, but wounds in vascular areas (e.g. face) may be delayed to up to 24 hours after trauma.

Secondary closure allows healing by secondary intention. The wound is left open to heal largely by the formation of granulation tissue and contraction. These wounds often have significant tissue loss precluding tension-free approximation of edges, with devitalized edges. Wound dressings are changed daily to aid in the formation of granulation tissue and subsequent contraction.

Tertiary closure, also known as delayed primary closure, results in a combination of healing by primary and secondary intention. The wound is thoroughly irrigated, debrided, and left open for 2 to 5 days before surgical closure. It is used for wounds that are grossly contaminated without significant tissue loss.
questions.learning: Tertiary intention Wound healing occurs by tertiary intention in this case. The wound is cleaned and left open for a few days.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The screening method for GDM recommended in India is done between:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 24-28 weeks of gestation

Universal screening for GDM is done for all pregnant women. The first testing should be done during the first antenatal contact as early as possible in pregnancy. The second testing should be done during 24-28 weeks of pregnancy if the first test is negative.

The screening method for GDM recommended in India is a 75 gram oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) irrespective of the last meal timing. A value of ≥140 mg/dL after 2 hours is considered a positive test, indicating GDM.

Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM) refers to any degree of glucose intolerance having its onset or first recognition during pregnancy.

For IADPSG criteria, an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) is done in the fasting state using 75 g of glucose, and gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is diagnosed if any one of the following cut-offs is met i.e.

* Fasting: >92 mg/dl

* 1 hour: >180 mg/dl

* 2 hour: >153 mg/dl

Earlier, a two-step approach was being used to diagnose GDM. In this, the first step (screening) is a 50-gram one-hour glucose challenge test (GCT). The patients having a positive result of >140mg/dl, are candidates for the OGTT. A 100-gram, three-hour oral glucose tolerance test (GTT), is the diagnostic test for gestational diabetes mellitus. GDM is diagnosed if two or more values are positive.

Diabetes in Pregnancy Societies of India(DIPSI) recommends a 1-step procedure with 75 g oral glucose without regard to the time of the last meal. A venous plasma glucose value at 2 hours >140 mg/dL is diagnosed as GDM.

Some complications of GDM include:

* Maternal

* Hypertension, preeclampsia

* Hydramnios

* Increased operative interventions

* Future development of diabetes mellitus

* Fetal and neonatal

* Fetal macrosomia

* Congenital anomalies

* Metabolic abnormalities such as hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, hyperbilirubinemia, and neonatal hypoglycemia.

* Respiratory distress syndrome

* Subsequent childhood and adolescent obesity

Screening is usually done at 24-28 weeks of gestation. Early diagnosis and treatment are important to prevent complications.
questions.learning: 24-28 weeks of gestation Universal screening for GDM is done for all pregnant women. The first testing should be done during the first antenatal contact as early as possible in pregnancy.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following tests is most appropriate for diagnosing this condition?
questions.explanation: The clinical image shows scaly plaques characteristic of psoriasis, for which the Grattage test is the most appropriate diagnostic bedside procedure. In this test, gentle scraping of the scales leads to their removal in a manner that reveals a shiny membrane (Auspitz sign) and pinpoint bleeding. The Nikolsky test (Option A) and Asboe-Hansen test (Option B) are used to diagnose autoimmune bullous diseases like pemphigus vulgaris, where the skin sloughs off with lateral pressure or blisters spread. A Tzanck smear (Option D) is specifically used for diagnosing viral infections, such as herpes simplex or varicella, by identifying multinucleated giant cells. Because the presented clinical features are scaly, erythematous, and well-demarcated plaques, they strongly point to psoriasis, making the Grattage test the definitive clinical maneuver for verification

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the most common defect in a ventricular septal defect?
options: Non-development of the perimembranous part of the septum
questions.explanation: The most common type of ventricular septal defect (VSD) is the membranous (or perimembranous) defect, accounting for approximately 80% of all cases. These defects occur in the membranous part of the interventricular septum, located below the crista supraventricularis. Muscular (trabecular) defects (Option A) are also common, particularly in infants, and may present as multiple defects known as "Swiss cheese" VSDs; they have a high rate of spontaneous closure. Inlet defects (Option C) represent about 8% of all VSDs and are frequently associated with Trisomy 21. Outlet or infundibular defects (Option D) are located below the semilunar valves (aortic and pulmonary) within the outlet septum of the right ventricle. VSDs generally result from the incomplete development or fusion of various septal components during embryonic cardiac formation. While muscular defects are prevalent, the membranous type remains the most frequently encountered in clinical practice and carries a high potential for spontaneous closure

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the most specific clinical use of Prostate-Specific Antigen (PSA) in the management of prostate cancer?
options: Monitoring the response to treatment in prostate cancer patients
Screening for prostate cancer in all men
Prognosis and survival of prostrate cancer patient
Confirming the diagnosis of prostate cancer
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Monitoring the response to treatment in prostate cancer patients

Monitoring the response to treatment is the most specific clinical use of PSA in prostate cancer management.

Carcinoma of the prostate is the most common malignancy in men above 65 years. The clinical features of prostate cancer are bladder outlet obstruction, pelvic pain, hematuria, arthritis, anaemia, and renal failure. Per rectal examination reveals a hard, nodular, irregularly indurated gland.

Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is useful in assessing the follow-up. PSA >10 ng/mL is suggestive of cancer and levels >35 ng/mL are diagnostic of advanced prostate cancer. The prostatic biopsy is indicated when there is a raised PSA level or suspicion of prostate cancer.

PSA's highest specificity comes into play when monitoring treatment response - whether after surgery, radiation, or hormonal therapy - as PSA levels should fall predictably after successful treatment and any rise can specifically indicate disease recurrence or treatment failure. This is particularly evident in post-prostatectomy patients, where PSA should be undetectable, making any detectable level highly specific for recurrence.

Other Options:

Option B: While PSA is used in screening, its specificity is actually lower in this context due to false positives from benign conditions like BPH and prostatitis.

Option C: PSA levels do correlate with prognosis, other factors like Gleason score and clinical stage are more specific prognostic indicators.

Option D: PSA's are also elevated in conditions like BPH, hence it cannot help confirm the diagnosis of prostate cancer.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A newborn presents with photophobia and excessive lacrimation. Examination reveals a patent tear drainage system, a clear but enlarged cornea, and the presence of Haab’s striae on ocular evaluation. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Buphthalmos, derived from the Greek for "ox eye," is the classic presentation of primary congenital glaucoma. In infants, the tissues of the eye are highly elastic; therefore, increased intraocular pressure (IOP) causes the entire globe and cornea to enlarge (megalocornea). The neonate’s symptoms—photophobia, lacrimation, and blepharospasm—form the classic symptomatic triad. "Haab's striae" are horizontal or curvilinear breaks in Descemet's membrane caused by the corneal stretching. Option B (Keratoconus) and Option D (Keratoglobus) are corneal ectasias that usually present later in life and are not associated with increased globe size or congenital glaucoma symptoms. Option C (Trachoma) is an infectious conjunctivitis that causes scarring, not globe enlargement. Congenital glaucoma is a surgical emergency caused by the maldevelopment of the trabecular meshwork (dysgenesis). Management typically involves goniotomy or trabeculotomy to lower the IOP and prevent permanent optic nerve damage and vision loss

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The biochemical form of amyloid in haemodialysis associated amylodosis is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Aβ2m

Patients on long-term hemodialysis for renal failure can develop amyloidosis as a result of the deposition of β2-microglobulin leading to major fibril protein Aβ2m.

This protein is present in high concentrations in the serum of persons with renal disease.Patients sometimes presented with carpal tunnel syndrome because of β2-microglobulin deposition.

Amyloidosis is a condition caused due to the deposition of abnormal fibrillar proteins in extracellular spaces. Abnormal fibrils are produced by the aggregation of misfolded proteins. The fibrillar deposits bind a wide variety of proteoglycans and glycosaminoglycans, including heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate, and plasma proteins, notably serum amyloid P component (SAP). Amyloid appears as an amorphous, eosinophilic, hyaline, extracellular substance.

Based on the involvement of organ systems it may be classified as systemic or localized. A hereditary amyloidosis is a separate group of heterogeneous disorders with many distinctive patterns of organ involvement.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A man came with complaints of recurrent discharge and pain due to lesions around the anus for 3 years. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fistula in ano

The given clinical scenario of recurrent pain and discharge due to lesions around the anus, shown in the image is likely to be a fistula-in-ano.

A fistula-in-ano is an abnormal connection between the anal canal and the perianal skin, lined with granulation tissue. It may follow the drainage of a perianal abscess or may be seen in association with diseases like tuberculosis or Crohn's disease.

Clinical features are perianal pain, swelling, and intermittent purulent discharge, which might be blood-stained. On examination, one or more external openings may be visible.

Goodsall’s rule can be used as a guide in determining the location of the internal opening of the fistula. Fistulas with an external opening anteriorly connect to the internal opening by a short, radial tract. Fistulas with an external opening posteriorly track in a curvilinear fashion to the posterior midline.

However, exceptions to this rule often occur. Fistulas with an anterior external opening greater than 3 cm from the anal margin usually track to the posterior midline.

The investigations done for fistula-in-ano can include a fistulogram, endoanal ultrasound with hydrogen peroxide, MRI, and computed tomography (CT) scan. An MRI is the gold standard investigation for fistula imaging. It helps us to identify the secondary extensions of the track, which when missed may cause persistence of the fistula.

Surgical management includes fistulotomy, fistulectomy, ligation of the intersphincteric fistula tract (LIFT), setons, or advancement flaps.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: While designing a banner on strategies to prevent the spread of non-communicable diseases, what major mistake did the intern make that prompted concern from the group of doctors?
questions.explanation: Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) like cardiovascular disease, cancer, and diabetes are largely driven by modifiable risk factors. Standard preventative measures include banning public smoking (Option A), restricting alcohol (Option B), and decreasing salt intake (Option D) to lower blood pressure. The intern's error was suggesting a shift from PUFA (Polyunsaturated Fatty Acids) with transfat. In reality, the medical recommendation is exactly the opposite: to eliminate transfats (which are highly harmful) and replace them with healthy PUFAs or MUFAs to improve the lipid profile. Transfats significantly increase LDL cholesterol and the risk of coronary heart disease. Promoting the intake of transfat would be a dangerous and erroneous medical instruction. This question emphasizes the need for accurate health communication in public health awareness campaigns to prevent providing misinformation that could worsen chronic disease outcomes

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A baby presents with diarrhea and characteristic skin lesions involving the perioral and perianal regions, as shown in the image. Which nutritional deficiency is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of perioral and perianal rashes combined with chronic diarrhea in a baby is a hallmark of zinc deficiency. This condition, known as acrodermatitis enteropathica, presents with characteristic acral and periorificial dermatitis featuring erythematous, scaly plaques. Other symptoms include growth retardation, alopecia, poor wound healing, and immune dysfunction. Niacin deficiency (Option B) causes pellagra, which involves the "3 Ds" (dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia), but the rash is typically photosensitive and occurs in sun-exposed areas like the neck (Casal's necklace), not primarily perioral. Selenium deficiency (Option C) primarily affects the cardiovascular system, leading to Keshan disease, and does not cause this specific rash pattern. Magnesium deficiency (Option D) presents with neuromuscular symptoms such as tetany, muscle cramps, or seizures rather than dermatological findings. Diagnosis is confirmed by low serum zinc levels, and treatment involves oral zinc supplementation

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the type of skin graft used in this image?
questions.explanation: The image demonstrates a split-thickness skin graft that has been "meshed". Meshing involves passing the harvested skin through a machine that creates a series of small, diamond-pattern slits. This allows the graft to be expanded to cover a much larger surface area than the original donor site, which is particularly useful in extensive burn management. Furthermore, the holes allow for the drainage of serum and blood, preventing the graft from lifting off the wound bed. Options B and C are variants of split-thickness grafts, but "Split thickness" (Option A) is the standard and most correct term for this appearance. A local flap (Option D) involves moving a piece of skin and its underlying blood supply from an adjacent area, which would not have this "mesh" appearance. While meshed grafts heal with a characteristic "lattice" scar, they are essential tools for providing coverage to large wounds that cannot be closed primarily

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 37-year-old man with hypertension and diabetes presented with blurred vision, photophobia, and increasing pain in his right eye. He has been using contact lenses for the past 2 years. He gave a history of swimming with his cousins, 2 weeks back, in a local pond. What is the most important risk factor for his diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Contact lenses

The above clinical scenario of a patient presenting with eye pain, photophobia, with a history of swimming in a local pond, followed by the characteristic ring lesion given in the image, is suggestive of Acanthamoeba keratitis, and the most common risk factor is wearing contact lenses.

Acanthamoeba keratitis is an infection of the eyes that typically develops from the entry of the amebic cyst through abrasions on the cornea. Most of the cases are associated with the use of contact lenses and individuals who swim or bathe in contaminated water.

Patients usually present with photophobia, excessive tearing, redness, and foreign body sensation, which can be bilateral in contact lens users. Pain is disproportionate to the degree of keratitis due to perineural invasion. It presents as a ring lesion or ring stromal infiltrate.

Diagnosis of amoebic keratitis is made by the demonstration of the cyst in corneal scrapings by wet mount, histology, and culture. The cysts are smaller (12-25 micrometers) and polygonal or star-shaped, as shown below.

Topical administration of biguanides or chlorhexidine with or without diamidine agents can be used for the management of acanthamoeba keratitis. In severe cases penetrating keratoplasty can be done.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child with infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis has multiple episodes of non-bilious vomiting. Which of the following metabolic abnormality is likely to be seen in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypochloremic, hypokalemic alkalosis

Multiple episodes of non-bilious vomiting in infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (IHPS) lead to hypochloremic hypokalemic alkalosis.

Emesis causes loss of gastric fluid containing H+ ions, leading to the release of bicarbonate into the bloodstream. Without normal neutralization in the small intestine, metabolic alkalosis develops. This is the generation phase of alkalosis.

Volume depletion during vomiting hinders the urinary excretion of bicarbonate. This is due to reduced glomerular filtration, increased proximal tubule resorption of sodium and bicarbonate, and elevated aldosterone levels promoting bicarbonate resorption and hydrogen ion secretion in the collecting duct. This is the maintenance phase.

Loss of chloride ions in the gastric acid leads to hypochloremia.

Hydrogen ions exit from the cells in exchange for potassium leading to hypokalemia. Loss of fluid due to excessive vomiting activates the RAAS pathway. This worsens hypokalemia as the aldosterone causes active reabsorption of sodium in exchange for the secretion of K+ and H+ ions into the urine.  The loss of H+ ions in urine lowers the urinary pH, resulting in paradoxical aciduria.

Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (IHPS) is associated with hypertrophy of the circular muscle of the pylorus resulting in constriction and obstruction of the gastric outlet. It is common between 3 and 6 weeks of age. First-born male infants are at the highest risk.

Infants usually present with projectile, non-bilious vomiting. Clinically, an olive-shaped mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium. When the infant is given a test feed, visible peristalsis is usually observed moving from left to right (not from right to left), followed by projectile vomiting. It is associated with hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria.

Ultrasound examination is the investigation of choice for this condition. The diagnostic criteria for pyloric stenosis are a muscle thickness of ≥4 mm and a pyloric length of ≥16 mm. The nipple sign is produced by the double-layered hypertrophic mucosa that protrudes into the stomach. The sonographic appearance of the hypertrophied pylorus resembles that of the uterine cervix and is therefore called the cervix sign.

The image below shows the cervix and nipple sign seen in IHPS:

Management includes the correction of metabolic abnormality prior to surgery. Administering 5% dextrose and 0.45% saline with added potassium at a rate of 150-175 mL/kg per 24 hours can correct the fluid deficit in infants. Monitoring urine output (>2 cc/kg/h) is important to ensure successful rehydration.

The hypertrophic pylorus is surgically corrected by Ramstedt’s pyloromyotomy (open or laparoscopic approach). It involves splitting the pyloric muscle while preserving the underlying submucosa.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Phase 4

* Population fails to grow.

* Demographic gap is 0.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A person is found dead in a bush with bound hands, cyanosis, petechial hemorrhages, abrasions and bruising around the mouth and lips, and marked facial congestion and edema. Which of the following causes of death is least likely in this case?
questions.explanation: The scene and autopsy findings provide strong evidence of foul play. The patient’s hands being bound is a clear indicator of restraint. Abrasions and bruises around the mouth and lips are classic signs of smothering (Option C), a form of mechanical asphyxia (Option A). Facial congestion, edema, and petechial hemorrhages (Tardieu spots) further support death by asphyxiation. Given these circumstances, a Homicide (Option D) is the most probable manner of death. It is physically impossible for a person to bind their own hands behind their back and then smother themselves to death effectively; thus, Suicide is the "least likely" cause (Option B). Smothering in adults is almost always homicidal, involving force to prevent breathing. The forensic indicators of struggle and mechanical obstruction of the airway make suicide an incompatible conclusion. Therefore, suicide is the correct outlier for this criminal forensic scenario
questions.learning: The scene and autopsy findings provide strong evidence of foul play. The patient’s hands being bound is a clear indicator of restraint.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the vertebral level of the abdominal plane labelled 2?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Upper border of L3

The plane marked 2 in the given image is the subcostal plane. It is at the level of the upper border of the third lumbar vertebra (L3).

The subcostal plane is an anatomical reference plane used in clinical and surgical practice. It is defined as a horizontal plane passing through the lower border of the 10th costal cartilage bilaterally. The 10th costal cartilage corresponds approximately to the level of the upper border of the third lumbar vertebra (L3).

The costal cartilages are extensions of the ribs that articulate with the sternum anteriorly. The 10th costal cartilage is the cartilage of the 10th rib.

In the given image, structure 2 represents the subcostal plane, which corresponds to the level of the lower border of the 10th costal cartilage. Since the 10th costal cartilage is at the level of the upper border of L3, it indicates that the subcostal plane is also at the level of the upper border of L3.

Pearl PF0627: Abdominal planes and their landmarks

Planes that divide the abdomen into 9 regions

* Horizontal planes

* L3 - Subcostal plane (between 10th costal cartilages). Corresponds to the 3rd part of the duodenum

* L5 - Transtubercular plane (between tubercles of iliac crests). Corresponds to the origin of Inferior vena cava.

* Vertical planes (Paramedian or lateral planes)

* Mid-clavicular point to mid-inguinal point on both sides

The nine regions of the abdomen include:

* Left hypochondriac, Epigastric, Right hypochondriac

* Left lumbar, Umbilical (Central), Right lumbar

* Left iliac, Hypogastric (Suprapubic), Right iliac

Other planes and angles in the abdomen

* Transpyloric (Addison's) plane passes midway between the suprasternal notch and the upper border of the pubic symphysis.

* The supracristal plane passing through the highest point of the iliac crest on both sides. Posteriorly, it corresponds to the level of the L4 body or L4/5 disc and its spinous process. It is an important landmark when performing a lumbar puncture or spinal injection. The bifurcation of the abdominal aorta lies approximately in this plane.

* The plane of the pubic crest passes through the upper border of the pubic symphysis. When supine, this plane intersects the tip of the coccyx and the femoral head.

* Renal angle is the angle between the 12th rib and the outer border of Erector spinae muscle. The lower border of normal kidneys may occasionally be felt here.

* Lumbar triangle (of Petit) is marked below by the iliac crest, anteriorly by external oblique and posteriorly by latissimus dorsi. Lumbar herniation can occur here.
questions.learning: Upper border of L3 — The plane marked 2 in the given image is the subcostal plane. It is at the level of the upper border of the third lumbar vertebra (L3).

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which of the following is not an OCD related disorder?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Temper tantrums

Temper tantrums are not OCD-related.

Obsessive-compulsive and related disorders are:

• Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
• Body Dysmorphic Disorder
• Hoarding Disorder
• Hair-Pulling Disorder (Trichotillomania)
• Excoriation (Skin-Picking) Disorder

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 65-year-old man’s chest X-ray shows bilateral blunting of the costophrenic angles along with a meniscus sign on the lateral view. Which condition is most consistent with these radiographic findings?
questions.explanation: The clinical hallmarks of a Pleural Effusion on a chest radiograph are the blunting of the costophrenic angle (where the lung meets the diaphragm) and the meniscus sign. The meniscus sign is a concave upper border of the fluid, created by the fluid climbing higher at the periphery due to capillary action and negative intrathoracic pressure. Emphysema (Option A) would show hyperinflated lungs with flattened diaphragms. Tension pneumothorax (Option B) would show a dark, air-filled pleural space without lung markings and a shifted mediastinum. Bronchiectasis (Option D) typically shows "tram-track" opacities or cystic changes, not localized fluid collection in the base. Therefore, the specific combination of angle blunting and a radiographic meniscus is definitive for fluid in the pleural cavity. Bilateral involvement in a 65-year-old often suggests a systemic cause like congestive heart failure
questions.learning: The clinical hallmarks of a Pleural Effusion on a chest radiograph are the blunting of the costophrenic angle (where the lung meets the diaphragm) and the meniscus sign.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A chronic alcoholic patient consuming alcohol for the last 20 years had his last drink 3 days back. He presents with altered sensorium, disorientation, tremors, and a feeling of insects crawling over his body. Which of the following should be given to this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lorazepam + thiamine

The given clinical scenario of alcohol withdrawal with altered sensorium, and a feeling of insects crawling over his body points towards the diagnosis of delirium tremens. Lorazepam + thiamine should be given to this patient.

Delirium tremens is treated using benzodiazepines like lorazepam starting with a higher dosage which is gradually tapered as withdrawal symptoms disappear. In cases of chronic alcohol use, vitamin deficiency (especially thiamine) may be co-existing and hence bolus doses of thiamine are given to prevent/treat Wernicke encephalopathy.

Delirium tremens occurs after 2-4 days of abstinence in a heavy or chronic drinker. It is characterized by autonomic hyperactivity, tremors, delusions, and hallucinations. It usually resolves spontaneously in 7 days but may cause the death of the patient due to cardiovascular collapse, infections or self-injury.

Haloperidol is generally not the first-line drug in case of alcoholic withdrawal. It might be used as an add-on in agitated patients. It decreases the seizure threshold and its use would be appropriate in a case of co-existing psychotic disorder like schizophrenia.
questions.learning: Lorazepam + thiamine — The given clinical scenario of alcohol withdrawal with altered sensorium, and a feeling of insects crawling over his body points towards the diagnosis of delirium tremens.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 3-year-old child has a long-standing history of rickets and malnutrition. The child’s growth is below the 5th percentile, and there has been no exposure to sunlight. Which of the following national programs specifically addresses nutritional deficiencies among children below 6 years of age?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. ICDS Program

The Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) programme is the primary national initiative addressing nutrition, growth, and development of children below 6 years of age.

The child in the question:

• Age 3 years
• Has malnutrition and rickets
• Falls under preschool age group (<6 years)

ICDS directly addresses these issues through nutrition supplementation and health services delivered via Anganwadi centres.

Target Beneficiaries of ICDS

Thus, ICDS is the primary national program for child nutrition below 6 years.

It provides supplementary nutrition, growth monitoring, health check-ups, immunization support, and nutrition education through Anganwadi centres.

Programs like Mid-Day Meal target school-age children, while Anemia Mukt Bharat and NNAPP focus on anemia rather than comprehensive early childhood nutrition.

Six Services Under ICDS

These services are delivered through Anganwadi centres
questions.learning: ICDS Program — The Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) programme is the primary national initiative addressing nutrition, growth, and development of children below 6 years of age.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Water from a broken septic tank is collected in a container and breeding mosquitoes are seen. The image of the larva is given below. Identify the species of the mosquito.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Culex

The species of mosquito that breeds in dirty water is Culex.

Culex fatigans are found everywhere in India and they transmit Bancroftian filariasis. Culex mosquitoes are also vectors for Japanese encephalitis, West Nile fever, and viral arthritis.

It can be identified by the presence of unspotted wings and hunched back. The larva has a head that is suspended downwards at an angle to the water surface and a siphon tube is present.

It breeds in dirty water collections like stagnant drains, septic tanks, and burrow pits. The peak biting time is during midnight. The preferred biting site is the legs, mainly below the knee.
questions.learning: Culex — The species of mosquito that breeds in dirty water is Culex. Culex fatigans are found everywhere in India and they transmit Bancroftian filariasis.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Gold standard investigation before Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (FESS) is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. CT scan

The gold standard investigation before FESS is a CT scan to rule out other pathologies and for confirmation of diagnosis. CT scan is better than MRI for visualizing bones and their anatomy.

Even while doing surgery, decisions on whether to open the mastoid antrum are based on CT findings and intraoperative findings. FESS is done for failed medical management of rhinosinusitis.

Other indications of FESS:

* Chronic bacterial sinusitis that is unresponsive to adequate medical treatment.

* Recurrent acute bacterial sinusitis

* Polypoid rhinosinusitis (diffuse nasal polyposis)

* Fungal sinusitis with a fungal ball or nasal polypi

* Antrochoanal polyp

* Mucocele of frontoethmoid or sphenoid sinus

* Control of epistaxis by endoscopic cautery.

* Removal of foreign body from the nose or sinus

* Endoscopic septoplasty

Advanced nasal endoscopic techniques

* Removal of benign tumors, e.g. inverted papillomas or angiofibromas.

* Orbital abscess or cellulitis management.

* Dacryocystorhinostomy

* Repair of CSF leak

* Pituitary surgery

* Optic nerve decompression

* Orbital decompression for Graves’ disease

* Control of posterior epistaxis (endoscopic clipping of sphenopalatine artery)

* Choanal atresia.
questions.learning: CT scan — The gold standard investigation before FESS is a CT scan to rule out other pathologies and for confirmation of diagnosis. CT scan is better than MRI for visualizing bones and their anatomy.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In the 2 vessels shown below, assume the pressure along both the vessels is the same and both follow linear flow pattern. What will be the amount of blood flow in A compared to B
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 8 times

The relationship between the flow in a long narrow tube, the viscosity of the fluid, and the radius of the tube is expressed mathematically in the formula called as Poiseuille's law :

Blood flow (F) inside the vessel depends on:

• Pressure difference: directly proportional
• Viscosity: inversely proportional
• Radius: directly proportional to the fourth power
• Length of the vessel: inversely proportional

Here, the radius is doubled so the flow increases by 2 to the power of 4 = 16.

the length of the vessel is also doubled, so the flow decreases by half (÷2) = 8

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following hypothalamic nuclei are responsible for leptin resistance?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Arcuate nucleus

Leptin is the body’s “fat thermostat hormone”

• Secreted by adipocytes
• Tells the brain: “We have enough energy, stop eating.”

But in obesity- Leptin is high, yet appetite persists → leptin resistance

The arcuate nucleus is the main hypothalamic leptin-sensing center containing POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons. Leptin resistance arises from impaired signaling in this nucleus, leading to failure of appetite suppression. It integrates peripheral energy signals.

| Nucleus | Function | Lesion Effect

| ------- | -------- | -------------

| Arcuate | Leptin integration | Leptin resistance

| Lateral | Hunger center | ↓ eating

| Ventromedial | Satiety center | Hyperphagia

| Paraventricular | Autonomic/endocrine control | Dysregulation

Extra Edge Points

1. POMC → α-MSH → acts on MC4 receptor → satiety
2. NPY = strongest appetite stimulant
3. AgRP blocks melanocortin receptors → promotes eating

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following is a secondary cause of headache?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Medication overuse headache

Headaches are classified into primary and secondary headaches according to the International Classification of Headache Disorders (ICHD-3).

• Primary headaches are disorders in which the headache itself is the disease (e.g., migraine, tension-type headache, trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias).
• Secondary headaches occur as a consequence of another condition, including medication overuse, infections, trauma, vascular disorders, or intracranial pathology.

Medication overuse headache (MOH) is the most common secondary chronic daily headache, resulting from the frequent use of acute headache medications.

Why not the other options?

• A. Migraine: A primary headache disorder.
• B. Tension-type headache: The most common primary headache.
• C. Trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia: A group of primary headache disorders, including cluster headache, paroxysmal hemicrania, and SUNCT.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the obstetric grip performed in the picture.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pelvic grip

The obstetric grip shown in the picture is a pelvic grip.

Leopold's manoeuvres help assess the fetal pole, lie, presenting part, engagement, and attitude of the fetal head. They are as follows:

* Fundal grip (first Leopold): Assesses the uterine fundus.

* Helps in the identification of fetal lie and determination of fetal pole at the fundus.

* The breech is felt as a large, irregular mass. The head feels hard and round and is more mobile.

* Lateral grip (second Leopold):  Assesses fetal orientation.

* The palms are placed on either side of the maternal abdomen, and gentle but deep pressure is exerted.

* The back is felt on one side as a hard, resistant structure. The fetal extremities are felt on the other side as numerous small, irregular, mobile parts.

* Pawlik's grip/ 1st pelvic grip (third Leopold): Assesses the presenting part.

* The thumb and fingers of one hand grasp the lower portion of the maternal abdomen just above the symphysis pubis.

* If the presenting part is not engaged, a movable mass will be felt, usually the head.

* Deep pelvic grip/ 2nd pelvic grip (fourth Leopold): Assesses the engagement and attitude of the fetal head.

* The examiner faces the mother's feet, and the fingertips of both hands are positioned on either side of the presenting part.

* They exert inward pressure and then slide along the axis of the pelvic outlet.
questions.learning: Pelvic grip — The obstetric grip shown in the picture is a pelvic grip. Leopold's manoeuvres help assess the fetal pole, lie, presenting part, engagement, and attitude of the fetal head.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Revised A 70-year-old man presents with chronic low back pain, fatigue, and headaches for the last few weeks. On examination, he has pallor and bony tenderness. Lab investigations revealed an increased ESR and his skull radiograph revealed several punched-out lytic lesions. Which of the following is the best investigation for this patient in the options given below ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Serum electrophoresis showing IgG

The given clinical condition is highly suggestive of multiple myeloma and in the given options,  serum electrophoresis showing M band in the gamma globulin region is preferred for multiple myeloma.

Bone marrow biopsy is diagnostic for multiple myeloma, where the neoplastic plasma cells can be seen.

Plasma cell dyscrasias are B-cell proliferations that contain neoplastic plasma cells that secrete a monoclonal Ig or Ig fragment.

* Multiple myelomas: Malignant neoplasm of plasma cells characterized by:

* Presence of monoclonal immunoglobulin or light chains in the serum and urine

* Bone destruction (lytic lesions)

* The disease of older adults, with a peak age of incidence of 65 to 70 years

* Signs and symptoms

* Hypercalcemia

* Pathologic fractures/lytic bone lesions

* Renal failure

* Anemia

* Radiography: Punched-out lytic lesions on X-ray

* Electrophoresis: Monoclonal elevation of one immunoglobulin

* Urinalysis: Free kappa and lambda light chains (Bence Jones proteins)

* Bone marrow biopsy: 10 to 20%plasma cells (normal is < 5%)

* Peripheral smear: Rouleaux formation (High level of M proteins in myeloma causes red cells in the peripheral blood smears to stick to one another in linear arrays, a finding referred to as rouleaux formation.)

* Plasma cell tumors are positive for CD138

Pearl PF0580: WHO Classification of Plasma Cell Neoplasms

Plasma cell neoplasms and variants

Plasma cell myeloma

• Non secretory: No secretion of Ig, No M component.

• Smoldering: M protein in serum ≥ 30 g/L and/or ≥10% clonal plasma cells in bone marrow, and no related organ or tissue impairment.

• Plasma-cell leukemia: >20% plasma cells in the peripheral blood or Absolute plasma cell count of >2 X 109/L.

Plasmacytoma

• Solitary plasmacytoma: Localized tumour of monoclonal plasma cells with no clinical features of plasma cell myeloma.

• Extramedullary(extraosseous) plasmacytoma: Localized plasma cell neoplasms that arise in tissues other than bone.

Monoclonal immunoglobulin deposition diseases

• Primary amyloidosis: Tumor secreting light chains that are deposited as beta-pleated sheet structure (amyloid light chain).

• Systemic light and heavy chain diseases: Secrete abnormal light or heavy chain or both, which do not form beta pleated sheet, stain Congo Red or contain amyloid P component.

Plasma cell neoplasms with associated paraneoplastic syndrome

POEMS syndrome- Polyneuropathy, organomegaly, Endocrinopathy, Monoclonal gammopathy, Skin changes.

TEMPI syndrome
questions.learning: Serum electrophoresis showing IgG — The given clinical condition is highly suggestive of multiple myeloma and in the given options, serum electrophoresis showing M band in the gamma globulin region is preferred for multiple myeloma.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which occupational exposure is most strongly linked to the development of mesothelioma?
questions.explanation: Malignant mesothelioma is a rare cancer of the pleura, peritoneum, or pericardium that is almost exclusively associated with asbestos exposure. Inhaled asbestos fibers lodge in the pleura, causing chronic inflammation and eventual malignant transformation over a long latency period of 20–40 years. Silica dust (Option B) causes silicosis and increases the risk of tuberculosis and lung cancer but is not a primary driver of mesothelioma. Cotton dust (Option C) is linked to byssinosis, an obstructive lung disease known as "Monday fever". Coal dust (Option D) results in coal workers' pneumoconiosis or "black lung". While asbestos is also the most common cause of general lung carcinoma, mesothelioma is its most "specific" neoplastic complication. High-risk occupations include shipbuilding, insulation manufacturing, and mining

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Out of the following areas of brain, which area is most commonly affected on brain imaging in Wilson’s disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Basal ganglia

Wilson’s disease (hepatolenticular degeneration) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene, leading to impaired biliary copper excretion and excessive copper accumulation. The basal ganglia, particularly the putamen, are the most commonly affected structures on brain MRI, explaining the characteristic movement disorders seen in the disease.

• Basal ganglia, especially the putamen, show the most frequent MRI abnormalities.
• MRI may demonstrate:

• Bilateral symmetric T2 hyperintensities in the putamen
• Globus pallidus involvement
• Caudate nucleus involvement
• Thalamic and brainstem involvement in advanced disease
• “Face of the giant panda” sign in the midbrain (classic MRI finding).

Why not the other options?

• A. Cerebellum – May be involved in advanced disease but is not the most commonly affected area.
• B. Sub-cortex – White matter involvement is less common than basal ganglia involvement.
• C. Thalamus – Can be affected but less frequently than the basal ganglia.
questions.learning: Basal ganglia Wilson’s disease (hepatolenticular degeneration) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene, leading to impaired biliary copper excretion and excessive copper accumulation.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: If a patient tests positive for a disease, which of the following represents the probability of her actually having the disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Positive predictive value

Positive predictive value implies the probability of a person with a positive test, actually having the disease.

It is the ability of a test to detect true positive(TP) out of total positive(TP+FP) and it is directly proportional to the prevalence of a disease.

PPV= TP/TP+FP

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is the primary surveillance tool in the Growth Restricted Fetus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Umbilical artery Doppler

• Umbilical artery Doppler is the first-line and most important surveillance modality in FGR. ⭐
• It evaluates placental blood flow by measuring:

• Pulsatility Index (PI)
• Resistance Index (RI)
• Systolic/Diastolic (S/D) ratio

• Progressive deterioration is indicated by:

• Increased PI
• Absent End-Diastolic Flow (AEDF)
• Reversed End-Diastolic Flow (REDF)

Why not the other options?

• A. Uterine artery Doppler: Used primarily as a screening tool in the second trimester (20–24 weeks) to predict FGR and preeclampsia, not for ongoing surveillance.
• B. Umbilical venous pulsation: Abnormal umbilical venous pulsations occur late and indicate severe fetal compromise.
• C. Middle cerebral artery (MCA) Doppler: MCA Doppler detects the brain-sparing effect (reduced PI due to cerebral vasodilatation) and complements umbilical artery Doppler but is not the primary surveillance tool.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which parameter is the best guide to monitor the adequacy of fluid resuscitation in a patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Urine output

Urine output is the best measure of organ perfusion and the best monitor for adequacy of fluid resuscitation.

Adequate end-organ perfusion is best indicated by urine output of  >0.5 to 1 mL/kg/h. However, it does not give a minute-to-minute value.

The level of consciousness is an important marker for cerebral perfusion.

The only clinical indicators of perfusion of the gastrointestinal tract and muscular beds are measures of lactic acidosis (lactate and base deficit) and mixed venous oxygen saturation.

Other options:

Option A: Central venous pressure (CVP) is the mean pressure in the superior vena cava, used for estimation of preload and right atrial pressure. Normal CVP ranges from 2 to 7 mm Hg (3 to 9 cm H2O). A sick or injured patient with a CVP <3 mm Hg is presumed to be volume depleted and may be given fluids with relative safety. However, CVP is unreliable in assessing volume status or left ventricular function with respect to resusitation.

Options C and D: Blood pressure and oxygen saturation do not reflect body fluid levels.
questions.learning: Urine output Urine output is the best measure of organ perfusion and the best monitor for adequacy of fluid resuscitation. Adequate end-organ perfusion is best indicated by urine output of >0.5 to 1 mL/kg/h.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is not seen in a case of otitis media?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Battle sign

Battle sign refers to retro auricular or mastoid ecchymosis that typically results from a fracture of the middle cranial fossa following head trauma. It is prominent when there is a fracture of the temporal bone. Battle sign is not seen in the case of otitis media.

Option A: Bezold abscess is a complication of acute otomastoiditis where the infection/pus breaks through the thin medial side of the tip of the mastoid and presents as a swelling in the upper part of the neck.

Option B: Griesinger sign refers to edema of the postauricular soft tissues overlying the mastoid process as a result of thrombosis of the mastoid emissary vein seen in sigmoid sinus thrombosis. It is a complication of acute otomastoiditis.

Option D: Delta sign is a contrast-enhanced CT finding seen in sagittal sinus thrombosis, which can occur as a complication of acute mastoiditis or chronic suppurative otitis media. It is a triangular area with rim enhancement and the central low-density area is seen in the posterior cranial fossa on axial cuts. MR venography is useful to assess the progression or resolution of a thrombus.

The image below depicts a filling defect (thrombus) outlined by contrast medium in the sagittal sinus.
questions.learning: Battle sign Battle sign refers to retro auricular or mastoid ecchymosis that typically results from a fracture of the middle cranial fossa following head trauma.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 60-year-old male presents with a hypopigmented patch behind the ear with loss of sensation. Physical examination reveals paraesthesias with associated numbness in extremities and a raised jugular venous pressure. A thickened nerve is observed as shown in the image below. Identify the structure marked by the arrow in the given image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Greater auricular nerve

In the given clinical scenario, the patient presents with a hypopigmented patch behind the ear accompanied by loss of sensation, and neck examination reveals a thickened structure suggestive of leprosy, and the thickened structure is the greater auricular nerve.

Great auricular nerve:

It is the largest ascending branch of the cervical plexus and arises from the second and third cervical spinal nerves. It winds over the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle and ascends upwards. On reaching the parotid gland, it divides into the anterior and posterior branches:

* The anterior branch supplies the facial skin over the parotid gland and joins the facial nerve in the gland.

* The posterior branch supplies the skin over the mastoid process and the lower part of the back of the auricle, lobule, and concha.

Clinical considerations:

* The nerve can be thickened in conditions like leprosy and can be palpated over the upper part of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. (as seen in the above image). Leprosy is a chronic granulomatous condition caused by Mycobacterium leprae. It affects the skin, cutaneous and peripheral nerves, and mucous membranes. The most commonly affected peripheral nerve is the posterior tibial nerve, followed by the ulnar, median, and lateral popliteal nerves. The most frequently involved cranial nerve is the facial nerve. It commonly presents as an area of numbness on the skin or a visible skin lesion, which could be a hypopigmented or erythematous macule.

* Cross-inervation between the somatic sensory supply (great auricular nerve) and the parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland is considered an anatomical basis for the phenomenon of Frey's syndrome (gustatory sweating).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents to PHC OPD in Chittoor, Andhra Pradesh with bowing of legs. He also complained about bone pain, stiffness, and restricted movement in joints. Which of the following would be useful in the management of the patient?
options: Checking the protein intake of the population
Addition of Lime and Alum to water
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Addition of Lime and Alum to water

The clinical features described are suggestive of skeletal fluorosis, caused by chronic excess fluoride intake from drinking water, which is endemic in parts of Andhra Pradesh.

Management focuses on reducing fluoride exposure by providing safe drinking water, using surface water sources, or applying defluoridation methods sucSh as lime and alum.

Fluoridation of water would worsen fluoride toxicity and therefore has no role in management.

Do not confuse it with Lathyrism!!
questions.learning: Addition of Lime and Alum to water — The clinical features described are suggestive of skeletal fluorosis, caused by chronic excess fluoride intake from drinking water, which is endemic in parts of Andhra Pradesh.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old male patient presented with sudden-onset palpitations, with a history of bypass surgery performed 2 years ago. He presented with stable vitals. An ECG was performed, as shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Atrial fibrillation

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia and is characterized by chaotic atrial electrical activity, resulting in absence of discrete P waves and an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm. It commonly occurs after cardiac surgery, including coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG).

• The ECG demonstrates:

• Absent P waves
• Irregularly irregular RR intervals
• Fibrillatory (f) waves in the baseline

• These findings are diagnostic of atrial fibrillation.

Why not the other options?

• B. Atrial flutter: Shows regular saw-tooth flutter (F) waves, typically with 2:1 or variable AV block.
• C. Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT): Usually a regular narrow-complex tachycardia with absent or retrograde P waves.
• D. Multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT): Characterized by ≥3 different P-wave morphologies, visible P waves, and an irregular rhythm; commonly seen in COPD.
questions.learning: Atrial fibrillation Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia and is characterized by chaotic atrial electrical activity, resulting in absence of discrete P waves and an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following cancers rarely metastasizes to the liver?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Prostate

Prostate cancers rarely metastasize to the liver.

The most common malignant tumors of the liver are metastatic lesions.  The liver is a common site of metastases from gastrointestinal tumors because of dissemination through the portal venous system.  The most relevant metastatic tumor of the liver to the surgeon is colorectal cancer because of the well-documented potential for long-term survival after complete resection.

The more frequent primary sites include carcinomas of the colon, pancreas, lung, and breast in adults, and neuroblastoma, Wilms tumor, and rhabdomyosarcoma in pediatric patients. Although the origin of the tumor is often known when metastases are biopsied, carcinomas of the pancreas, stomach, and lung are particularly notorious for being occult primary neoplasms.
questions.learning: Prostate Prostate cancers rarely metastasize to the liver. The most common malignant tumors of the liver are metastatic lesions.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presented with a Type 1 Choledochal cyst. All of the following statements are correct except?
options: Cyst opened and drainage is done
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cyst opened and drainage is done

In the given clinical scenario, a patient presented with a Type 1 Choledochal cyst. Cyst opening and drainage will not be done in this patient. the preferred course of action involves the complete surgical excision of the cyst. Complete resection of the cyst is essential because there is a risk of malignant transformation (cholangiocarcinoma). (Option A)

Choledochal cysts are congenital cystic dilations of the intrahepatic and/or extrahepatic biliary tree. They present with a triad of jaundice, a palpable upper quadrant mass, and abdominal pain.

The clinical triad (abdominal pain, mass, and jaundice) and the MRCP (Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography) findings suggest choledochal cyst. According to the Todani classification, the type III choledochal cyst opens into the duodenum. The treatment of choice for type III choledochal cyst is Endoscopic sphincterotomy followed by surveillance.

Choledochal cysts are congenital dilations of the intra and/or extrahepatic biliary system.

Pathogenesis involves an Anomalous Pancreaticobiliary Junction (APBJ) which may allow reflux into the biliary tract, leading to inflammation, increased biliary pressure, and cyst formation. (Option D)

Clinical features of choledochal cysts are as follows

• 60% of cases are diagnosed before the age of 10 years
• more common in females than in males (4:1)
• The classic symptom triad includes abdominal pain, right upper quadrant mass, and jaundice (most consistent symptom)
• Other symptoms- nausea, weight loss, fever, pruritus, etc

Complications include

• Cholangitis (may lead to cirrhosis and portal hypertension)
• Pancreatitis
• Bile peritonitis (due to cyst rupture)
• Cholangiocarcinoma

Diagnostic investigations for choledochal cysts are as follows:

• Ultrasonography:

• Confirms the presence of an abnormal cyst
• Define the dimensions of the cyst
• Define its relationship to the vascular structures in the porta hepatis, as well as the intrahepatic ductal configuration

• Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI/MRCP) is the investigation of choice. It reveals the anatomy of the ducts
• CT - delineates the extent of the intra- or extrahepatic dilatation
• ERCP - defines the distal biliary tree

Todani classification (Option C) of the choledochal cysts along with their management is as shown below,

Type of choledochal cyst
Surgical management

Type I -  fusiform dilatation of the bile duct (most common - seen in 75% of patients)
complete surgical excision, cholecystectomy, and Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy

Type II - saccular diverticulum from the common bile duct
Diverticulectomy, cholecystectomy, and common bile duct repair

Type III- diverticulum within the pancreas, also known as choledochoceles
ERCP + sphincterotomy (Only cyst in which reconstruction is not required)

Type IV
a - multiple cysts (both intrahepatic and extrahepatic)
Liver transplant

b - multiple cysts limited to the extrahepatic biliary tree
Kasai procedure (Portoenterostomy)

Type V - multiple cysts involving only intrahepatic ducts (Caroli's disease)
Liver transplant

Biliary-enteric reconstruction is not required in Type III choledochal cyst as it has the lowest risk of malignancy, and it may not be associated with ABPJ (anomalous pancreaticobiliary junction). Therefore, endoscopic drainage is sufficient.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following groups is not included in the high-risk core population for HIV transmission?
options: Men who have sex with men
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Long-distance truck drivers

Long-distance truck drivers are not included in the high-risk core population for HIV transmission. They are part of the bridge population.

Target interventions for the control of AIDS transmission are done for high-risk core populations like:

• sex workers
• Men who have sex with men
• Transgender
• Injecting drug users

Bridge populations like migrants and long-distance truckers also receive targeted interventions for the control of AIDS transmission.

The services offered through targeted interventions include detection and treatment for sexually transmitted diseases and condom distribution.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The population of an area is 90,000. On January 1, there were 30 existing TB cases. During the year, 15 new cases occurred with no deaths or migration. Calculate the period prevalence per 1,000 population.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 0.5

• Period prevalence includes existing + new cases during the specified period.
• Total TB cases = 30 + 15 = 45.
• Population = 90,000.
• Formula:

• Existing cases contribute to prevalence.
• Newly diagnosed cases during the period are also included.
• Since there were no deaths or migration, all 45 cases remain.
• Prevalence measures disease burden, not risk.
• Incidence would include only the 15 new cases.
