questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 22-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with high-grade fever, diffuse erythematous rash, hypotension, and shock. She started menstruating 3 days ago and reports using superabsorbent tampons. Which of the following is the most likely reason responsible for her condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Superantigen like TSST-1

The presentation is classic for toxic shock syndrome associated with tampon use.

It is caused by TSST-1 produced by Staphylococcus aureus, which acts as a superantigen.

Superantigens cause non-specific activation of a large number of T cells with massive cytokine release.

This cytokine storm leads to fever, rash, hypotension, and shock.

TSST-1 (superantigen)

↓

Bridges MHC II and TCR (non-specific)

↓

Massive T-cell activation

↓

Cytokine storm:

• IL-1 → fever

• IL-2 → T-cell proliferation

• TNF-α → hypotension, shock

↓

Toxic Shock Syndrome

| Feature | Normal Antigen | Superantigen

| ------- | -------------- | ------------

| Processing | Required | Not required

| T-cell activation | Specific (\~0.01%) | Massive (20–30%)

| Binding | Specific peptide-MHC | Direct MHC–TCR binding

| Cytokines | Controlled | Explosive (storm)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-week pregnant woman presents with mild bleeding. Her blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, and fetal heart rate is 140 bpm. There were no contractions. TAS is shown below. What is the best next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hospitalisation and expectant management

Placenta previa occurs when the placenta partially or completely covers the internal cervical os.

Classic presentation

• Painless vaginal bleeding
• Occurs in 2nd or 3rd trimester
• Soft, non-tender uterus
• Normal fetal heart rate

At 30 weeks, the fetus is preterm. If both mother and fetus are stable, the goal is : Prolong pregnancy to improve fetal maturity.

Management includes Mc-Afee Johnson regimen:

• Hospital admission
• Bed rest
• Monitoring of bleeding
• Fetal monitoring
• Corticosteroids (betamethasone) for lung maturity
• Blood availability
• Avoid vaginal examination

Delivery is planned later unless bleeding becomes severe.

Stable placenta previa before 36–37 weeks → expectant management

A. Induction of Labour with Oxytocin

Induction is contraindicated in placenta previa because:

• Placenta blocks the cervical opening
• Vaginal delivery can cause massive hemorrhage

C. Immediate LSCS

Immediate cesarean section is indicated only when:

• Severe bleeding
• Maternal hemodynamic instability
• Fetal distress
• Gestation ≥37 weeks

In this question:

• Mother stable
• Fetal heart normal
• Bleeding mild

D. Amniotomy

Amniotomy may be used in placental abruption, not placenta previa.

In placenta previa it can:

• Tear placental attachment
• Cause catastrophic bleeding

| Condition | Management

| --------- | ----------

| <36 weeks, mild bleeding | Expectant management

| ≥37 weeks | Elective LSCS

| Severe bleeding anytime | Emergency LSCS

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following mechanisms explains how atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) produces its physiological effects?
questions.explanation: Atrial Natriuretic Peptide (ANP) is a hormone released by the cardiac atria in response to stretch, serving to lower blood pressure and volume. Its mechanism of action begins when it binds to its specific receptor (NPR-A), which possesses intrinsic guanylyl cyclase activity. This leads to the direct conversion of GTP into cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) . cGMP then acts as the secondary messenger to activate protein kinase G, resulting in vasodilation and increased renal sodium excretion . cAMP (Option A) is the secondary messenger for hormones like glucagon and epinephrine. IP3-DAG (Option C) is utilized by hormones such as oxytocin and vasopressin acting on V1 receptors. The JAK/STAT pathway (Option D) is typical for growth hormone and cytokines. Therefore, because ANP receptors act through the guanylyl cyclase system, cGMP is the definitive secondary messenger that elucidates its physiological effects

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: 'a' wave in JVP corresponds to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Right atrial contraction

The "a" wave in jugular venous pressure (JVP) is a positive wave, which corresponds to right atrial contraction.

The waveforms seen in a normal JVP are:

• a wave corresponds to atrial contraction and occurs just after the P wave (on ECG) and just before the first heart sound.
• c wave represents the bulging of the tricuspid valve into the right atrium during ventricular systole.
• x descent corresponds to the atrial relaxation during atrial diastole.
• v wave represents atrial filling during ventricular systole and peaks at the second heart sound.
• y descent represents passive emptying of the right atrium into the right ventricle after tricuspid valve opening.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presented with dysuria and pain in the back. His lumbar spine X-ray shows the below finding. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hyperparathyroidism

The given clinical scenario and X-ray showing diffuse calcification of both kidneys are suggestive of nephrocalcinosis which is seen in hyperparathyroidism.

Nephrocalcinosis is the deposition of calcium in the kidney parenchyma or tubules which is seen in conditions causing hypercalcemia like hyperparathyroidism.

Clinical features of hyperparathyroidism:

• Bones:

• Pathological fractures
• Subperiosteal bone resorption - 2nd and 3rd digits, most common in the radial aspect
• Salt and pepper skull
• Osteitis fibrosa cystica or VonReckling Hausen’s disease of bone

• Stones

• Multiple and recurrent renal stones - most common
• Nephrocalcinosis

• Abdominal groans - colicky due to pancreatitis
• Psychiatric overtones - raised PTH causing CNS depression and psychiatric symptoms
• Band keratopathy
• Features of hypercalcemia -

• Vomiting
• Confusion
• ECG changes: increased PR interval, shortened QT interval

Investigations done in primary hyperparathyroidism:

• Ultrasonography of the neck is a safe and widely used technique for the localization of abnormal parathyroid glands.
• Nuclear medicine scanning with radiolabeled Sestamibi is also a widely used technique. Sestamibi accumulates in parathyroid adenomas. This radionuclide is concentrated in the thyroid and parathyroid tissue but usually washes out of normal thyroid tissue in under an hour. It persists in abnormal parathyroid tissue.
• Dual-energy radiographic absorptiometry is a useful tool to demonstrate skeletal involvement in primary hyperparathyroidism.
questions.learning: Hyperparathyroidism — The given clinical scenario and X-ray showing diffuse calcification of both kidneys are suggestive of nephrocalcinosis which is seen in hyperparathyroidism.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient who presents to the OPD has a visual field defect as shown below. What is the probable site of the lesion based on the image displayed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 3

The visual field defect in the image is indicative of bitemporal hemianopia, so the probable site of the lesion is the optic chiasma marked as 3 in the image given.

Options marked in the image are:

1. Left optic nerve
3. Otic chiasma
4. Left optic tract
5. Left lateral geniculate nucleus

Hemianopia or hemianopsia refers to loss of sight in half the visual field. Bitemporal hemianopia refers to loss of sight in the temporal halves of the visual field, seen in lesions affecting the optic chiasma. The most common cause of this is pituitary gland tumours. Other causes include suprasellar aneurysms, chronic arachnoiditis, and suprasellar tumours like craniopharyngioma and suprasellar meningioma.

Damage to the middle part of the optic chiasm affects fibres crossing at the nasal retina of each eye, leaving the uncrossed fibres from the temporal retinas intact. The resulting loss of vision is confined to the temporal visual field of each eye and this is known as bitemporal hemianopia. It is also called heteronymous hemianopia to emphasize the fact that the parts of the visual field that are lost in each eye do not overlap.

Individuals with this condition are able to see in both left and right central visual fields, with both eyes open. However, all information from the most peripheral parts of visual fields (which are seen only by the nasal retinas) is lost.

Pearl PF1675: Lesions in the optic pathway

Transection of the pathways at the locations indicated by the letters causes the visual field defects shown in the diagram above.

* The fibers from the nasal half of each retina decussate in the optic chiasm, so that the fibers in the optic tracts are those from the temporal half of one retina and the nasal half of the other.

* A lesion that interrupts the optic nerve causes blindness in that eye.

* Lesions affecting the optic chiasma destroy fibers from both nasal hemiretinas and produce a heteronymous (opposite sides of the visual fields) hemianopia.

* A lesion in one optic tract causes blindness in half of the visual field and is called homonymous (same side of both visual fields) hemianopia (half-blindness).

* Occipital lesions may spare the fibers from the macula because of the separation in the brain of these fibers from the other subserving vision.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A mother brings her child to the pediatric outpatient department complaining of recurrent infections. On examination, her child has a length-for-age less than–2 standard deviations below the median. There is a history of improper feeding in the past. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Stunting

A length-for-age less than –2 standard deviations (SD) below the median is called stunting according to WHO.

Classification of nutritional status depending on the anthropometry (height/length for age):

Classification
Criteria

Moderate stunting (or) moderate chronic malnutrition
Height/length-for-age < –2 SD and > –3 SD

Severe stunting (or) severe chronic malnutrition
Height/length-for-age < –3 SD

The nutritional status of a child is assessed in terms of anthropometry:

The World Health Organization (WHO) has established international standards for normal child growth from birth to 5 years of age. The normalization of the anthropometric measures is done in terms of z-scores (standard deviation scores). The anthropometric indicators are marked in a growth chart which is compared with a reference curve.

The anthropometric measures used are weight for age, height for age, weight for height, BMI, and mid-upper arm circumference.

* Low weight for height, or wasting, indicates acute malnutrition. It is also mentioned as wasting.

* High weight-for-height indicates overweight.

* Low height-for-age, or stunting, indicates chronic malnutrition. This is the best indicator of long-term nutritional status in the pediatric population.

* Low weight-for-age indicates acute or chronic malnutrition. It does not differentiate between wasting and stunting. Hence, it has limited clinical significance.

Other options:

Option A: To diagnose a child as underweight, weight for age charts are used. If the weight for the age of a child is less than -2 SD, then the child is said to be moderately underweight. If it is less than -3SD, it is called severe underweight.

Option B: A diagnosis of wasting can be made with mid-upper arm circumference measurements and weight for height. A weight for height below -2 SD is called moderate wasting. A mid-upper arm circumference of less than 115mm or weight for height below -3SD is called severe wasting.

Option C: Malnutrition refers to any deficiencies in the dietary intake of a person. Although it means both undernutrition and overnutrition, in practice it is used interchangeably with undernutrition.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding skeletal is/are incorrect? 1. Skeletal muscle contraction is initiated by calcium binding to troponin T. 2. Skeletal muscle fibers contain a single nucleus. 3. Skeletal muscle contractions are voluntary. 4. Gap junctions are present in skeletal muscle.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4 only

Let's evaluate each statement:

1. Skeletal muscle contraction is initiated by calcium binding to troponin T. ❌ Incorrect

• Calcium binds to troponin C (TnC), not troponin T (TnT).
• Troponin T attaches the troponin complex to tropomyosin, while troponin I inhibits actin-myosin interaction.
• Calcium binding to TnC shifts tropomyosin away from the myosin-binding sites on actin, initiating contraction.

2. Skeletal muscle fibers contain a single nucleus. ❌ Incorrect

• Skeletal muscle fibers are multinucleated due to fusion of myoblasts during development.
• The nuclei are located peripherally beneath the sarcolemma.

3. Skeletal muscle contractions are voluntary. ✅ Correct

• Skeletal muscle is supplied by the somatic nervous system, making its contractions voluntary.

4. Gap junctions are present in skeletal muscle. ❌ Incorrect

• Skeletal muscle fibers function independently and lack gap junctions.
• Gap junctions are characteristic of cardiac muscle (intercalated discs) and single-unit smooth muscle.

Therefore, the incorrect statements are 1, 2, and 4.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient is evaluated for meningitis. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis reveals lymphocytic predominance, low glucose levels, and elevated protein concentration. What is the most likely etiological agent?
questions.explanation: Analyzing CSF parameters is vital for identifying the type of meningitis. Tuberculous meningitis (TBM) characteristically presents with a lymphocytic pleocytosis (lymphocytosis), significantly decreased glucose, and marked elevation of protein. This profile reflects a chronic granulomatous inflammatory process. Acute bacterial pathogens like S. pneumoniae (Option A), H. influenzae (Option B), and N. meningitidis (Option C) would typically show a neutrophilic predominance (not lymphocytosis) alongside low glucose and high protein. Viral meningitis would show lymphocytosis but with normal glucose levels. TBM is a medical emergency with an insidious onset; it often results in thick basal exudates and cranial nerve palsies. Definitive diagnosis involves AFB staining, GeneXpert, or liquid culture (MGIT). Treatment requires a prolonged course of anti-tubercular therapy combined with corticosteroids to reduce inflammation and prevent neurological sequelae

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the probable diagnosis based on the image of the scan given below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Craniopharyngioma

The given MRI of the brain demonstrates a craniopharyngioma, which is a suprasellar tumour that arises from remnants of Rathke's pouch.

The two variants of craniopharyngioma are:

• Adamantinomatous type (common in children):  Predominantly solid with cystic components. Diagnostic features include compact lamellar keratin ("wet keratin") and areas of dystrophic calcification.
• Papillary type (common in adults): Contains both solid sheets and papillae lined by well-differentiated non-keratinized squamous epithelium.

These tumours are usually large and heterogeneous, displaying solid and cystic components. The cysts contain a cholesterol-rich, thick brownish-yellow fluid that is compared to 'machine oil'.

Clinical features include headaches (most common), visual abnormalities - decreased acuity and bitemporal hemianopia, GH deficiency, growth failure, delayed sexual maturation due to pituitary hypofunction, and polyuria (central diabetes insipidus).

Radiologically:

• CT may show calcifications associated with the solid and cystic wall components
• MRI is the imaging modality of choice which shows:

Cysts

T1
Iso to hyperintense to the brain (due to high protein content "machinery oil cysts")

T2
Mostly hyperintense

Solid component

T1
Vivid enhancement

T2
Variable or mixed

Craniopharyngiomas tend not to expand the pituitary fossa unless they become huge, which is a differentiating feature from pituitary macroadenomas.

Other options:

Option A: Pituitary apoplexy is an acute clinical condition associated with the rapid expansion of the pituitary gland, which is evident on an MRI as enhancement around a non-enhancing infarcted centre.
Option B: Pituitary macroadenoma (with cystic degeneration or necrosis) shows indentation at the diaphragma sellae, giving rise to a snowman/figure of eight appearance/cottage loaf. Calcification is often absent. The image below shows the snowman appearance:

Option C: Rathke cleft cyst shows no solid or enhancing component. Calcification is rare. It is unilocular and the majority are completely or mostly intrasellar.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the marked structure in the given histopathology slide.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Brunner's gland

The slide shows section of the duodenum and marked structures glands located on the duodenum called Brunner's glands

Brunner's glands (or duodenal glands) are compound tubular submucosal glands present in the upper duodenum (above the sphincter of Oddi).

The alveoli of duodenal glands are lined mostly by mucous secreting columnar cells. Their ducts pass through the muscularis mucosae and empty into the intestinal crypts (of Lieberkuhn).

The duodenum can be easily differentiated from the jejunum or ileum by the presence of these submucosal glands. The jejunum and ileum do not have glands in their submucosa.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: You are conducting an experiment on mitochondrial respiration. You add malate/pyruvate and respiration is normal. You add succinate and respiration is normal. When you add another substance in the presence of pyruvate/succinate and malate, respiration is blocked. Which of the following substances is most likely added?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Oligomycin

In the experiment conducted on mitochondrial respiration, respiration will be blocked by the addition of oligomycin, an antibiotic, when added in the presence of pyruvate/ succinate and malate. Oligomycin inhibits oxidative phosphorylation in the mitochondria and hence blocks respiration.

Electron transport chain (ETC)/respiratory chain is the final pathway by which all the electrons derived from the oxidation of carbohydrates, fatty acids, and amino acids are directed towards the final reaction with oxygen, to form water and adenosine triphosphate (ATP).

The chemiosmotic theory states that the flow of electrons through the respiratory chain generates a proton motive force. This force drives the formation of ATP by the process of oxidative phosphorylation.

Complexes of ETC
Inhibitors

Complex I: NADH-CoQ oxidoreductase
Piericidin, amobarbital, rotenone

Complex II: Succinate-CoQ reductase
TTFA (thenoyltrifluoroacetone), carboxin, malonate

Complex III: CoQH2-cytochrome c oxidoreductase
BAL(British anti-lewisite), antimycin A

Complex IV: cytochrome oxidase
Hydrogen sulfide, carbon monoxide, cyanide

Complex V (informally): ATP Synthase
Atractyloside, oligomycin

In the given experiment, malate and pyruvate are electron donors (NADH) at complex I of the ETC, and succinate is the electron donor (FADH2) at complex II. Normal respiration is observed on the addition of substances at both complexes I and II i.e., both oxygen consumption and ATP synthesis from ADP (adenosine diphosphate) take place.

Oligomycin is a competitive inhibitor of the Fo (oligomycin-sensitive) complex of ATP synthase (complex V) and blocks oxidation and phosphorylation by stopping the flow of protons through the ATP synthase enzyme complex. Hence the addition of oligomycin will inhibit complex V and stop respiration.

Other options:

Options A and B: Rotenone (option A) if added, will inhibit complex I. Electron transfer before complex I will be blocked but not after. Hence, normal respiration will occur. Similarly, antimycin A (option B) inhibits complex III, and electron transfer prior to complex III will be blocked and not after. Hence, respiration will not be completely hindered.

Option C: 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP) is an uncoupler that dissociates oxidation in the respiratory chain from phosphorylation. Hence, respiration continues without ATP synthesis.
questions.learning: Oligomycin — In the experiment conducted on mitochondrial respiration, respiration will be blocked by the addition of oligomycin, an antibiotic, when added in the presence of pyruvate/ succinate and malate.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A child was brought to the hospital by his mother after being struck by a ball. In addition to double vision, he feels pain when opening his jaw. On examination, there was flattening of the malar eminence and periorbital emphysema. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Zygomatic fracture

In the given scenario, the child presenting with diplopia, flattening of the malar eminence and periorbital emphysema points to the diagnosis of zygomatic fracture.

Zygomatic fractures often result in facial asymmetry and visual disturbances due to involvement of the orbit.

After nasal bones, the zygoma is the second most frequently fractured bone. Usually, the cause is direct trauma. The lower segment of the zygoma is pushed medially and posteriorly, resulting in flattening of the malar prominence and a step deformity at the infraorbital margin.

Zygomatic bone following injury presents with:

* Flattening of the malar eminence

* Anaesthesia of the cheek in the distribution of the infraorbital nerve

* Periorbital emphysema

* Step deformity of infraorbital margins

* Restricted ocular movements

* Trismus

* Diplopia

It is diagnosed on the Waters’ or exaggerated Waters’ view, which shows the fracture and displacement the best.

Other options:

Option B: Maxillary bone fractures present with malocclusion of the teeth, elongation of the midface, mobility of the maxilla and CSF rhinorrhoea.

Option C: Nasal bone fractures usually result from direct trauma such as fights, falls, sports injuries, or road accidents. Clinical examination may show deformity, swelling, bruising, and nasal obstruction. Imaging may aid in the diagnosis, but the diagnosis is mainly made on the basis of physical examination.

Option D: Naso-orbito-ethmoid fractures are associated with CSF rhinorrhea, pug nose, telecanthus and displacement of eyeball.

Pearl PF1981: Le-Fort's classification of Maxillary Fracture

Le-Fort I is a transverse fracture of the maxilla

* Fracture line passes through the lower part of nasal septum, maxillary antra and the pterygoid plates

* It separates palate from the rest of the face leading to floating teeth or palate

* Also called Guerin’s fracture.

Le-Fort II is a pyramidal fracture

* Fracture line passes through the root of the nose, lacrimal bone, floor of the orbit, upper part of the maxillary sinus and pterygoid plates

* X-ray or CT appears like hanging maxilla

* It is associated with CSF rhinorrhea.

Le-Fort III is craniofacial dysjunction i.e., facial skeleton completely disconnected from its cranial attachment

* Fracture line passes through the root of the nose, ethmo-frontal junction, superior orbital fissure, lateral wall of the orbit, fronto-zygomatic and temporo-zygomatic sutures and the upper part of pterygoid plates

* It is also associated with CSF rhinorrhea.
questions.learning: Zygomatic fracture — In the given scenario, the child presenting with diplopia, flattening of the malar eminence and periorbital emphysema points to the diagnosis of zygomatic fracture.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the type of gland marked in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Holocrine

The correct answer is Holocrine.

Sebaceous glands are holocrine glands where entire cells disintegrate to release sebum into the hair follicle.

Merocrine secretion (e.g., salivary glands, pancreas) releases products by exocytosis without cell loss, while eccrine glands are sweat glands using merocrine mechanism, not a separate mode.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the most effective method for educating an urban slum community about the use of oral rehydration solution (ORS)?
questions.explanation: Health education in community settings, particularly in low-literacy areas like urban slums, requires methods that are practical and easy to follow. A Demonstration (Option D) is the most effective approach for teaching the preparation and use of ORS. This "learning by seeing" method allows community members to observe the exact measurements and mixing process, which ensures accuracy and builds confidence in their ability to perform the task at home. A Lecture (Option A) is often too passive and less effective for procedural skills. Roleplay (Option B) is good for teaching social behaviors but not technical prep. Flashcards (Option C) are useful visual aids but do not provide the step-by-step practical instruction of a live demonstration. Therefore, because ORS prep is a specific, life-saving skill that must be done correctly to be effective, demonstration is the definitive educational standard
questions.learning: Health education in community settings, particularly in low-literacy areas like urban slums, requires methods that are practical and easy to follow. A Demonstration (Option D) is the most effective approach for teaching the preparation and use of ORS.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Liver synthesizes all of the following except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Immunoglobulins

Immunoglobulins are not synthesized by the liver. They are produced by plasma cells.

Plasma proteins synthesized by the liver are:

• Albumin
• Coagulation/clotting factors
• Acute-phase proteins
• Steroid binding and other hormone-binding proteins

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a well-designed cancer study, similar remission rates were obtained for a new treatment (33.2%) and the usual treatment (32.2%), with the p-value being 0.04. Which of the following statements is true regarding the study?
options: Both the treatments are equally effective
Neither of the treatments is effective
The new treatment is more effective than the usual treatment
The information given is not adequate to compare the efficacy of the treatments
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. The new treatment is more effective than the usual treatment

As the p-value is 0.04, we can conclude that the new treatment is more effective than the usual treatment.

Even though both treatments have similar rates of remission, a valid statistical test is required to determine the difference in their effectiveness. Statistically, p-value < 0.05 implies that the alternate hypothesis is true.

In this scenario, we can consider:

• Null hypothesis: Both the treatments are equally effective (in other terms, there is no difference between the effect of the two treatments).
• Alternative hypothesis: New treatment is more effective than the usual treatment.

As the p-value is 0.04, which is statistically significant (<0.05), the null hypothesis is rejected and the alternative hypothesis is accepted. Hence the new treatment is more effective than the usual treatment.
questions.learning: The new treatment is more effective than the usual treatment As the p-value is 0.04, we can conclude that the new treatment is more effective than the usual treatment.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which among the following is an ideal treatment for a 55 year old with simple hyperplasia of endometrium with atypia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Simple hysterectomy

Simple hysterectomy is the best treatment in the above case.

Best treatment of atypical hyperplasia in a post-menopausal woman is hysterectomy.

Management of Endometrial hyperplasia:

1) Non-atypical hyperplasia:

* Pre-menopausal women: Progesterone therapy

* Post menopausal women:

* Simple hyperplasia without atypia: Follow up without therapy

* Complex hyperplasia without atypia: Progesterone therapy

2) Atypical hyperplasia:

* Pre-menopausal women: High-dose progesterone therapy

* Post-menopausal women: Hysterectomy

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 27-year-old IT professional has presented to you with intense watering, redness, and foreign body sensation in the eye for the past 2 months. He took out his contact lens and applied eye lubricants to help alleviate his ailment, but it didn't provide any relief. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Giant papillary conjunctivitis

The clinical history of watering, redness, and foreign body sensation in a contact lens user, along with the image showing giant papillae in the conjunctiva, suggests a probable diagnosis of giant papillary conjunctivitis.

Giant papillary conjunctivitis is a severe form of mechanically induced papillary conjunctivitis. It is most commonly associated with contact lens wear. It can also be associated with ocular prostheses, exposed sutures, and scleral buckles.

Patients usually present with redness, foreign body sensation, increased mucus production, itching, blurring, and loss of contact lens tolerance. On examination, giant papillae are seen on the upper tarsal conjunctiva with hyperemia. Focal apical ulceration and whitish scarring may develop on larger papillae.

Papillae are reddish, flat-topped, raised areas that give a red and velvety appearance to the tarsal conjunctiva. These are caused by the hyperplasia of the normal vascular system, with glomerulus-like bunches of capillaries growing into the epithelium.

The image below shows papillae in the tarsal conjunctiva.

Treatment includes the removal of the offending cause. Mast cell stabilizers, such as sodium cromoglycate, and drugs like azelastine and olopatadine, which have combined antihistamine and mast cell–stabilizing effects, are effective. Steroids can be used for resistant cases.

Other options:

Option A: In acute trachoma, sago-like follicles are characteristically seen. It is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis. The SAFE strategy is used in the management of trachoma.

The image below shows sago-like follicles in trachoma.

Option B: In follicular conjunctivitis, follicles are seen. It is most commonly caused by herpes and adenoviruses. Follicles are greyish-white raised areas on fornices and palpebral conjunctiva. These are formed due to the localized aggregations of lymphocytes in the sub-epithelial adenoid layer.

The image shows follicles.

Option D: In spring catarrh (vernal catarrh), cobblestone appearance is a papillary reaction in the palpebral conjunctiva, ropy discharge, and Maxwell-Lyon sign are present. Horner-Trantas spots that are discrete, whitish, raised dots along the limbus can also be seen. It is more common during summer.

The image below shows Horner-Trantas spots.
questions.learning: Giant papillary conjunctivitis — The clinical history of watering, redness, and foreign body sensation in a contact lens user, along with the image showing giant papillae in the conjunctiva, suggests a probable diagnosis of giant papillary conjunctivitis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text:
A 30-year-old male is found to be positive for HBsAg and HBeAg and is diagnosed with chronic hepatitis B. The viral load of the patient was 2 x 100000 and SGPT is found to be doubled. What is the appropriate management in this patient?

SGPT- Serum glutamate pyruvate transaminase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tenofovir for > 40 weeks

The appropriate treatment for this patient based on the given clinical scenario is to administer tenofovir for more than 40 weeks.

The serological markers present in the case of chronic hepatitis B are

1. HBsAg (Remains detectable beyond six months)
2. Anti-HBc (Primarily of IgG class)
3. HBeAg (Qualitative marker of replicative phase)
4. HBV DNA (Quantitative marker of replicative phase)

Treatment of chronic hepatitis B is focused on suppressing the level of virus replication.

Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) is an acyclic nucleotide analog that is used as first-line therapy for the treatment of chronic hepatitis B and lamivudine-resistant chronic hepatitis B. It is a potent antiretroviral agent used in the treatment of HIV infection. It is more potent in suppressing HBV DNA and is active against both wild-type and lamivudine-resistant HBV. It is given as an oral once-daily dose of 300 mg for 48 weeks. Tenofovir therapy provided histologic improvement, reduction in fibrosis score, and regression of cirrhosis in patients. Side effects are acute renal failure and low blood phosphate levels.

Other options:

Option A: Lamivudine is a nucleoside analog that inhibits reverse transcriptase activity of both HIV and HBV  and is an effective agent for chronic hepatitis B. It is given at a daily dose of 100 mg for 48-52 weeks. It is no longer preferred.

Option C: Pegylated interferon is recommended as one of the first-line agents for hepatitis B. It is given as a subcutaneous injection at a dose of 180 μg/week for 48-52 weeks. It is not preferred over oral agents because of its poor tolerability.

Option D: The combination of lamivudine and pegylated interferon is found to suppress HBV DNA more profoundly during therapy than monotherapy. However, usage of these drugs for a year provides results similar to drugs given as monotherapy. Hence, this options is not preferred.
questions.learning: Tenofovir for > 40 weeks — The appropriate treatment for this patient based on the given clinical scenario is to administer tenofovir for more than 40 weeks.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the co-test in cervical cancer screening?
questions.explanation: Co-testing for cervical cancer screening involves the simultaneous performance of HPV DNA testing and a Pap smear (cytology). This dual approach is highly effective because HPV testing identifies the presence of the causative virus (high-risk strains 16 and 18), while the Pap smear detects pre-malignant cellular changes. VIA (Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid) (Options B and C) is a low-cost screening method used primarily in resource-limited settings. Colposcopy (Option D) is a diagnostic follow-up tool used to investigate abnormal screening results rather than a primary screening "co-test". In standard guidelines, co-testing with HPV and Pap smear is the gold standard for women aged 30–65

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with breast skin dimpling as shown in the image. This occurs due to the infiltration of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cooper's ligament

Skin dimpling of the breast occurs due to traction on Cooper’s ligaments by a carcinoma. The fibrous bands shorten as they are infiltrated and pulled by tumor or associated fibrosis, producing the characteristic puckering or dimpling on the breast surface.

The condition is most often seen in carcinoma of the breast, where the tumor induces fibrosis and collagen deposition (desmoplastic reaction). As the tumor increases in size and invades adjacent breast parenchyma, it contracts the fibrous tissue (Cooper’s ligaments), leading to tethering of the overlying skin. This leads to the signs of dimpling or puckering during clinical examination.

Other options:

Option B: Lactiferous duct: Infiltration of these ducts results in nipple retraction.

Option C: Dermal lymphatics: Their involvement causes peau d’orange (orange peel appearance) due to edema.

Option D: Suspensory fascia: It is part of the superficial fascia.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Given below is an instrument which is used to measure air humidity. Identify the instrument.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sling psychrometer

The instrument seen in the image is a Sling Psychrometer, It is used to measure the humidity/ moisture content in the air.

Sling Psychrometer has 2 mercury thermometers (wet and dry) in it. The wet bulb is moistened first with distilled water and the instrument is whirled/rotated standing with the back to the sun. The reading is noted twice.

Later the dry bulb is taken up for the reading and the relative air humidity is obtained by use of suitable tables and charts.

Pearl PF1005: Measurement of Air Temperature

* A number of thermometers which employ mercury or alcohol are used for measuring air temperature.

* These thermometers are mounted on a special screen called Stevenson screen as air should have free access to their bulbs and they must be protected from radiant heat.

* The instruments used to measure air temperature are:

* Dry bulb thermometers:

* These are ordinary mercury thermometers mounted on a Stevenson screen at about 1.20 to 1.80 metres above sea level

* Wet bulb thermometers

* These are just like the dry bulb variants but the bulb is kept wet by a muslin cloth that is fed with water from a bottle through a wick.

* Maximum thermometer

* This is a mercury thermometer which has a very fine constriction near the neck of the bulb

* Minimum thermometer

* The liquid in this thermometer is spirit which has a dumb-bell shaped index immersed in it

* Six’s maximum-minimum thermometer

* This thermometer has both mercury and alcohol

* It measures the maximum and minimum air temperatures reached over a period of time

* A mercury-free variant of this thermometer is available

* Globe thermometer:

* It is used for the direct measurement of mean radiant temperature of the surroundings.

* It has a hollow metal bulb (6 inches diameter) which has a matte black paint which absorbs radiant heat. A specially calibrated mercury bulb thermometer is kept inside.

* The difference between the readings of the globe thermometer and the bulb thermometer is the measure of the radiant heat.

* Kata thermometers:

* It is an alcohol thermometer and consists of a wet kata and a dry kata.

* A wet kata reading of 20 and above and a dry kata reading of 6 and above were taken as indices of thermal comfort.

* It was originally used to measure the cooling power of air (air temperature, humidity and air movement) but currently it is used only as an anemometer to measure low air velocities.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient presents to you with complaints of mass descending per vaginum for the past 6 months. On examination, you notice a grade 3 uterovaginal prolapse and a decubitus ulcer over the prolapse. Which of the following is a cause for this decubitus ulcer and treatment?
options: Venous congestion and reduction of the prolapsed part into the vagina and daily packing with glycerine and acriflavine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Venous congestion and reduction of the prolapsed part into the vagina and daily packing with glycerine and acriflavine

The given case scenario is suggestive of pelvic organ prolapse with a decubitus ulcer. It is due to venous congestion and local circulatory changes.

Friction, congestion and circulatory changes in the dependent part of prolapse cause keratinization and pigmentation of the vaginal mucosa, as well as ulceration of the prolapsed tissue with a clean edge.

Treatment includes the reduction of the prolapsed part into the vagina and daily packing with glycerine and acriflavine. Acriflavine is an antiseptic agent while glycerine is a hygroscopic agent. This helps in the healing of the ulcer within a week or two.

Complications of prolapse:

* Kinking of the ureter with resulting renal damage can occur in procidentia and enterocele.

* Chronic Urinary tract infection due to retention of urine in a cystocele, and can lead to upper renal tract infection and renal damage.

* Decubitus ulcer due to venous congestion and local circulatory changes.

* Stress incontinence occurs when the internal urinary meatus and neck of the bladder descend below the level of pelvic floor muscles.

* Cancer of the vagina can rarely occur over the decubitus ulcer and if the ring pessary is left in over a long period.
questions.learning: Venous congestion and reduction of the prolapsed part into the vagina and daily packing with glycerine and acriflavine The given case scenario is suggestive of pelvic organ prolapse with a decubitus ulcer.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A six-year-old child presented with the given deformity. Identify the deformity.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cubitus valgus

The image shows the cubitus valgus deformity of left elbow most probably arising as a complication of lateral condyle fracture humerus which the patient had 3 years back.

Treatment of cubitus valgus is Medial closed wedge osteotomy or lateral open wedge osteotomy.

Option A: Cubitus varus deformity is also called gunstock deformity. It happens due to the malunion of supracondylar fracture in childhood. Injury to the brachial artery is an important complication.

Option C: Coxa vara is a hip deformity characterized by a reduced angle (less than 120 degrees) between the femoral neck and the femoral shaft.

OptionD : Coxa valga is a hip condition where the angle between the femoral neck and the femoral shaft exceeds 135 degrees.

A combination of coxa vara in one leg and coxa valga in the other (Wind-swept deformity) is seen in rickets
questions.learning: Cubitus valgus — The image shows the cubitus valgus deformity of left elbow most probably arising as a complication of lateral condyle fracture humerus which the patient had 3 years back.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient from a North-Eastern state is diagnosed with Plasmodium falciparum malaria. Considering regional drug-resistance patterns and the malaria species, which treatment option is most appropriate for effectively managing this infection?
questions.explanation: The treatment of Plasmodium falciparum malaria in India is guided by regional drug resistance patterns. In the North-Eastern states, there is widespread resistance to both Chloroquine (Option C) and the combination of Sulfadoxine-Pyrimethamine (Option B). Therefore, national guidelines mandate the use of Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy (ACT). The specific ACT recommended in these resistance-prone regions is Artemether plus Lumefantrine (Option A). This combination is highly effective at rapidly reducing the parasite load and preventing the development of severe malaria. Mefloquine (Option D) is generally used for prophylaxis or as part of other combinations rather than as primary monotherapy for North-Eastern P. falciparum. Because the patient is in a high-resistance zone, the use of the modern Artemether-Lumefantrine combination is the definitive clinical standard for ensuring cure and preventing mortality
questions.learning: The treatment of Plasmodium falciparum malaria in India is guided by regional drug resistance patterns. In the North-Eastern states, there is widespread resistance to both Chloroquine (Option C) and the combination of Sulfadoxine-Pyrimethamine (Option B).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The following cost-effective investigations are routinely recommended in the screening of antenatal mothers except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Echocardiography for cardiac disease

Except for echocardiography for cardiac disease, all other tests (urine analysis for bacteriuria, blood sugar levels for GDM, VDRL for syphilis) are cost-effective investigations routinely recommended in the screening of antenatal mothers.

Echocardiography is an expensive investigation and is not routinely recommended to look for cardiac abnormalities in all pregnant ladies. Indications for fetal echocardiography include:

• Abnormality in routine genetic screening such as USG to look for nuchal translucency (NT). NT is the space between the fetal skin and the underlying soft tissue near the neck of the fetus filled with fluid. NT of >3mm is abnormal and warrants the need for detailed USG and fetal echocardiography
• Gestational diabetes mellitus for early detection of fetal anomalies. Done at 20-22 weeks.
• Heart disease in pregnancy like congenital heart disease or Marfan's syndrome needs routine echocardiography (color doppler) at mid-pregnancy to look for structural abnormalities, valve anatomy, etc.

Routine investigations during pregnancy:

• 1st trimester:

• Hemoglobin, hematocrit, blood grouping, blood glucose, and VDRL.
• Midstream urine to look for protein, sugar, pus cells, and evidence of urinary tract infections or bacteriuria by dipstick test (for nitrites).
• Serology for rubella, hepatitis B virus, and HIV.
• Genetic screening like maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein.
• Ultrasound scan to look for gross fetal abnormalities, number of fetuses, and dating of pregnancy.

• 2nd trimester:

• Ultrasound scan (booking scan at 18-20 weeks) is done to look for cardiac activity, structural abnormalities, amniotic fluid index and placental location.
• Triple test at 11-13 weeks for a high risk mother.
• Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) at 24-26 weeks with a 1-hour 50-gram glucose load or a diagnostic 2-hour 75-gram glucose load. This is to look for gestational diabetes mellitus.

• 3rd trimester:

• Repeat hemoglobin, hematocrit, and serology for syphilis and HIV.
• Vaginal examination to look for Streptococcus agalactiae.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is the most important determinant of malignant potential in the papillary type of renal tumor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Size

The most important determinant of malignant potential in the papillary type of renal tumor is the size of the tumor.

The papillary type of renal tumors includes:

• Renal papillary adenoma (≤ 1.5 cm)
• Papillary type of renal cell carcinoma (RCC) - > 1.5 cm

Small renal papillary growths are fairly common and incidentally found. Ruling out of malignancy is one of the processes carried out during the evaluation of donor transplant kidneys.

Papillary renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is the second most common type of renal cell carcinoma and it arises from proximal tubules. It can be multifocal or bilateral. It is typically hemorrhagic and cystic, especially when large.

It is often a circumscribed tumor composed of papillae formed by delicate fibrovascular cores that often contain foamy macrophages and Psammoma bodies.

It has two histological types:

• Type 1 papillary RCC - single layer of cells on the basement membrane and low-grade nuclear features
• Type 2 papillary RCC - pseudostratification of cells and usually has high-grade nuclear features

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: All are true about renal tubular acidosis in children except
options: Type 4 is due to defective ammoniagenesis and aldosterone resistance
Type 2 is Fanconi and hypophosphatemic rickets
Type 4 with paradoxical aciduria and hypokalemia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Type 4 with paradoxical aciduria and hypokalemia

Hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis are features of type 4 renal tubular acidosis

Type IV (hyperkalemic) renal tubular acidosis: Hyperkalemia with distal RTA occurring due to aldosterone resistance or deficiency is termed type 4 RT A. Aldosterone directly stimulates the proton pump, increases Na+ absorption resulting in negative intrahibular potential and increases urinary K+ losses and stimulates basolateral Na+ /K+ ATPase. Hence, aldosterone deficiency or resistance is expected to cause hyperkalemia and acidosis.

The clinical features seen in Type IV RTA are as follows:

• Hyperkalemia: Hypoaldosteronism results in an increase in potassium concentration.
• Metabolic acidosis: The important buffers in urine are ammonia and phosphate. Hyperkalemia impairs ammonia production in the proximal tubule, which reduces the buffering of hydrogen ions. This results in decreased hydrogen ion excretion.
• Urinary pH<5.5: Due to the decreased production of ammonia in the proximal tubule, excess protons are excreted in the renal tubules, thus decreasing the urinary pH.

RTA type I (distal RTA) is seen in autoimmune diseases like Sjogren's syndrome, systemic lupus erythematosus, systemic sclerosis, medullary sponge kidney disease, cirrhosis, drugs like amphotericin B, lithium, etc. The patients develop hypokalemia and metabolic acidosis with alkaline urine (urinary pH >5.5).

RTA type II (proximal RTA) is seen in Fanconi syndrome, Wilson's disease, heavy metals ingestion, etc., The patients develop hypokalemia and metabolic acidosis with acidic urine (urinary pH <5.5). It occurs due to generalized proximal tubule dysfunction. Defective HCO3- resorption is the primary dysfunctional mechanism causing metabolic acidosis and is also associated with glycosuria, aminoaciduria, and phosphaturia. Rickets is rare in isolated proximal RTA but common in Fanconi syndrome.

RTA type III (mixed RTA) is seen in inherited mutations of carbonic anhydrase II. A combined pathology of type I and type II RTA is seen in this type. It results in hypokalemia and metabolic acidosis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text:
Choose the correct statements for cystic fibrosis:

i. Increased Cl- in sweat.

ii. Decreased Cl- in sweat.

iii. Increased Cl- in pancreatic juice.

iv. Decreased Cl- in pancreatic juice.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. i and iv

In cystic fibrosis, there are increased chloride levels in sweat and decreased Chloride levels in pancreatic juice. The chloride level of sweat, known as the sweat test, is used to diagnose cystic fibrosis (CF). A sweat chloride level of >60 mmol/L is diagnostic of CF.

Cystic fibrosis or mucoviscidosis is an autosomal recessive disorder with a mutation in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane regulator (CFTR) gene on chromosome 7q. The most common CFTR mutation is F508 deletion.

CFTR gene encodes for ATP-gated chloride channels in the apical membranes of epithelial cells. The function of the CFTR gene on chloride channels is organ-specific. In sweat glands, the normal function of the CFTR gene is to reabsorb chloride ions. But in the pancreatic ducts and respiratory airways, the normal function of the CFTR gene is to secrete chloride ions. So, in cystic fibrosis, due to defect in the chloride channels, chloride levels in the sweat increase, and chloride levels in the pancreatic juices decreases. Excessive loss of salt in the sweat predisposes young children to salt-depletion episodes. Therefore, these children present with hypochloremic alkalosis, resulting in increased serum bicarbonate levels.

Clinical manifestations/ complications of cystic fibrosis include:

• Sinusitis and nasal polyps
• Respiratory - copious hyper-viscous and adherent pulmonary secretions with abnormal mucociliary clearance obstruct small and medium-sized airways leading to respiratory compromise. The disease can be further complicated by bronchiectasis and allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA).
• Gastrointestinal -

• Thick and adherent exocrine secretions obstruct pancreatic ducts and impair the production and flow of digestive enzymes
• Tissue destruction of the exocrine pancreas, with fibrotic scarring, cyst proliferation, and loss of acinar tissue - fat malabsorption, steatorrhea, fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies
• Obstruction of intrahepatic bile ducts and parenchymal fibrosis leading to hepatic insufficiency and focal biliary cirrhosis
• Distal intestinal obstructive syndrome in adults and meconium ileus in neonates

• Reproductive - males have infertility due to the congenital absence of bilateral vas deferens and defective sperm transport, resulting in obstructive azoospermia. Females have infertility due to abnormalities of the reproductive tract secretions.

The diagnosis is confirmed if both of the following criteria are met:

• Presence of

• Clinical symptoms affecting at least one organ system (respiratory, gastrointestinal, or genitourinary) or
• Positive newborn screening or
• A sibling with cystic fibrosis

• Evidence of dysfunction of the CFTR gene by

• Two positive sweat chloride test results were obtained on separate days or
• Identification of two CFTR mutations by genetic testing or
• An abnormal measurement of nasal potential difference

Cystic fibrosis requires a multidisciplinary approach to management. The correction of the defect can be via:

• Lumacaftor, an FDA-approved drug that corrects the misfolding and reverts the Phe508del mutation defect
• Ivacaftor potentiates CFTR channel opening and stimulates ion transport

End-stage pulmonary failure requires lung transplantation.
questions.learning: i and iv In cystic fibrosis, there are increased chloride levels in sweat and decreased Chloride levels in pancreatic juice. The chloride level of sweat, known as the sweat test, is used to diagnose cystic fibrosis (CF).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the structure given in the image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Incus

The structure given in the image is the incus.

It is one of the three ossicles that are in the middle ear cavity i.e, malleus, incus, and stapes. Ossicles conduct sound energy from the tympanic membrane to the oval window and then to the inner ear fluid.

Incus is shaped like an anvil. It has a body, a short process, and a long process. It has a saddle-shaped articular facet on its anterior surface that articulates with the malleus. The long process descends vertically and ends as a rounded lenticular process.

Incus has a single nutrient vessel within the long process and no collateral circulation. Thus, it is more susceptible to aseptic necrosis following a middle ear infection.

The malleus (option A) is the largest ossicle and is shaped like a mallet. The parts of the malleus are the head, neck, handle (manubrium), and anterior and lateral processes. The head and neck lie in the attic. The tympanic membrane is connected to the handle of the malleus.

The stapes (option C) has a head, neck, footplate, and anterior and posterior crura. The annular ligament holds the footplate of stapes in the oval window.

The joints between the ear ossicles are synovial joints. A saddle-shaped joint is present between the incus and malleus. Incus and stapes articulate via a ball and socket joint.

Option D- The vomer is a small bone in the posteroinferior part of the nasal septum. Along with perpendicular plate of the ethmoid, and the septal cartilage, it forms the nasal septum.
questions.learning: Incus — The structure given in the image is the incus. It is one of the three ossicles that are in the middle ear cavity i.e, malleus, incus, and stapes.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A renal biopsy section is provided in the image. Identify the type of cells indicated by the marked area in this histological specimen.
questions.explanation: The marked cells in the renal biopsy are Lacis cells, also known as extraglomerular mesangial cells or Goormaghtigh cells. These cells are a critical component of the juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA) and are located in the triangular space between the afferent and efferent arterioles and the macula densa. Their primary role is to facilitate signal transmission between the macula densa and the JG cells, thereby regulating renin secretion and blood pressure. Macula densa cells (Option A) are specialized tubular cells in the distal tubule that sense sodium concentration. Juxtaglomerular (JG) cells (Option B) are modified smooth muscle cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole that produce renin. Podocytes (Option D) are epithelial cells covering the glomerular capillaries, forming the filtration barrier. Given the specific anatomical location between the arterioles, the marked cells are Lacis cells

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 30 year old female developed pruritic papules with excoriated plaques in the interdigital web spaces. Later the lesion spread to the groin and under-surface of the breasts. The lady gives a history of intense pruritus which is more severe at night. Given below is the organism responsible for this condition. Identify the wrong statement about the same.
options: The entire life cycle takes about 15 days
Male parasite burrows into the epidermis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Male parasite burrows into the epidermis

The clinical background is probably suggestive Scabies. The given image depicts Itch mite also called Sarcoptes scabiei. The female parasite burrows into the stratum corneum layer of the epidermis and lays eggs in the burrow.

A single female may lay about 30 eggs at a rate of 2 to 3 per day, and ultimately dies at the end of the burrow.

The life cycle has 4 stages: Egg, Larva, Nymph, and Adult. The adult mites live for 1 to 2 months.

Itching is a hypersensitivity reaction to the eggs and dead parasite in the epidermis.

Permethrin cream - 5% is the treatment of choice.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient presents to the ER with complaints of headache, seizures and blurred vision. His BP was recorded as 220/120 mmHg. Which of the following will be the next best step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. IV labetalol

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of a hypertensive crisis (BP > 160/110 mmHg). The preferred drug to manage a hypertensive patient in an emergency is IV labetalol.

Intravenous labetalol is the drug of choice for controlling BP in a hypertensive crisis. It is effective, has a rapid onset of action, and has a good safety profile.

Labetalol is a nonselective β blocker and vascular α blocker. It should be avoided in patients with asthma and congestive heart failure due to bronchoconstriction.

It is available in oral form for the treatment of chronic hypertension and as an intravenous formulation for use in hypertensive emergencies. It can be used in the setting of a pregnancy-induced hypertensive crisis.

Other options:

Option A: IV Hydralazine: It is a vasodilator used in the treatment of heart failure, and hypertensive emergencies, especially preeclampsia. The drug is used as a combination pill containing isosorbide dinitrate (BiDil) in the treatment of heart failure. The important side effect of hydralazine is drug-induced lupus.

Option B: Oral Nifedipine: It is a calcium channel blocker (CCB), a class of medications commonly used to lower blood pressure by relaxing the blood vessels. They work by blocking the influx of calcium into smooth muscle cells, leading to vasodilation and reduced peripheral resistance. They are safer alternatives to use in pregnant patients with Asthma as they do not cause vasoconstriction and would not worsen it.

Option D: Oral Methydopa: Methyldopa is a selective alpha-2 receptor agonist and is preferred for chronic hypertension in pregnancy based on its safety and efficacy data for both mother and fetus.
questions.learning: IV labetalol — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of a hypertensive crisis (BP > 160/110 mmHg). The preferred drug to manage a hypertensive patient in an emergency is IV labetalol.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: According to the New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional classification, into which class does a person fall if they have mild limitation of physical activity, develop dyspnea with ordinary activities, but are comfortable at rest?
questions.explanation: The New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional classification provides a simple way of classifying the extent of heart failure. Class II (Option B) is defined as "slight limitation of physical activity" where patients are comfortable at rest, but ordinary physical activity (such as walking on level ground or climbing one flight of stairs) results in fatigue, palpitations, or dyspnea. Class I (Option A) involves no limitation of physical activity. Class III (Option C) involves a "marked limitation" where even less-than-ordinary activity causes symptoms. Class IV (Option D) is characterized by an inability to carry out any physical activity without discomfort and symptoms may be present even at rest. This classification is widely used to monitor the progression of heart failure and the response to medical therapy. Therefore, the description of mild restriction during ordinary activity corresponds precisely to NYHA Class II

questions.text: Cells with prolific smooth endoplasmic reticulum secrete_______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Steroid hormones

Cells with prolific smooth endoplasmic reticulum secrete steroid hormones.

The endoplasmic reticulum contains a complex series of tubules in the cytoplasm of the cell.

• Ribosomes are attached to the cytoplasmic side of the membrane in the rough(granular) endoplasmic reticulum. Protein synthesis and the initial folding of polypeptide chains with the formation of disulfide bonds are the functions of rough ER.
• Ribosomes are absent in the smooth (agranular) endoplasmic reticulum. Free ribosomes are found in the cytoplasm. It is the site of steroid synthesis in steroid-secreting cells and the site of detoxification processes in other cells.

The sarcoplasmic reticulum is a modified endoplasmic reticulum, that functions as an intracellular calcium store, which releases calcium into the cytoplasm stimulating cell contraction, proliferation, and migration.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: An 80-year-old woman sustains a fall in the bathroom and presents with severe pain, inability to walk, and a shortened, externally rotated left lower limb, suggestive of a hip fracture. An X-ray confirms the injury, as shown below. What is the most appropriate management approach for this patient?
questions.explanation: For an 80-year-old patient with a displaced femoral neck fracture, the standard of care is hemiarthroplasty (replacing the femoral head with a prosthesis). In the elderly, femoral neck fractures have a very high risk of non-union and avascular necrosis (AVN) due to the precarious blood supply to the femoral head. Replacing the head allows for immediate weight-bearing and avoids the complications of a second surgery if internal fixation fails. Internal fixation (Option A) is preferred in "young" patients (usually years) to preserve their native joint. Meyer’s operation (Option B) is a muscle-pedicle bone graft used to treat non-union in younger patients. McMurray’s osteotomy (Option D) is an obsolete procedure for hip osteoarthritis or non-union. Therefore, in a low-demand elderly patient, the goal is rapid mobilization, which is best achieved via hemiarthroplasty

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text:
Ketosis is common in type 1 DM due to:

1. Decreased beta-oxidation of fatty acids
2. Increased mobilization of fat from the adipose cell
3. Decreased acetyl CoA in TCA cycle
4. Increased beta-hydroxy butyrate dehydrogenase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2,3 and 4

2, 3 and 4 statements correctly explain the reason behind increased ketogenesis as seen in type1 DM.

Type 1 DM is characterized by a deficiency in insulin production. Since insulin is deficient, GLUT4 (insulin-dependent uptake) mediated glucose uptake is not possible in the heart or skeletal muscles. So adipose tissue mobilizes fat to be used as an energy source. These FFA (free fatty acids) are oxidized to acetoacetyl CoA which serves as a precursor for ketone body synthesis.

As the level of serum FFA is raised, proportionately more of the acetyl-CoA produced from their breakdown is converted to ketone bodies and less is oxidized via the citric acid cycle to CO2. A fall in the concentration of oxaloacetate, particularly within the mitochondria, can impair the ability of the citric acid cycle to metabolize acetyl-CoA and divert fatty acid oxidation toward ketogenesis. Such a fall may occur because of an increase in the (NADH)/(NAD+) ratio caused when increased β-oxidation alters the equilibrium between oxaloacetate and malate so that the concentration of oxaloacetate is decreased.

Beta-hydroxy butyrate dehydrogenase is one of the enzymes used in ketone body synthesis. Increased rate of ketone body synthesis in insulin-deficient state implies an increased activity of beta-hydroxy butyrate dehydrogenase enzyme.
questions.learning: 2,3 and 4 2, 3 and 4 statements correctly explain the reason behind increased ketogenesis as seen in type1 DM. Type 1 DM is characterized by a deficiency in insulin production.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the mechanism of action (MOA) of Rivaroxaban?
questions.explanation: Rivaroxaban belongs to a class of medications known as Direct Oral Anticoagulants (DOACs) that work by directly inhibiting Factor Xa. Factor Xa is a critical enzyme at the convergence of the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways, responsible for the "thrombin burst" that converts prothrombin to thrombin. By blocking Factor Xa, Rivaroxaban effectively prevents blood clot formation. Inhibition of thrombin (Factor IIa) (Option A) is the mechanism for drugs like Dabigatran. Activation of antithrombin III (Option C) is how heparin and its derivatives function. Inhibition of platelet aggregation (Option D) describes antiplatelet drugs like aspirin or clopidogrel. Rivaroxaban is commonly used for the prevention of stroke in atrial fibrillation and for the treatment of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE). Its advantages over warfarin include a rapid onset, a predictable dose-response, and the lack of a need for routine blood monitoring (PT/INR)

questions.text: IL-1 is activated by :

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman arrives at the emergency department about 6 hours after consuming a large overdose of paracetamol tablets. What is the most likely clinical course or progression of paracetamol poisoning in this situation?
options: Increase in liver enzymes within 24 hours
Paracetamol achieves peak concentration within 4 hours
questions.explanation: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) toxicity occurs when the normal metabolic pathways are overwhelmed, leading to the production of the toxic metabolite NAPQI via CYP2E1. In Stage I (0–24 hours post-ingestion), patients are often asymptomatic or have minor symptoms like nausea. However, subclinical hepatotoxicity begins, and a measurable increase in liver enzymes (AST, ALT) can occur within this first 24-hour window as damage starts. Clinical liver failure (Option B) typically develops in Stage III, which is 72–96 hours post-ingestion, not within the first day. While paracetamol reaches peak plasma levels within 2 hours, toxicity is not defined by this peak (Option C). Recovery (Option D) or progression to organ failure happens after 5 days, whereas 72 hours marks the peak of hepatic damage. Therefore, monitoring for early enzyme elevation is the most likely first sign of progression
questions.learning: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) toxicity occurs when the normal metabolic pathways are overwhelmed, leading to the production of the toxic metabolite NAPQI via CYP2E1.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the use of the Mallampati classification?
options: To evaluate the risk of surgery
To evaluate the pros and cons of surgery
To evaluate the fitness of the patient
questions.explanation: The Mallampati classification is a standard clinical tool used by anesthesiologists during the preoperative assessment to predict the ease of endotracheal intubation. By asking the patient to open their mouth and protrude their tongue without phonating, the physician assesses how much of the soft palate, fauces, and uvula are visible. There are four classes; Class I (complete visibility) suggests an easy intubation, while Class IV (only the hard palate is visible) predicts a "difficult airway". It does not evaluate the overall risk of surgery (Option B), the pros and cons of the procedure (Option C), or the patient's general fitness (Option D). The American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) physical status classification is used for overall surgical risk and fitness assessment. Correctly identifying a difficult airway using Mallampati is essential for the anesthetic team to prepare appropriate equipment, such as a video laryngoscope or fiberoptic scope, to ensure patient safety during the induction of anesthesia
questions.learning: The Mallampati classification is a standard clinical tool used by anesthesiologists during the preoperative assessment to predict the ease of endotracheal intubation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following are true about structure marked A except:
options: Supplied by sacral nerves S3 and S4 and pudendal nerve.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Attached to pelvic brim

The marked structure A represents the levator ani muscle, the major component of the pelvic diaphragm, which supports pelvic organs and maintains continence.

The levator ani consists of:

• Pubococcygeus
• Iliococcygeus
• (Often also includes puborectalis)

Innervation: Branches from S3–S4 and the pudendal nerve

Direction of fibers: Run downward and medially to form a sling around pelvic viscera

Function:

• Supports pelvic organs
• Maintains fecal and urinary continence
• Important during childbirth and defecation

Levator ani arises from:

1. Body of pubis
2. Tendinous arch of obturator fascia
3. Ischial spine

It is not attached to the pelvic brim. The pelvic brim is related to the pelvic inlet, not the levator ani.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which statement correctly explains the key features of the Michaelis–Menten enzyme kinetics curve?
options: Km is directly proportional to substrate concentration
Km doesn't vary with the enzyme concentration
Km is indirectly proportional to substrate concentration
Km has no relation to substrate concentration
questions.explanation: The Michaelis constant (Km) is a fundamental parameter in enzyme kinetics that reflects the affinity of an enzyme for its substrate. By definition, Km is equal to the substrate concentration at which the reaction velocity is exactly half of the maximum velocity (Vmax). A critical characteristic of Km is that it is an intrinsic property of the enzyme-substrate pair; therefore, it does not change regardless of the amount of enzyme present in the system. Statements A, C, and D are incorrect because Km is defined at a specific substrate concentration but is not proportional or inversely proportional to it as a variable; rather, Km is a constant used to describe the enzyme's behavior. While Vmax increases with higher enzyme concentration, Km remains stable. Consequently, understanding that Km is independent of enzyme concentration is vital for analyzing how different enzymes interact with their substrates in metabolic pathways

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient had a cataract surgery 3 years back, now complains of decrease in vision and presented with the following slit lamp image. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Posterior capsular opacification

Posterior capsular opacification (PCO) is the most common late complication of cataract surgery, presenting months to years later with gradual, painless decrease in vision.

• Proliferation and migration of residual lens epithelial cells onto the posterior capsule
• Leads to fibrosis or pearl (Elschnig pearls) formation → opacification

Key clinical features:

• Gradual painless visual decline after initially good post-op vision
• Glare and decreased contrast sensitivity
• Slit lamp: opacified posterior capsule behind IOL

Management: Nd: YAG laser posterior capsulotomy → creates a central opening in the capsule → restores vision

Why not others:

• Pseudophakic bullous keratopathy: Corneal edema, painful, epithelial bullae
• Corneal dystrophy: Bilateral, hereditary corneal changes
• Posterior subcapsular cataract: Occurs in natural lens, not after IOL implantation

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 55-year-old woman undergoes a routine check-up, during which a suspicious breast lump is identified. Biopsy confirms breast cancer. Which histological subtype of breast cancer is associated with the most favorable prognosis?
questions.explanation: In the molecular classification of breast cancer, the Luminal A subtype is recognized as having the most favorable prognosis . Luminal A tumors are characterized by being Estrogen Receptor (ER) positive and Progesterone Receptor (PR) positive, while being HER2 negative. Most importantly, they have a low Ki-67 index, indicating that the tumor cells are growing slowly. Luminal B (Option B) tumors are also ER-positive but have a higher growth rate and potentially poorer prognosis. ER-negative (Option C) and Basal-like (Option D, often triple-negative) subtypes are generally more aggressive, have higher recurrence rates, and carry a significantly worse prognosis than the Luminal A category. Therefore, because Luminal A tumors are well-differentiated and respond excellently to endocrine therapy, they represent the "best-case" molecular subtype for long-term survival. Recognizing these subtypes is essential for customizing the oncology treatment plan

questions.text: A patient with heart disease presented with breathlessness. The feature of the patient is given in the image below. Which of the following is the best drug for the treatment of edema in this patient?
options: Na-K-2Cl symporter inhibitor in loop of Henle
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Na-K-2Cl symporter inhibitor in loop of Henle

The given clinical scenario of a patient with heart failure with acute symptoms of breathlessness and pitting edema as shown in the image is sugestive of Acute decompensated heart failure. LOOP DIURETICS - Na-K-2Cl symporter inhibitor in loop of Henle are used as first line therapy for treatment of edema in heart failure.

Loop diuretics (furosemide, torasemide, bumetanide) inhibit the Na-K-2Cl symporter in the ascending limb of the loop of Henle and has a strong diuretic action.

They reduce salt and water retention, edema, and symptoms. They have no direct effect on cardiac contractility; their major mechanism of action in heart failure is to reduce venous pressure and ventricular preload.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What are the characteristic symptoms commonly observed in a patient with Reinke's edema?
options: Dysphagia of liquids more than solids
Dysphagia of solids more than liquids
questions.explanation: Reinke’s edema involves accumulation of fluid in the superficial lamina propria (Reinke’s space) of the vocal cords, leading to bulky, floppy, and often asymmetrical vocal folds. Because of this uneven mass and laxity, the two vocal cords may vibrate at different frequencies, producing two distinct tones simultaneously. This phenomenon is known as diplophonia (double voice) and is considered a characteristic feature in such questions. Although dysphonia (hoarseness) is commonly present, it is a nonspecific symptom seen in many laryngeal disorders. In contrast, diplophonia reflects abnormal, asynchronous vibration, making it more specific to conditions like Reinke’s edema in exam settings. Why Other Options Are Wrong (B) Dysphonia: Common but nonspecific (C) & (D) Dysphagia: Not related to vocal cord pathology
questions.learning: Reinke’s edema involves accumulation of fluid in the superficial lamina propria (Reinke’s space) of the vocal cords, leading to bulky, floppy, and often asymmetrical vocal folds.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a rural Type-A Primary Health Center (PHC), approximately how many deliveries are performed per month?
questions.explanation: In the Indian public health system, Primary Health Centers (PHCs) are classified based on their caseload to optimize resource allocation. A Type-A PHC is a facility that handles a low volume of deliveries, typically defined as less than 20 deliveries per month. These centers focus primarily on outpatient care and essential maternal health services but refer more complex cases to higher facilities. A Type-B PHC is one that handles a higher load, specifically 20 or more deliveries per month (Option B). Options C and D ( and ) are not the standard cut-off values used in the official classification system. Type-B PHCs are required to have more extensive labor room facilities and staff to manage the increased delivery burden. This classification helps in determining the necessary staffing, equipment, and supply chain needs for each center. Encouraging institutional deliveries at PHCs is a core strategy of the National Health Mission to reduce maternal and infant mortality rates
