questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is/are useful in the treatment of Listeria monocytogenes infection? 1. Ceftriaxone 2. Gentamicin 3. Ampicillin 4. Sulfamethoxazole Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2, 3 and 4 only

Ampicillin is the drug of choice for Listeria monocytogenes infection. Gentamicin is often added for synergistic bactericidal activity in severe infections such as meningitis or endocarditis. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) is the preferred alternative in patients allergic to penicillin.

Why not the other option?

• Ceftriaxone: Listeria is intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins; therefore, ceftriaxone is ineffective despite being commonly used for bacterial meningitis.
questions.learning: 2, 3 and 4 only Ampicillin is the drug of choice for Listeria monocytogenes infection. Gentamicin is often added for synergistic bactericidal activity in severe infections such as meningitis or endocarditis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · Acute Coronary Syndrome Mi
questions.text: A 50-year-old man presents with a history of chest pain with each episode lasting for 20-30 minutes and partial response with sublingual nitrate. ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy with ST depression and T wave inversion. He is a known case of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and hypercholesterolemia currently on aspirin, atenolol, metformin, and lovastatin. What is the next best step in management?
options: Increase the dose of beta blocker
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Injection enoxaparin

This patient has features of unstable angina / NSTEMI—recurrent chest pain lasting 20–30 minutes, only partial nitrate relief, and ischemic ECG changes (ST depression and flat T waves) in a high-risk patient (HTN, DM, dyslipidemia). The next best step is anticoagulation with LMWH (enoxaparin) to prevent thrombus propagation.

A. IV GTN infusion – Helps symptom control, but does not address thrombosis.

C. Add clopidogrel – Important, but anticoagulation is prioritized first in acute setting.

D. Increase beta-blocker dose – Useful for rate/ischemia control, but not indicated that its not optimal here.
questions.learning: Injection enoxaparin — This patient has features of unstable angina / NSTEMI—recurrent chest pain lasting 20–30 minutes, only partial nitrate relief, and ischemic ECG changes (ST depression and flat T waves) in a high-risk patient (HTN, DM, dyslipidemia).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 55-year-old woman presents with dizziness and palpitations. An ECG has been performed (shown below). What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation: The ECG strip shows a regular, narrow-complex tachycardia, most consistent with paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT). The patient presents with palpitations and dizziness, typical symptoms of this arrhythmia. The first-line management in a hemodynamically stable patient with PSVT is: 1. Vagal maneuvers (e.g., Valsalva) 2. If unsuccessful → Adenosine Since the question asks for the most appropriate treatment, adenosine is the drug of choice because: 1. It causes transient AV nodal block 2. Rapidly terminates re-entrant tachycardias 3. Has a very short half-life, making it safe and effective Why other options are incorrect: (B) Amiodarone → Used for ventricular arrhythmias or refractory cases (C) Beta-blocker → Second-line, slower onset (D) Valsalva maneuver → First step, but often insufficient alone

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is a facility offered by Ayushman AROGYA mandirs?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Essential drugs

Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (formerly Health & Wellness Centres) are mandated to provide free and essential medicines as part of comprehensive primary healthcare services.

Ayushman Arogya Mandirs are envisaged to deliver an expanded range of services that go beyond Maternal and child health care services to include care for non-communicable diseases, palliative and rehabilitative care, Oral, Eye and ENT care, mental health and first-level care for emergencies and trauma, including free essential drugs and diagnostic services.

Ayushman Arogya Mandir represents a shift from a selective model of healthcare to one that offers a comprehensive package of services, including preventive, promotive, curative, rehabilitative, and palliative care. The scheme has two complementary components. The first aims to establish 1,50,000 Ayushman Arogya Mandirs to provide universal, free, and comprehensive primary health care, with an emphasis on wellness and expanded services delivered closer to communities. The second component is the Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY), which offers health insurance coverage of ₹5 lakhs per year to more than poor and vulnerable families for secondary and tertiary level treatments.
questions.learning: Essential drugs Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (formerly Health & Wellness Centres) are mandated to provide free and essential medicines as part of comprehensive primary healthcare services.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 22-year-old woman presents within 8 hours seeking emergency contraception and prefers a single-dose pill. Which option would you recommend?
questions.explanation: For emergency contraception following unprotected intercourse, Levonorgestrel (LNG) is the standard hormonal choice. It works by delaying or inhibiting ovulation and is most effective when taken as soon as possible. While the original regimen involved two doses of 0.75 mg (Option A) taken 12 hours apart, current guidelines recommend a single dose of 1.5 mg (Option C) for improved patient compliance and convenience. Ethinyl estradiol + levonorgestrel (Option B) refers to the "Yuzpe regimen," which is older, less effective, and associated with more nausea and vomiting. Desogestrel 3 mg (Option D) is not a standard emergency contraceptive dose. LNG 1.5 mg is available over-the-counter in many regions (e.g., "Plan B One-Step") and is effective up to 72 hours, although it is ideal within the first 12–24 hours. Because the patient specifically requested a "single pill," the 1.5 mg formulation is the correct recommendation
questions.learning: For emergency contraception following unprotected intercourse, Levonorgestrel (LNG) is the standard hormonal choice. It works by delaying or inhibiting ovulation and is most effective when taken as soon as possible.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following organisms are associated with acute haemorrhagic conjunctivitis? I. Coxsackie B II. Coxsackie A III. Enterovirus 70 IV. Polio virus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. I, II and III

Acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis is a contagious viral conjunctivitis characterized by sudden onset redness, subconjunctival hemorrhage, pain, and watering.

Causative organisms:

• Enterovirus 70 → classic and most common cause in epidemics
• Coxsackie A (especially A24 variant)
• Coxsackie B (less common but associated)

Why not Poliovirus:

• Poliovirus primarily affects the central nervous system → causes poliomyelitis
• Not associated with hemorrhagic conjunctivitis
questions.learning: I, II and III Acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis is a contagious viral conjunctivitis characterized by sudden onset redness, subconjunctival hemorrhage, pain, and watering.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 12-year-old boy was brought to OPD with complaint of fatigue. Serum investigations revealed findings as given below. What is the likely diagnosis? Hemoglobin – 9 g/dl Mean cell volume (MCV) – 60 fL Mean cell Hb (MCH) – 20 pg Serum Ferritin – 185 mcg/L Total leukocyte count – Elevated lymphocyte and Neutrophils [Normal values: Serum Ferritin: 50-200 mcg/L; Mean cell volume (MCV) - 80-100 fL; Mean cell Hb (MCH) - 27-31 pg]
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thalassemia

Thalassemia should be suspected in a patient with microcytic hypochromic anemia (low MCV, low MCH) but normal or increased serum ferritin, indicating adequate iron stores.

• Low MCV and MCH (microcytic hypochromic anemia)
• Normal/high ferritin → rules out iron deficiency anemia
• Often normal or elevated RBC count relative to Hb
• Peripheral smear may show target cells
• Confirmed by hemoglobin electrophoresis

Differentiation:

A. Anemia of chronic disease: usually normocytic or mild microcytic with low iron/TIBC

C. Iron deficiency anemia: low ferritin

D. Sickle cell anemia: normocytic with sickled RBCs

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 50-year-old man was prescribed +12D glasses. He has deep anterior chamber with a deep jet-black pupil and no lens was seen on the slit lamp examination. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Aphakia

The need for +12 D glasses, a deep anterior chamber with jet-black pupil, and absence of lens on slit lamp are classical findings that together confirm aphakia.

Aphakia is the absence of the natural crystalline lens of the eye, usually caused by surgical removal, trauma, or congenital absence.

Signs of surgical aphakia include the following:

* Limbal scar

* Anterior chamber deeper than normal

* Iridodonesis (tremulousness of the iris)

* Jet black color of the pupil

* Only the first and second images (normally, four images are seen) seen on Purkinje’s image test

* Small disc seen on fundus examination

* High hypermetropia seen on retinoscopy

Aphakic eyes (eyes without a lens) only produce two Purkinje images, as the absence of the lens eliminates the reflections from the anterior and posterior lens surfaces. The test helps differentiate pseudophakia from aphakia and is useful for confirming the presence of an IOL.

Intraocular lens (IOL) implantation is done to correct aphakia following cataract surgeries. Singh and Worst’s lens is fixed on the iris by enclavating the mid-peripheral iris stroma into claw-shaped haptics, without sutures. Haptics refer to the supporting structures that hold the lens in place within the eye. They are associated with a high incidence of postoperative complications.

Posterior chamber lenses (PCIOLs) are placed entirely behind the iris. Anterior chamber IOLs are placed entirely in front of the iris. They are supported at the angle of the anterior chamber.

Other options:

Option B: Pseudophakia is wrong because in pseudophakia, the patient has an intraocular lens implant (IOL) after cataract surgery. On slit lamp examination, the IOL would be clearly visible within the pupillary area.

Option C: Hypermetropia has the lens present and usually needs only low-to-moderate (+1D to +6D) correction.

Option D: Myopia necessitates the use of minus (–) power lenses, not +12D. In this case, the patient requires strong positive correction due to an absent lens, thereby excluding a diagnosis of myopia.
questions.learning: Aphakia — The need for +12 D glasses, a deep anterior chamber with jet-black pupil, and absence of lens on slit lamp are classical findings that together confirm aphakia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The waveform shown in the image represents which of the following physiological parameters?
questions.explanation: The provided image is a capnogram, which measures the concentration of carbon dioxide in the exhaled air. Specifically, it represents End-tidal carbon dioxide (EtCO2). The waveform shows the transition from inspiration (zero CO2) to the rapid rise of mixed air during expiration, concluding with the alveolar plateau. The highest point at the end of expiration (Point E) is the EtCO2 value. Arterial oxygen saturation (Option A) is measured by pulse oximetry and displayed as a plethysmographic waveform. Functional residual capacity (Option C) is a volume measurement that cannot be visualized on a real-time monitor. Tidal volume (Option D) is the amount of air inhaled/exhaled, which can be inferred from respiration but is not the parameter directly plotted on this CO2 concentration graph. Capnography is essential for confirming ET tube placement and monitoring ventilation quality
questions.learning: The provided image is a capnogram, which measures the concentration of carbon dioxide in the exhaled air. Specifically, it represents End-tidal carbon dioxide (EtCO2).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Baroreceptor provides ________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Negative feedback

Baroreceptors provide negative feedback in response to an increase in blood pressure.

Increased baroreceptor discharge inhibits the tonic discharge of sympathetic nerves and excites the vagal innervation of the heart.

Baroreceptor reflex

• Increased BP → stimulation of baroreceptors → stimulation of NTS → inhibition of RVLM → inhibition of sympathetic system
• Stimulation of NTS also stimulates CVC → parasympathetic stimulation
• Net effect = sympathetic inhibition and parasympathetic stimulation → decreased HR and BP

NTS - Nucleus tractus solitarius

CVC - Cardiovagal center

RVLM - Rostral ventrolateral medulla

HR- Heart rate

BP - Blood pressure
questions.learning: Negative feedback Baroreceptors provide negative feedback in response to an increase in blood pressure. Increased baroreceptor discharge inhibits the tonic discharge of sympathetic nerves and excites the vagal innervation of the heart.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following abnormalities occur from vitamin D deficiency in children? 1. Craniotabes 2. Bossing of frontal and parietal bones 3. Muscle hypotonia 4. Shrinking of epiphysis at the lower end of radius Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

Vitamin D deficiency in children causes rickets, characterized by defective mineralization of the growing bone. Clinical features include craniotabes, frontal/parietal bossing, muscle hypotonia, widening of wrists, rachitic rosary, bow legs, and delayed closure of fontanelles.

Why not the other option?

• 4. Shrinking of epiphysis at the lower end of radius: Incorrect. Rickets causes widening, cupping, fraying, and splaying of the metaphysis at the distal radius, not shrinking of the epiphysis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 2-week-old infant presents with jaundice characterized by elevated conjugated (direct) bilirubin, dark urine, and pale (clay-colored) stools. The baby is otherwise feeding well on examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The presentation of conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, dark urine, and clay-colored (pale) stools in a 2-week-old infant is a classic hallmark of biliary atresia. Clay-colored stools occur because bile pigments cannot reach the intestine due to obstructed or absent bile ducts. Dark urine results from the renal excretion of water-soluble conjugated bilirubin. Gilbert's syndrome (Option B) and Crigler-Najjar syndrome (Option C) both cause unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and would not present with pale stools or dark urine. Physiological jaundice (Option D) is also unconjugated, typically peaks within the first week, and leaves stool and urine color unaffected. Biliary atresia is a progressive condition; while infants may appear healthy initially and feed well, the jaundice will worsen without surgical intervention (the Kasai procedure)
questions.learning: The presentation of conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, dark urine, and clay-colored (pale) stools in a 2-week-old infant is a classic hallmark of biliary atresia.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Postmortem examination of a dead body reveals contraction of the hands with absent primary relaxation. What is this suggestive of?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cadaveric spasm

Postmortem examination of a dead body with contraction of the hands and the absence of primary relaxation is suggestive of cadaveric spasm.

Cadaveric spasm/Instantaneous rigor is a phenomenon where a group of muscles that are in a state of contraction at the time of death remains contracted after death till molecular death occurs. It occurs immediately after death. There is no stage of primary relaxation.

It is most commonly seen in voluntary muscles, especially hands. It is seen in cases of death associated with emotional disturbances like cases of excitement, fear, severe pain, and exhaustion at the time of death. It is an antemortem phenomenon and it indicates the manner of death and not the time since death.

Other options:

Option A: Rigor mortis (cadaveric rigidity or death stiffening) refers to the stiffening and shortening of muscles following death. The order of appearance of rigor mortis: Myocardium of the heart is affected first. Nysten's rule describes the sequential onset of rigor mortis in the various muscle groups. It starts in the eyelids, neck, lower jaw, and muscles of the face and progresses downwards to involve the muscles of the chest, upper limbs, abdomen, and lower limbs. The fingers and toes are affected last.

Option B: Livor mortis/Postmortem hypostasis/Postmortem staining/Postmortem lividity/Suggilation refers to bluish-purple or reddish-purple discoloration of the superficial layers of the dermis. It is an early postmortem change that occurs due to the stagnation of blood in the vessels of the dependent parts due to the effect of gravity.

Option D: Algor mortis/postmortem cooling is one of the early changes occurring after death. The body loses heat mainly by conduction and convection after death.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the preferred treatment for a benign tumor of the superficial parathyroid gland?
questions.explanation: (Note: The question likely refers to the parotid gland, not the parathyroid, given the options.) For a benign tumor (like a pleomorphic adenoma) located in the superficial lobe of the parotid gland, the preferred and standard treatment is a superficial parotidectomy. This procedure involves removing the entire superficial lobe along with the tumor, which allows the surgeon to definitively identify and preserve the facial nerve. Simple enucleation (Option A)—just "shelling out" the tumor—is strictly avoided because it leads to a very high rate of recurrence (up to 25%) due to microscopic extensions of the tumor through its capsule. Chemotherapy (Option C) and Radiation therapy (Option D) have no role in the primary treatment of benign parotid neoplasms. During a superficial parotidectomy, the facial nerve acts as the anatomical plane dividing the gland. Preserving this nerve while ensuring an adequate margin around the tumor is the primary goal. Accurate surgical technique is critical to prevent complications like facial palsy or Frey's syndrome

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman presented to your OPD with complaints of non-foul-smelling curdy white vaginal discharge accompanied by itching and burning. Microscopic examination revealed gram-positive budding yeast and pseudohyphae. What is the causative organism in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Candida albicans

In the given clinical scenario, symptoms of non-foul smelling curdy white vaginal discharge and budding yeast cells and pseudohyphae on microscopy are suggestive of vulvovaginal candidiasis caused by Candida albicans.

Candida species are yeast-like fungi, which normally inhabit the skin and mucosa. Vulvovaginal candidiasis occurs in conditions that decrease the normal genital microbiota(e.g., long-term antibiotic use), allowing the yeasts to proliferate and produce symptoms.

Candida albicans is an ovoid or spherical budding cell, which produces pseudohyphae both in tissues and in culture. Unlike other species of candida, yeast cells of Candida albicans will begin to form germ tubes after incubation in serum maintained at 37°C for about 90 minutes. This is known as the Reynolds-Braude phenomenon.

The clinical symptoms of vulvovaginal candidiasis include curdy white vaginal discharge, dysuria, and intense itching with vaginal pH <4.5.

Diagnosis includes:

* Wet smear with 10% KOH solution- shows budding yeast cells and pseudohyphae as seen in the image below:

* Gram staining - Gram-positive budding cells with pseudohyphae

* Sabouraud agar culture - Creamy white smooth colonies with yeasty odour.

* Corn meal agar culture - Candida albicans form chlamydospores.

* CHROMagar - Candida albicans colonies appear green.

Treatment involves oral fluconazole 150 mg single dose or local intravaginal application of antifungal agents such as imidazole miconazole, clotrimazole, vaginal pessaries or creams used for 3-6 days is effective.
questions.learning: Candida albicans — In the given clinical scenario, symptoms of non-foul smelling curdy white vaginal discharge and budding yeast cells and pseudohyphae on microscopy are suggestive of vulvovaginal candidiasis caused by Candida albicans.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A patient presents with low mood, loss of appetite, excessive sleep, and low energy persisting for 2 months. She had a similar episode 5 months ago that resolved with medication. What is the most likely disorder?
questions.explanation: The patient is experiencing a second distinct episode of classic depressive symptoms (low mood, energy, and changes in appetite and sleep) lasting at least two weeks. The history of a previous episode that responded to treatment five months ago defines this as Recurrent Depressive Disorder. While she is currently depressed (Option A), "recurrent" is the most specific diagnosis describing her longitudinal course. Dysthymia (Option C) is a chronic, low-grade depression lasting for at least two years without remission. Cyclothymia (Option D) involves a two-year period of fluctuating periods of mild depression and mild elevation (hypomania). Recurrent depressive disorder is a common psychiatric condition requiring long-term maintenance therapy with antidepressants to prevent further relapses. Each subsequent episode increases the risk of future recurrences, making consistent pharmacological and psychotherapeutic intervention critical for the patient's long-term functional stability
questions.learning: The patient is experiencing a second distinct episode of classic depressive symptoms (low mood, energy, and changes in appetite and sleep) lasting at least two weeks.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following are true about the right coronary artery except _____
options: It's diameter is less than left coronary artery
It arises from the anterior aortic sinus
It gives rise to circumflex coronary branch
Right conal artery is it's first branch
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It gives rise to circumflex coronary branch

The right coronary artery does not give rise to the circumflex coronary artery.

The right coronary artery arises from the anterior aortic sinus (right coronary sinus) of the ascending aorta. It passes anteriorly and descends vertically in the coronary sulcus between the right atrium and the right ventricle. On reaching the inferior margin, it turns posteriorly and continues in the sulcus onto the diaphragmatic surface and the base of the heart.

The diameter of the right coronary artery is less than that of the left coronary artery.

The right conal artery is, usually the first branch of the right coronary artery.

The circumflex coronary artery is a branch of the left coronary artery and is the exclusive supplier to the right bundle branch.
questions.learning: It gives rise to circumflex coronary branch — The right coronary artery does not give rise to the circumflex coronary artery. The right coronary artery arises from the anterior aortic sinus (right coronary sinus) of the ascending aorta.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A diabetic man presents with facial pain and blackish discoloration of the nasal cavity. CT imaging reveals sinus involvement with bone erosion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Uncontrolled diabetes is a major risk factor for mucormycosis, a fulminant and angioinvasive fungal infection. The presence of a black eschar (necrotic tissue) on the nasal mucosa or palate is a hallmark clinical sign. The fungus, usually Rhizopus species, invades blood vessels causing thrombosis, infarction, and invasive bone destruction as seen on the CT. Acute bacterial sinusitis (Option A) causes purulent discharge and pain but lacks tissue necrosis and bone erosion. Allergic fungal sinusitis (Option B) is a non-invasive condition that expands rather than destroys bone. Nasal polyps (Option C) are benign mucosal growths that do not cause pain or necrotic changes. Management requires urgent surgical debridement and high-dose IV liposomal amphotericin B
questions.learning: Uncontrolled diabetes is a major risk factor for mucormycosis, a fulminant and angioinvasive fungal infection. The presence of a black eschar (necrotic tissue) on the nasal mucosa or palate is a hallmark clinical sign.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which of the following is a formal thought disorder?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Derailment

Derailment is a formal thought disorder.

It is a breakdown in both the logical connection between ideas and the overall sense of being goal-oriented. It is generally identified in schizophrenic patients as a generalized loosening of associations.

For example, a person with derailment thought disorder might jump from talking about rabbits to the hair on their head to your sweater. They talk in chains of semi-related ideas. Their communication style has a generalized loosening of associations. Their ideas often fall further and further from the topic.

Formal thought disorders are:

• Circumstantiality is the overinclusion of trivial or irrelevant details that impedes the sense of getting to the point.
• Clang association is an association of thoughts with the sound of words rather than by their meaning (e.g., through rhyming).
• Derailment is the breakdown in both the logical connection between ideas and the overall sense of goal-directedness. The words make sentences, but the sentences do not make sense.
• Flight of ideas is a succession of multiple associations so that thoughts seem to move abruptly from idea to idea, through rapid, pressured speech.
• Neologism is the invention of new words or phrases or the use of conventional words in idiosyncratic ways.
• Perseveration is the repetition of out-of-context words, phrases, or ideas.
• Tangentiality is responding to a question, that is appropriate to the general topic without actually answering the question.
• Thought blocking is a sudden disruption of thought or a break in the flow of ideas.

Other options:

Option A - An obsession is a recurrent and intrusive thought, feeling, idea, or sensation.

Option C - A delusion is defined as a false belief based on incorrect inference about external reality that firmly sustains despite evidence to the contrary.

Option D - Thought insertion is a type of delusion where the patient believes that thoughts are not his/her own and have been inserted into his/her mind.
questions.learning: Derailment Derailment is a formal thought disorder. It is a breakdown in both the logical connection between ideas and the overall sense of being goal-oriented.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 24-year-old woman at 16 weeks of gestation is found to have anemia on routine antenatal screening. She is otherwise asymptomatic, and laboratory evaluation is consistent with iron deficiency anemia. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
options: 100 mg iron + 500 mcg folic acid once daily
60 mg iron + 500 mcg folic acid once daily
100 mg iron + 500 mcg folic acid twice daily
60 mg iron + 500 mcg folic acid twice daily
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 60 mg iron + 500 mcg folic acid twice daily

Iron deficiency anemia diagnosed during pregnancy should be treated with therapeutic oral iron, not the prophylactic dose. In a hemodynamically stable pregnant woman with mild-to-moderate iron deficiency anemia, the recommended treatment is 60 mg elemental iron + 500 mcg folic acid twice daily, along with dietary counseling and assessment of response.

Why not the other options?

• A. 100 mg iron + 500 mcg folic acid once daily: Not the standard recommended therapeutic regimen in national antenatal programs.
• B. 60 mg iron + 500 mcg folic acid once daily: This is the prophylactic dose used to prevent anemia during pregnancy.
• C. 100 mg iron + 500 mcg folic acid twice daily: Higher than the recommended routine therapeutic dose for uncomplicated iron deficiency anemia.
questions.learning: 60 mg iron + 500 mcg folic acid twice daily Iron deficiency anemia diagnosed during pregnancy should be treated with therapeutic oral iron, not the prophylactic dose.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, at 16 weeks’ gestation presents for a prenatal visit. She reports increased urinary frequency but otherwise feels well. Urinalysis reveals mild glucosuria. Laboratory studies show a non-fasting serum glucose concentration of 100 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient’s glucosuria?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Increased glomerular filtration rate

During normal pregnancy, there is a physiologic increase in renal plasma flow and glomerular filtration rate (GFR) by approximately 40–50%.

Because of this increased GFR, a larger amount of glucose is filtered at the glomerulus.

The renal tubules may not completely reabsorb this increased glucose load, resulting in mild physiologic glucosuria, even when serum glucose levels are normal.

Key features of physiologic glucosuria in pregnancy:

• Occurs due to increased GFR

• Normal blood glucose levels

• Common finding in pregnancy

• Not diagnostic of gestational diabetes

Why other options are incorrect:

• Decreased SGLT2 expression → not the physiologic change in pregnancy

• Increased glomerular filtration barrier permeability → would cause proteinuria, not glucosuria

• Splay phenomenon → refers to variability in nephron glucose reabsorption but is not the primary mechanism here
questions.learning: Increased glomerular filtration rate During normal pregnancy, there is a physiologic increase in renal plasma flow and glomerular filtration rate (GFR) by approximately 40–50%.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A lady presented with a pelvic mass which was hyperintense on T1-weighted image, hyperintense on T1-fat saturated image, and hypointense on T2-weighted image with T2 shading. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Endometrioma

Endometriomas (chocolate cysts) show T1 hyperintensity due to blood, remain bright on fat-sat, and T2 shading from repeated hemorrhage. Teratomas contain fat, carcinoma/dysgerminoma lack these features.

Key Radiological Signs

1. T1 Hyperintensity

• Due to blood products (methemoglobin)

2. No Fat Suppression

• Remains bright on T1 fat-sat → confirms blood, not fat

3. T2 Shading Sign

• Progressive loss of signal on T2
• Due to chronic repeated hemorrhage

| Feature | Endometrioma | Teratoma | Ovarian Carcinoma | Dysgerminoma

| ------- | ------------ | -------- | ----------------- | ------------

| T1 | Hyperintense | Hyperintense | Variable | Iso/hypo

| Fat suppression | ❌ No | ✅ Yes | No | No

| T2 | Shading (hypo) | Variable | Heterogeneous | Solid

| Nature | Blood cyst | Fat tumor | Malignant | Solid tumor

| Key sign | T2 shading ⭐ | Fat suppression | Solid nodules | Lobulated mass
questions.learning: Endometrioma Endometriomas (chocolate cysts) show T1 hyperintensity due to blood, remain bright on fat-sat, and T2 shading from repeated hemorrhage. Teratomas contain fat, carcinoma/dysgerminoma lack these features.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 60-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus develops vaginal candidiasis. Which antidiabetic (hypoglycemic) agent should be avoided in this patient?
questions.explanation: Gliflozins (SGLT2 inhibitors), such as canagliflozin or empagliflozin, work by inhibiting glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubules of the kidney, leading to glycosuria (glucose in the urine). While effective for blood sugar control and providing cardiovascular benefits, the increased urinary glucose concentration promotes the growth of fungi. Therefore, a major and common side effect of Gliflozins is an increased risk of genitourinary infections, particularly vaginal candidiasis and urinary tract infections. In a patient already suffering from candidiasis, these drugs should be avoided as they will likely exacerbate the infection. Acarbose (Option A), Metformin (Option B), and Linagliptin (Option D) do not cause glycosuria and are not associated with an increased risk of fungal infections. Clinical management requires weighing the significant renal and cardiac benefits of SGLT2 inhibitors against the risk of recurrent infections, often necessitating counseling on proper hygiene and prompt treatment of any symptomatic episodes
questions.learning: Gliflozins (SGLT2 inhibitors), such as canagliflozin or empagliflozin, work by inhibiting glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubules of the kidney, leading to glycosuria (glucose in the urine).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which media is most suitable for the optimal growth of E.coli?
questions.explanation: Escherichia coli is a gram-negative rod and a member of the Enterobacteriaceae family. The most suitable and standard media for its optimal growth and identification is MacConkey agar (Option D). MacConkey agar is both selective (inhibiting gram-positives) and differential. E. coli is a strong lactose fermenter, so it produces bright pink-colored colonies on this medium. Chocolate agar (Option A) is an enriched medium for fastidious organisms like H. influenzae. Thayer-Martin (Option B) is a specialized medium for Neisseria species. SDA (Sabouraud Dextrose Agar, Option C) is used for the cultivation of fungi. Because MacConkey agar allows for the rapid differentiation of E. coli from non-lactose fermenting gut pathogens, it is the definitive choice for standard enteric bacteriology
questions.learning: Escherichia coli is a gram-negative rod and a member of the Enterobacteriaceae family. The most suitable and standard media for its optimal growth and identification is MacConkey agar (Option D).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which one of the following disorders are caused by enzymatic defects in the heme biosynthesis pathway?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Porphyrias

Porphyrias are a group of inherited or acquired disorders caused by deficiency of enzymes involved in the heme biosynthesis pathway, leading to the accumulation of porphyrins or their precursors in tissues. Clinical manifestations depend on the site of accumulation and are characterized by neurovisceral symptoms, photosensitivity, or both.

• A. Porphyrias: Caused by enzyme defects in the heme synthesis pathway, resulting in accumulation of toxic heme precursors.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. Myelodysplastic syndrome: A clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorder causing ineffective hematopoiesis; unrelated to heme biosynthesis.
• C. Hemophilias: Inherited coagulation factor deficiencies (Factor VIII or IX), not disorders of heme synthesis.
• D. Plasma cell disorders: Disorders of monoclonal plasma cell proliferation (e.g., multiple myeloma), unrelated to the heme pathway.
questions.learning: Porphyrias Porphyrias are a group of inherited or acquired disorders caused by deficiency of enzymes involved in the heme biosynthesis pathway, leading to the accumulation of porphyrins or their precursors in tissues.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Identify the postmortem change shown in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tache noire

The image shows Tache noire.

If the eyelids remain open for a few hours after death, a layer of cell debris and mucus forms a yellow triangle on the sclera at either side adjacent to the iris. The base of the triangle is towards the margin of the cornea and the apex is towards the canthus of the eye. This debris turns brown when the dust settles on them. It appears within 3-4 hours of death.

Other postmortem changes occurring in the eye:

* Cornea: Dull, and opaque due to the lack of lacrimal moistening.

* Flaccidity of eyeballs occurs due to a fall in intraocular pressure.

* Pupils- Soon after death, pupils are slightly dilated due to the relaxation of the iris muscles. At the onset of rigor, the pupils become constricted.

* Increase in potassium concentration in the vitreous. It is helpful in determining the time since death.

* Kevorkian sign(Option C)- It is characterized by fragmentation of the blood column in the retinal vessels. It appears within minutes after death and lasts for about 1 hour.
questions.learning: Tache noire — The image shows Tache noire. If the eyelids remain open for a few hours after death, a layer of cell debris and mucus forms a yellow triangle on the sclera at either side adjacent to the iris.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: All of the following are causes of secondary osteoarthritis of the hip, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diabetes

Secondary osteoarthritis (OA) of the hip occurs due to an identifiable underlying condition that damages the hip joint.

• (a) Trauma — Correct: Previous hip trauma or fracture can lead to secondary OA.
• (b) Diabetes — Incorrect → Diabetes is not a classical direct cause of secondary hip OA.
• (c) Perthes’ disease — Correct: Childhood avascular necrosis of the femoral head can cause deformity and subsequent secondary OA.
• (d) Avascular necrosis — Correct: Collapse and deformity of the femoral head can result in secondary OA.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following substances enhances the absorption of iron from the diet?
questions.explanation: Iron absorption occurs mainly in the duodenum and proximal jejunum and is strongly influenced by the oxidation state of iron. Dietary non-heme iron is predominantly present in the ferric (Fe³⁺) form, which is poorly absorbed. For absorption to occur, ferric iron must be reduced to the ferrous (Fe²⁺) form, which can then be transported across the intestinal mucosa via Divalent Metal Transporter-1 (DMT1). Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) plays a crucial role in this process. It acts as a powerful reducing agent, converting Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺, thereby enhancing iron solubility and absorption. This is why vitamin C markedly increases the bioavailability of non-heme iron. Why the other options are incorrect: 1. Calcium (Option A): Inhibits iron absorption when taken simultaneously in large amounts 2. Vitamin D (Option C): Regulates calcium and phosphate metabolism, not iron absorption 3. Vitamin K (Option D): Required for synthesis of clotting factors and bone health
questions.learning: Iron absorption occurs mainly in the duodenum and proximal jejunum and is strongly influenced by the oxidation state of iron. Dietary non-heme iron is predominantly present in the ferric (Fe³⁺) form, which is poorly absorbed.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which artery is most commonly affected in bleeding from the nose?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sphenopalatine artery

The most commonly affected artery in bleeding from the nose is the sphenopalatine artery. It is called the artery of epistaxis because of the same

Arterial supply of lateral wall of nose is given

Sites of epistaxis

* Little’s area: It is the site in 90% of the patients with epistaxis. Four arteries form a vascular plexus called “Kiesselbach’s plexus” in the antero-inferior part of the nasal septum just above the vestibule. It is more prone to finger nail trauma and the drying effect of air.

* Above the level of middle turbinate: The bleeding usually occurs from the anterior and posterior ethmoidalvessels (internal carotid system).

* Below the level of middle turbinate: The bleeding is from the branches of sphenopalatine artery.

* Posterior part of the nasal cavity or the nasopharynx: The blood flows into the pharynx.

* Woodruff’s venous plexus: It is the site of posterior epistaxis in adults and is situated inferior to the posterior end of inferior turbinate.

* Diffuse: It is often indicative of general systemic disorders and blood dyscrasias.

The stepwise management of epistaxis:

* Pinching of the nose with thumb and index finger for about 5 minutes compresses the vessels of the Little’s area.

* Cauterization of the bleeding point with silver nitrate or electrocautery. This is done under topical anesthesia.

* Anterior nasal packing.

* Posterior nasal packing for which patients should be hospitalized.

* Endoscopic cauterization of the bleeding point.

* Elevation of the mucoperichondrial flap and submucosal resection operation- for persistent and recurrent bleeds from the septum.

* Ligation of vessels.

The recommended hierarchy of ligation of vessels in a patient of epistaxis is Sphenopalatine artery → Internal maxillary artery→ External carotid artery → Anterior /posterior ethmoidal artery.

* Transnasal endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation (TESPAL) is done under topical anesthesia with sedation or under general anesthesia. It is effective in controlling refractory posterior bleeds.

* Embolization of the internal maxillary artery by an interventional radiologist, via femoral artery catheterization.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old male with a history of heart surgery now presents with the chest X-ray shown below. What is the finding indicated by the '?' on the X-ray?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Prosthetic mitral valve

The structure marked in the image shows a prosthetic mitral valve and a pacemaker also in place.

Prosthetic heart valves are common. The most commonly replaced are aortic and mitral valves.

Replacements may be tissue or metallic valves.

In recent times, aortic valves in select circumstances are being replaced via a transcatheter approach, called transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) from a femoral artery approach.

Prosthetic valves are subdivided into two categories -mechanical and bioprosthetic

* Mechanical valves

* ball cage valves

* tilting disk valves

* Bioprosthetic valves

* homografts

* heterografts

* stented

* stentless

Transesophageal echocardiography is the modality of choice to assess the status of a prosthetic heart valve after placement of a valve.

Complications:

* Obstruction

* maybe due to thrombus or pannus

* Infective endocarditis

* with or without valvular vegetation or paravalvular abscess

* Paravalvular regurgitation

* Valve failure

* mechanical failure in mechanical valves

* degeneration of a biological valve

* Hemolytic anemia
questions.learning: Prosthetic mitral valve — The structure marked in the image shows a prosthetic mitral valve and a pacemaker also in place. Prosthetic heart valves are common.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 35-year-old patient undergoes endoscopic evaluation for recurrent abdominal discomfort and altered bowel habits. Which anatomical structure is indicated by the arrow in the provided image?
questions.explanation: The given histological image represents a section of the duodenum, which can be identified by the presence of finger-like villi in the mucosa and prominent glandular structures in the submucosa. The arrow is pointing to clusters of mucous-secreting glands located beneath the mucosal layer. These are Brunner’s glands, a distinctive feature of the duodenum. Brunner’s glands secrete an alkaline mucus rich in bicarbonate ions, which plays a crucial role in neutralizing the acidic chyme entering from the stomach. This protective mechanism helps prevent damage to the intestinal lining and provides an optimal pH for pancreatic enzyme activity. Why Other Options Are Incorrect (B) Interstitial cells of Cajal: These are microscopic pacemaker cells and are not visible as large glandular clusters (C) Crypts of Lieberkühn: Present in the mucosa, not in the submucosa (D) Peyer’s patches: Lymphoid aggregates found in the ileum, not in the duodenum
questions.learning: The given histological image represents a section of the duodenum, which can be identified by the presence of finger-like villi in the mucosa and prominent glandular structures in the submucosa.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is correct about Finerenone? 1. It causes less hyperkalemia than spironolactone 2. It has a cardioprotective effect 3. It gets accumulated in the kidneys 4. It causes a significant reduction in blood pressure
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 and 2

Solution – Finerenone:

• It is a non-steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA)
• Used mainly in:

• Chronic kidney disease (CKD) with diabetes
• Cardiovascular protection

Statement 3: Gets accumulated in kidneys

• Opposite is true
• Finerenone has Even distribution (heart + kidney)

• Unlike eplerenone/spironolactone→ kidney accumulation

Statement 4: Significant BP reduction

• Only mild antihypertensive effect
• Not used as a primary antihypertensive

Steroidal MRAs (spironolactone, eplerenone) → kidney-predominant distribution → more BP reduction + more hyperkalemia

Finerenone (non-steroidal) → equal heart:kidney distribution → cardioprotective + less hyperkalemia + minimal BP effect

| Feature | Finerenone | Spironolactone

| ------- | ---------- | --------------

| Type | Non-steroidal MRA | Steroidal MRA

| Tissue distribution | Balanced (heart + kidney) | Kidney predominant

| Hyperkalemia | Less | More

| Anti-androgen effects | None | Gynecomastia

| Cardioprotection | Strong | Moderate

| BP reduction | Mild | Moderate

| CKD use | Preferred | Limited

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A worker employed in a groundnut processing unit develops features of food poisoning after eating groundnuts that had been stored for a long duration. What is the most probable cause of this illness?
questions.explanation: Aflatoxins are potent mycotoxins produced by the molds Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus parasiticus, which commonly contaminate "groundnuts" (peanuts), maize, and other crops stored in damp conditions. Acute ingestion of high levels of aflatoxin can cause severe toxic hepatitis, while chronic exposure is one of the strongest risk factors for hepatocellular carcinoma. Beta oxalyl amino alanine (BOAA) (Option A) is the neurotoxin found in Lathyrus sativus (Khesari dal) that causes neurolathyrism. Option B is an environmental pollutant. Sanguinarine (Option C) is the toxin found in Argemone mexicana (prickly poppy) seeds; when mixed with mustard oil, it causes Epidemic Dropsy. In the context of "stored groundnuts," aflatoxin is the most probable epidemiological culprit. Public health efforts focus on proper agricultural storage and the monitoring of moisture levels to prevent the fungal growth that produces these dangerous toxins
questions.learning: Aflatoxins are potent mycotoxins produced by the molds Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus parasiticus, which commonly contaminate "groundnuts" (peanuts), maize, and other crops stored in damp conditions.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 61-year-old university professor presents with sudden loss of vision in his left eye, describing it as a curtain descending over the eye. He also reports experiencing flashes of light and floaters about a week earlier. His medical history is significant for cataract surgery in the same eye three weeks ago. A B-scan image of the left eye is provided. Based on this presentation, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s history of "flashing lights" (photopsia) and "floaters" followed by a vision loss described as a "curtain being pulled" is the classic clinical triad for Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment (RD). Post-cataract surgery (pseudophakia) is a well-known risk factor for RD. The provided B-scan ultrasound provides definitive radiological evidence, showing a high-reflective, undulating membrane within the vitreous cavity that remains attached to the optic nerve head, forming a classic funnel shape. Glaucoma (Option A) causes progressive peripheral field loss, not an acute "curtain" effect. A retinal tumor (Option B) would appear as a solid, vascularized mass on B-scan. A corneal ulcer (Option D) would be visible on external examination and not require a B-scan for diagnosis. Therefore, the combination of clinical symptoms and the pathognomonic B-scan image confirms the diagnosis of Retinal Detachment
questions.learning: The patient’s history of "flashing lights" (photopsia) and "floaters" followed by a vision loss described as a "curtain being pulled" is the classic clinical triad for Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment (RD).

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 38-year-old professor with depression requests you to prescribe an antidepressant that would be least likely to cause sexual dysfunction. Which of the following drugs would you prescribe?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bupropion

Bupropion can be prescribed as it decreases the chance of causing sexual dysfunction.

* It enhances both noradrenergic and dopaminergic neurotransmission by inhibiting reuptake.

* Used for aiding smoking cessation and for the treatment of depression in combination with SSRIs.

* Adverse effects of bupropion include stimulant side effects like tachycardia, insomnia, headache, and seizures in anorexic/bulimic patients.

* It decreases the risk of sexual dysfunction and weight gain compared to other antidepressants.

Venlafaxine is a serotonin noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor used in the treatment of major depression, generalized anxiety disorder, and panic disorder. Adverse effects are nausea, sexual dysfunction, and sustained elevation of blood pressure.

Escitalopram and fluoxetine are selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors used in the treatment of major depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder, bulimia and anorexia nervosa, and generalized anxiety disorders. Adverse effects are dry mouth, urinary retention, and sexual dysfunction.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the correct arrangement for the levels of Health Care?
options: 1→ Medical colleges and Hospitals, 2→CHC, 3 → subcentre and PHC
1 → CHC, 2→ Subcentre, PHC , 3→ Medical colleges and Hospitals
1→Subcentre and PHC, 2→ CHC, 3→Medical colleges and Hospitals
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1→Subcentre and PHC, 2→ CHC, 3→Medical colleges and Hospitals

The correct arrangement for the levels of Health Care is as follows, Primary, Subcentre and PHC → Secondary, CHC→ Tertiary, Medical colleges and Hospitals.

The NPHCE was established for geriatric care and includes provisions at primary, secondary, and tertiary levels.

Centres
Services according to NPHCE

PHCs (primary)

• Weekly geriatric clinics at PHC.
• Treatment of minor ailments.
• Referral services to higher centres.

Sub-centres (primary)

• ANMs/ male health workers make domiciliary visits to the elderly.
• Arrange supportive devices for the disabled.
• Treatment of minor ailments

CHCs (secondary)

• Dedicated geriatric clinics twice weekly.
• Rehabilitation unit with trained physiotherapists.

The tertiary component of the program has been renamed RVJSY and has the following provisions:

* Geriatrics departments at 20 super speciality institutions:

* 30-bed inpatient facility and referral treatment.

* Research and manpower development.

* Development of training, IEC material, and guidelines.

* Geriatric units at district hospitals (tertiary)-

* 10-bed geriatric ward.

* Dedicated geriatric OPD.

Pearl PF1670: Levels of Healthcare System in India

Pearl PF1669: Elements and Principles of Primary Health Care

A. Elements of Primary Health Care

(Mnemonic: ELEMENTS)

* Education about health problems and their prevention and control

* Locally endemic diseases – prevention and control

* Essential drugs

* Maternal and child health care

* Expanded programme of immunization against vaccine preventable diseases

* Nutrition and proper food supply

* Treatment of common diseases and injuries

* Safe water and sanitation

B. Principles/Pillars of Primary Health Care

* Equitable distribution

* Community participation

* Intersectoral coordination

* Appropriate technology

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is a recommended treatment for esophageal varices?
questions.explanation: Endoscopic variceal ligation (EVL) is the first-line treatment for both the management of acute variceal hemorrhage and secondary prophylaxis. It involves placing elastic bands around the varices to cause thrombosis and eventual obliteration. TIPS (Option B) is an effective procedure but is reserved as a salvage therapy when endoscopic and pharmacological treatments fail to control bleeding. Intravenous labetalol (Option C) is not used; instead, non-selective beta-blockers like propranolol are used for primary prophylaxis to reduce portal pressure. While prophylactic antibiotics are standard in variceal bleeding (usually ceftriaxone), oral amoxicillin (Option D) is not the standard choice and has no role in the direct control of bleeding. Thus, EVL is the definitive recommended endoscopic intervention
questions.learning: Endoscopic variceal ligation (EVL) is the first-line treatment for both the management of acute variceal hemorrhage and secondary prophylaxis. It involves placing elastic bands around the varices to cause thrombosis and eventual obliteration.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: True statement for Wolf Parkinson's white syndrome?
questions.explanation: Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome is a pre-excitation syndrome caused by an accessory electrical pathway (Bundle of Kent) that bypasses the AV node. The classic ECG findings include a short PR interval (less than 120 ms), a slurred upstroke of the QRS complex known as a delta wave, and a resulting widened QRS complex. While the QRS is technically broadened, "Short PR Interval" is the most characteristic and defining initial diagnostic finding. A broad QRS interval (Option B) is too general, as it occurs in many conditions like bundle branch blocks. Tall tented T waves (Option C) are the hallmark of hyperkalemia. A prolonged PR interval (Option D) defines a first-degree AV block, which is the pathophysiological opposite of pre-excitation. WPW predisposes patients to paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardias (AVRT). Management includes avoiding certain AV-nodal blocking drugs and definitive treatment via radiofrequency catheter ablation of the accessory pathway to prevent future arrhythmias and potential sudden cardiac death
questions.learning: Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome is a pre-excitation syndrome caused by an accessory electrical pathway (Bundle of Kent) that bypasses the AV node.

questions.text: A 75 kg person is administered a drug with a half-life of 3 hours. What is the approximate clearance of the drug? (Given: Vd = mL/kg)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient has sustained an injury resulting in nerve damage. Based on the findings shown in the provided image, which nerve is affected?
questions.explanation: The provided image demonstrates a "wrist drop" deformity, which is the hallmark clinical presentation of a Radial nerve injury. The radial nerve provides motor innervation to the extensor muscles of the wrist and fingers. When the nerve is damaged—classically at the spiral groove of the humerus due to a mid-shaft fracture or "Saturday night palsy"—the patient loses the ability to extend the hand against gravity. Ulnar nerve injury (Option A) typically results in a "claw hand" affecting the ring and little fingers. Median nerve damage (Option C) often leads to the "ape hand" deformity or "hand of benediction" during an attempt to make a fist. Axillary nerve injury (Option D) affects the deltoid muscle, causing impaired shoulder abduction rather than distal hand weakness. Physical examination for sensory loss in the first dorsal web space further confirms radial nerve involvement. Management involves splinting the wrist in extension to prevent contractures while the nerve recovers

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is used to obtain consensus forecasts among a large number of people?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Delphi method

Delphi method is a systematic interactive forecasting method, which is used to obtain a consensus forecast, i.e., to determine the degree of agreement on a topic. This can help in setting priorities or selecting alternatives in planning. This method uses questionnaires, which are answered by experts in two or more rounds.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 22-year-old student presented with high-grade fever, and purpuric rash as shown in the image below. CSF sample showed gram-negative diplococci. Which of the following is the most likely aetiology?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Neisseria meningitidis

This patient has a high-grade fever and is a student, so he presumably spends a lot of time in crowded areas. The above image shows a purpuric rash. This patient's features are seen in meningococcemia caused by Neisseria meningitidis, which are gram-negative diplococci.

The organism enters the body through the nasopharynx by attaching to the epithelial cells with the help of pili. From the nasopharynx, they enter the bloodstream producing bacteremia, and the symptoms may resemble upper respiratory tract infection.

Fulminant meningococcemia is the severe form, where the patient presents with high-grade fever and hemorrhagic rash. There is thrombosis of several small blood vessels in various organs with perivascular infiltration and petechial hemorrhages. Some patients with fulminant meningococcemia may also develop disseminated intravascular coagulation, and circulatory collapse, a condition known as Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome.
questions.learning: Neisseria meningitidis — This patient has a high-grade fever and is a student, so he presumably spends a lot of time in crowded areas. The above image shows a purpuric rash.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 16-year-old male presents with subacute, painless, bilateral vision loss. Family history reveals his mother and maternal uncle had similar vision problems in their teens, but his father is unaffected and none of his father's relatives are affected. Which mitochondrial complex is implicated, and what inheritance pattern explains why only maternal relatives are affected?
options: Complex IV mutation; autosomal dominant inheritance
Complex III mutation; X-linked inheritance, explaining male predominance
Complex II mutation; autosomal recessive inheritance with consanguinity
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Complex I mutation; mitochondrial (maternal) inheritance

Leber hereditary optic neuropathy = mutations in Complex I of the electron transport chain → neuronal death in retina/optic nerve → subacute bilateral vision loss in teens/young adults (males > females in expression, though inheritance is maternal). Mitochondrial DNA is transmitted only through the mother — explaining why maternal relatives (mother, maternal uncle) are affected while paternal relatives are entirely unaffected, regardless of the patient's own sex.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What is the typical Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) in a healthy adult?
questions.explanation: The Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) is a measure of how much filtrate the kidneys produce each minute. In a healthy adult, the typical GFR is approximately 125 ml/min. This equates to roughly 180 liters per day. However, about 99% of this filtrate is reabsorbed, resulting in a normal urine output of 1-2 liters per day. Values like 200 ml/min (Option B) are abnormally high (hyperfiltration), while 100 ml/min (Option C) or 150 ml/min (Option D) are outside the standard "normal" range. GFR is the gold standard for assessing kidney function. It is often estimated (eGFR) in clinical practice using the patient's serum creatinine level, age, sex, and race. A persistent decline in GFR below 60 ml/min for more than three months is diagnostic of Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD). Maintaining a steady GFR is essential for regulating the body's fluid balance, electrolyte levels, and the excretion of nitrogenous waste products like urea and creatinine
questions.learning: The Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) is a measure of how much filtrate the kidneys produce each minute. In a healthy adult, the typical GFR is approximately 125 ml/min.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which drug is used to test for Myasthenia Gravis?
questions.explanation: Edrophonium is a short-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used in the Tensilon test to diagnose Myasthenia Gravis (MG). In patients with MG, who have a deficiency of functional acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, edrophonium briefly increases the amount of available acetylcholine, leading to a rapid, temporary improvement in muscle strength (e.g., resolution of ptosis). Its rapid onset and very short duration of action (minutes) make it ideal for this diagnostic test. Pyridostigmine (Option A) and Neostigmine (Option B) are longer-acting inhibitors used for the treatment of MG, not typically for the initial diagnosis. Atropine (Option D) is a muscarinic antagonist used to counteract the cholinergic side effects (like bradycardia or salivation) that can occur during the edrophonium test. While the Tensilon test has largely been replaced by antibody testing and electromyography (SFEMG), it remains a classic pharmacological principle for understanding the pathophysiology of the neuromuscular junction

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An intern finds a patient unresponsive and performs an urgent ECG showing a persistent arrhythmia. Despite delivering a DC shock, the arrhythmia continues, and the patient remains unresponsive. What is the next best step in managing this patient?
questions.explanation: The provided ECG shows Ventricular Fibrillation (VF), a disorganized pulseless rhythm. According to standard ACLS guidelines, after a DC shock (defibrillation) is delivered, the immediate and absolute next step is to resume high-quality chest compressions (CPR) for two minutes before re-checking the rhythm or pulse. Synchronized cardioversion (Option A) is strictly contraindicated for VF; it is used for organized tachycardias with a pulse. Delivering another immediate shock (Option C) is incorrect, as the heart requires mechanical support between attempts. Epinephrine 1 mg (Option D) is administered after the second shock, but the immediate step after any shock is resuming CPR to maintain organ perfusion. Therefore, because the shock has just been delivered and the patient remains unresponsive, initiating the next cycle of CPR is the standard of care to maximize the success of subsequent interventions

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The number of births per 1,000 women in the reproductive age group is called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. General fertility rate

Number of live births per 1000 women in the reproductive age group (15 - 49 years) in a given year is called the general fertility rate

* GFR = Number of live births in an area in a year x 1000/Mid-year population of women in reproductive age in the same area in the same year.

* It is a better indicator of fertility than crude birth rate

* The demerit of this indicator is that not all women in the denominator are exposed to childbirth

Pearl PF1746: Fertility Indicators

Crude birth rate

* It is the simplest measure of fertility although its usage is unsatisfactory

* India, as per SRS bulletin 2018, had a birth rate of 20.0 per 1000 population

General Fertility Rate

* It is a better indicator of fertility than crude birth rate

* The demerit of this indicator is that not all women in the denominator are exposed to childbirth

Age-specific fertility rates is a more precise measure of fertility and is also a sensitive indicator of family planning achievement.

Total Fertility Rate

* It is the sum of all age-specific fertility rates multiplied by 5

* This measure gives the approximate magnitude of completed family size

Gross Reproductive Rate is the average number of girls that would be born to a woman if she experiences the current fertility pattern throughout her reproductive span, assuming no mortality.

Net Reproduction Rate

* It is a demographic indicator

* NRR of 1 is equivalent to approximately the 2 child norm

* If the NRR is less than 1, then the reproductive performance of the population is said to be inadequate

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 28-year-old patient presents with severe ear pain and unilateral facial weakness. Examination reveals vesicular lesions in the external auditory canal and on the tympanic membrane, along with inability to smile or close the eye on the affected side. What is the most likely diagnosis, and which part of the nervous system is involved?
options: Ramsay Hunt syndrome and basal ganglion
Ramsay Hunt syndrome and geniculate ganglion
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of facial nerve palsy (difficulty smiling/closing eyelids), severe ear pain, and vesicular eruptions in the external ear canal is pathognomonic for Ramsay Hunt syndrome (Herpes Zoster Oticus). This condition results from the reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus specifically within the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve (Cranial Nerve VII). Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome (Options C and D) is a rare neurological disorder characterized by a triad of recurrent facial paralysis, swelling of the face and lips, and a fissured tongue, but it does not involve painful vesicles. The basal ganglion (Option A) is involved in movement disorders like Parkinson's, not peripheral nerve palsies. Management of Ramsay Hunt syndrome requires urgent initiation of antiviral medications (acyclovir) and oral corticosteroids to reduce nerve inflammation. Early treatment is critical, as the prognosis for facial nerve recovery in Ramsay Hunt is generally poorer than in standard Bell's palsy
questions.learning: The clinical triad of facial nerve palsy (difficulty smiling/closing eyelids), severe ear pain, and vesicular eruptions in the external ear canal is pathognomonic for Ramsay Hunt syndrome (Herpes Zoster Oticus).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: An image shows a lateral view of the face with a highlighted area located anterior to the ear. Which type of abscess is most likely to occur in this region?
questions.explanation: Luc's abscess is a subperiosteal abscess located in the region of the external auditory canal or preauricular area. It occurs when pus from the mastoid antrum erodes through the outer cortex without involving the mastoid tip. It is more common in children due to their thinner, softer mastoid bone. Citelli's abscess (Option A) tracks into the posterior belly of the digastric muscle, presenting in the upper neck behind the mandible. Bezold's abscess (Option C) results from pus eroding the mastoid tip and tracking deep to the sternocleidomastoid muscle into the neck. Zygomatic abscess (Option D) spreads to the zygomatic root cells, appearing higher in the temporal region above the ear. Based on the specific anatomical highlight toward the external canal in the image, Luc's abscess is the most likely diagnosis
questions.learning: Luc's abscess is a subperiosteal abscess located in the region of the external auditory canal or preauricular area. It occurs when pus from the mastoid antrum erodes through the outer cortex without involving the mastoid tip.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with a history of recurrent pilonidal sinus underwent surgery as shown in the image. What kind of flap procedure is used here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Rhomboid flap

The following image shows a rhomboid flap done in pilonidal sinus surgery.

A pilonidal sinus is defined as a blind track lined by granulation tissue leading from an epithelial surface to surrounding tissue. Pilonidal sinus disease, also called jeep/driver’s bottom, is commonly seen in the natal cleft, more in men, usually after puberty.

Buttock friction and shearing forces (drivers are commonly affected) in this area allow broken hairs to enter the skin and create a subcutaneous, chronically infected midline track. An infected hair follicle can also form such a track. Secondary tracks can also form and are lined with granulation tissue and discharge.

Patients complain of intermittent pain, swelling, and discharge at the base of the spine. A foreign-body-type reaction may then lead to the formation of an abscess.

Treatment includes non-surgical and surgical approaches:

Non-surgical approaches include conservative treatment with proper hygiene and regular shaving of hair in the area. In case of an abscess- adequate rest, baths, local antiseptic dressings, and broad-spectrum antibiotics are advised.

Surgical approaches for the management of pilonidal sinus disease include:

Incision and drainage- for pilonidal abscess refractory to medical treatment.
Bascom's procedure- is a cleft lift procedure in which hair follicles parallel to the natal cleft are removed under local anesthesia
Others- VY advancement flaps, and Z-plasty.

A rhomboid flap is an example of a transposition flap that are rectangular or square and turn laterally to reach the defect . They rely on the looseness of adjacent skin to transfer a rhomboid-shaped flap into a defect that has been converted into a similar rhomboid shape.
questions.learning: Rhomboid flap — The following image shows a rhomboid flap done in pilonidal sinus surgery. A pilonidal sinus is defined as a blind track lined by granulation tissue leading from an epithelial surface to surrounding tissue.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A child lacks thymus and inferior parathyroid glands. Defective development of which of the following structures is likely to be the cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of DiGeorge syndrome. Defective development of the third pharyngeal pouch marked as 3 causes this condition.

A child with DiGeorge syndrome lacks thymus and inferior parathyroid glands due to defective development of the 3rd pharyngeal pouch. The child can also lack superior parathyroid glands, due to defective development of the 4th pharyngeal pouch. It is caused by chromosome 22q deletion and is characterized by the following (Mnemonic: CATCH-22)

• Cleft palate
• Abnormal facies
• Thymic aplasia leading to T-cell deficiency and recurrent infections
• Cardiac defects
• Hypocalcemia, secondary to parathyroid aplasia.

Derivatives of the Pharyngeal Pouches

1st Pouch

• Tympanic cavity (middle ear cavity)
• Auditory tube (eustachian tube)

2nd Pouch

• Palatine tonsils
• Tonsillar fossa

3rd Pouch

• Inferior parathyroid glands
• Thymus

4th Pouch

• Superior parathyroid glands
• Ultimobranchial body - gives rise to parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid gland

The medulla of the thymus has Hassall’s corpuscles. They are small rounded structures formed from whorls of medullary epithelial cells with a central partially keratinized core appearing as an eosinophilic-staining mass.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 56-year-old patient presents with prominent, dilated veins on the legs. Which diagnostic test is most appropriate for evaluating varicose veins in this patient?
questions.explanation: For the evaluation of varicose veins and chronic venous insufficiency, a Duplex ultrasound scan is considered the gold standard and most appropriate diagnostic test. It is non-invasive and provides both anatomical information (identifying the location of dilated veins) and functional information (demonstrating the direction of blood flow and the presence of valvular reflux). This precise mapping is essential for planning treatments such as endovenous laser ablation or sclerotherapy. Plethysmography (Option B) measures changes in limb volume and can assess global venous function but lacks the anatomical detail of Duplex. MRI (Option C) and CT (Option D) are rarely indicated for simple varicose veins, although they may be used for complex pelvic venous congestion syndromes. Clinicians use the Duplex scan to evaluate the saphenofemoral and saphenopopliteal junctions for incompetence. Accurate diagnostic mapping significantly reduces the risk of recurrence after surgical or minimally invasive interventions
questions.learning: For the evaluation of varicose veins and chronic venous insufficiency, a Duplex ultrasound scan is considered the gold standard and most appropriate diagnostic test.

questions.text: What would be the diagnosis in case the axis aligns with the "?" mark as depicted in the below diagram?

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 40-year-old male presents with increased thirst and increased frequency and volume of urination. His random blood sugar was 205 mg/dl, what appropriate investigations should be done? i) HbA1c ii) Urine ACR iii) Echocardiography iv) Fundoscopy v) ECG vi) Serum protein electrophoresis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. i, ii, iv, v

In a patient with suspected or newly diagnosed diabetes mellitus, evaluation should include confirmation of glycemic status and screening for early diabetic complications.

Appropriate initial investigations include:

• HbA1c → assesses long-term glycemic control (average glucose over \~3 months).
• Urine albumin–creatinine ratio (ACR) → screens for diabetic nephropathy (microalbuminuria).
• Fundoscopy → detects diabetic retinopathy.
• ECG → evaluates cardiovascular disease, which is common in diabetics.

Tests like echocardiography and serum protein electrophoresis are not routine initial investigations for newly diagnosed diabetes unless specific clinical indications are present.
questions.learning: i, ii, iv, v In a patient with suspected or newly diagnosed diabetes mellitus, evaluation should include confirmation of glycemic status and screening for early diabetic complications.
