questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient on anti-depressants presented to you with hypotension. An ECG was done, which showed wide QRS complexes and right axis deviation. How will you manage this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Intravenous sodium bicarbonate

The given clinical scenario along the ECG changes described suggests a diagnosis of tricyclic antidepressant toxicity. This can be managed with intravenous sodium bicarbonate.

Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) are used in the treatment of psychotic depression, insomnia, and several pain conditions. Their mechanism of action is inhibition of norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake. They have a quinidine-like sodium channel blockade effect on cardiac conduction. Hence, they cause QT prolongation. Other cardiotoxic effects include atrioventricular (AV) block and hypotension. Rightward-axis deviation is also an associated finding.

TCA toxicity can result in ventricular tachyarrhythmias, status epilepticus, hyperthermia, and coma. It can also result in anticholinergic syndrome due to muscarinic receptor antagonism. Symptoms include dilated pupils, high temperature, dry mouth, and myoclonic movements. It is managed with intravenous sodium bicarbonate bolus (50-100 mEq). This helps in the reversal of sodium channel blockade. Gastric lavage and administration of activated charcoal can be carried out in cases of recent ingestion.

Other side effects of TCAs include urinary retention, tachycardia, and postural hypotension. ECG changes such as T wave inversion or suppression are also common.

In some cases, it can result in polymorphic ventricular tachycardias with QT prolongation known as torsades de pointes. Recurrent episodes can be treated with intravenous magnesium sulfate.

Other options:

Option A: Class IA, IC, and III antiarrhythmic drugs are contraindicated as they potentiate the action of TCAs.

Option B: Propranolol is a class II antiarrhythmic that can cause wide QRS complexes. It is used for rate control in atrial fibrillation, angina, and hypertension.

Option D: Phenytoin is an antiepileptic used for the treatment of generalized tonic-clonic seizures and focal seizures. It inactivates sodium channels and stabilizes neuronal membranes. It can displace TCAs from their protein binding sites which can result in transient overdose symptoms.
questions.learning: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate — The given clinical scenario along the ECG changes described suggests a diagnosis of tricyclic antidepressant toxicity. This can be managed with intravenous sodium bicarbonate.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 32-year-old woman presents to the breast clinic with a painless lump in her left breast that she discovered during a self-examination. On examination, a well-defined, mobile, firm, and non-tender mass of 2 cm is palpated in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast. The overlying skin is smooth, and there is no nipple discharge or lymphadenopathy. Mammogram is shown below. Classify the following mammography lesion as per BIRADS staging:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. BIRADS 2

BI-RADS 2 (benign) lesions show classic benign features such as well-defined margins, coarse “popcorn” calcifications, simple cysts, or fibroadenoma, with no suspicious features. These findings have 0% malignancy risk and require routine screening only, not biopsy or short-interval follow-up.

BI-RADS Scoring System (Mammography):

• BI-RADS 0: Incomplete – need additional imaging
• BI-RADS 1: Negative (normal)
• BI-RADS 2: Benign lesion (0% malignancy) → routine screening
• BI-RADS 3: Probably benign (<2% risk) → short-interval follow-up (6 months)
• BI-RADS 4: Suspicious (2–95% risk) → biopsy required

o    4A: Low suspicion

o    4B: Moderate

o    4C: High
• BI-RADS 5: Highly suggestive of malignancy (>95%) → treat as cancer
• BI-RADS 6: Known biopsy-proven malignancy
questions.learning: BIRADS 2 BI-RADS 2 (benign) lesions show classic benign features such as well-defined margins, coarse “popcorn” calcifications, simple cysts, or fibroadenoma, with no suspicious features.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 30-year-old male presents with nonaxial proptosis of the left eye. The patient gives a history of a road traffic accident 15 years back. The CT image is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Frontal mucocele

A frontal mucocele is a slow-growing, mucus-filled expansile lesion of the paranasal sinus that can cause non-axial proptosis due to orbital displacement.

• Cause: Obstruction of sinus drainage (often post-trauma or surgery)
• Leads to progressive expansion → bone erosion → orbital extension
• Presents with painless, non-axial proptosis (eye displaced downward/outward)

Imaging features (CT):

• Homogeneous expansile lesion in frontal sinus
• Thinning/erosion of sinus walls
• Displacement of orbit and surrounding structures

Why not other options:

• B. Frontal meningioma: Intracranial, not sinus-based expansile lesion
• C. JNA: Nasopharyngeal vascular tumor in adolescent males
• D. Orbital pseudotumor: Inflammatory, painful, no sinus expansion

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What represents the marked area in the given histology of lymph node?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Mantle zone

The area marked in the image is the mantle zone of a lymph node.

Lymph node has primary follicle composed of small, quiescent lymphocytes, and a secondary follicle with germinal centre composed mainly of antigen-stimulated B cells.

The mantle zone is produced as surrounding cells are marginalised by the rapidly growing germinal centre. It is populated by mainly quiescent B cells with condensed heterochromatic nuclei and little cytoplasm (hence the deeply basophilic staining of this region in routine preparations), a few helper T cells, Follicular Dendritic cells and macrophages.

In peripheral lymph nodes, the marginal zone are often inapparent because they are mixed with the mantle zone cells. And often not well developed in lymph nodes.

The paracortex lies between the cortical follicles and the medulla and is populated mainly by T cells, which are not organised into follicles

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Revised A patient underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy for cholelithiasis. Picture of the resected gall bladder is shown as below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gall bladder carcinoma

The diagnosis is gallbladder carcinoma.

The gross specimen shows a resected gallbladder with multiple gallstones impacted in the lumen. The irregularly thickened wall, mucosal changes, and firm, indurated areas indicate tumor growth and inflammation.

Gallbladder carcinoma

* Gallbladder carcinoma is a rare malignancy that affects the elderly population; it is associated with a poor prognosis, except when diagnosed at the early stages.

* The histologic subtypes are papillary, nodular, and tubular carcinomas.

Clinical features:

* It is usually indistinguishable from cholecystitis or cholelithiasis.

* Features include right upper quadrant pain, abdominal discomfort, nausea, and vomiting.

Diagnosis:

* It is usually diagnosed when patients undergo cholecystectomy for gallstones.

* Laboratory diagnosis in 80% of the cases is made by detection of elevated levels of carbohydrate antigen (CA) 19-9 in assays.

* Ultrasonography (USG) is often indicative of a thickened irregular gallbladder wall or a lesion replacing the gallbladder.

* Computed tomography (CT) can detect the presence of a tumour and its invasion and can be used for identifying its stage of development

* Percutaneous transhepatic or endoscopic retrograde cholangiography and subsequent bile cytology can help establish the diagnosis of gallbladder cancer.

* Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography is a non-invasive imaging method that allows for a complete clinical assessment of the vascular, nodal, and hepatic architecture and other adjacent organs.

Treatment options for carcinoma gall bladder found incidentally after cholecystectomy:

* Up to stage Ia and stage Ib with negative margins: Standard cholecystectomy

* Stage Ib with perineural, lymphatic, vascular invasion and stage II: Extended cholecystectomy

* Chemotherapy is not required in an early gall bladder cancer. Radiation has no role.

Treatment of gallbladder carcinoma (in general):

T1a: Simple cholecystectomy

T1b, T2, T3: Radical cholecystectomy

T4: Unresectable, chemotherapy and palliative nonsurgical therapy are provided.

N1: Regional lymphadenectomy

N2: Radical cholecystectomy plus hepatopancreatic duodenectomy
questions.learning: Gall bladder carcinoma — The diagnosis is gallbladder carcinoma. The gross specimen shows a resected gallbladder with multiple gallstones impacted in the lumen.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A young patient came with complaints of acute abdominal pain on and off and tingling sensation of limbs and at times weakness of limbs. She had a history of eating paint from the wall of a newly built house. Which of the following enzyme defect will be the cause of her condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. ALA dehydratase

A child with acute abdominal pain, tingling sensation and weakness of limbs with history of eating paint likely has lead poisoning. It is characterized by impaired ALA dehydratase enzyme activity.

Lead is a potent inhibitor of both ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase/ heme synthase (option C). However, it has the greatest inhibitory action on ALA dehydratase. Lead poisonining thus leads to the buildup of protoporphyrin and ALA. Lead also substitutes for calcium in many fundamental cellular processes. It can cross red blood cell membranes as well as the blood-brain barrier and enter the neuroglial cells which support brain function. The fatal dose of lead is 20g of lead acetate and the fatal period is 1 to 2 days.

Other options:

Option A: ALA synthase 2 defect causes X-linked protoporphyria.
Option C: Heme synthase, or ferrochelatase, defect causes erythropoeitic protoporphyria.
Option D: Coproporphyrinogen oxidase defect causes hereditary corproporphyria.
questions.learning: ALA dehydratase — A child with acute abdominal pain, tingling sensation and weakness of limbs with history of eating paint likely has lead poisoning. It is characterized by impaired ALA dehydratase enzyme activity.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man with multiple sexual partners presents with a palmoplantar rash as seen below. On examination, he has epitrochlear lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Secondary syphilis

This clinical scenario of maculopapular rash with flu-like symptoms and epitrochlear lymphadenopathy points to secondary syphilis.

Secondary syphilis occurs within 6 weeks to 8 weeks of the onset of the primary chancre.

It is characterized by the following:

* Onset of systemic manifestations includes symptoms such as malaise, headache, loss of appetite, sore throat

* Generalized symmetric, asymptomatic maculopapular rash on the palms and soles.

* Generalized adenopathy in 50% of cases

* Condyloma lata is the classic finding. They are highly contagious exophytic broad excrescences that ulcerate. These are commonly seen on the vulva, perianal area, and upper thighs.

The image below shows mucosal and cutaneous lesion of secondary syphilis.

Other options:

Option A: Psoriasis presents with itching and a papulosquamous rash commonly on the scalp, trunk, and extensor surfaces of the limbs. The lesions are red, scaly, and have well demarcation from the normal skin. They can also be encircled by a clear peripheral zone called the Woronoff ring.

Option C: Meningococcemia caused by Neisseria meningitidis presents as acute fever with chills, malaise, and prostration. A petechial rash is seen early in the disease. Metastatic involvement of the joints, ears, eyes, lungs, and adrenals may occur.

Option D: Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) are severe mucocutaneous reactions, usually to drugs, characterized by blistering and epithelial sloughing. The two terms describe phenotypes within a severity spectrum, where SJS is the less extensive form and TEN is the more extensive.

Pearl PF1554: Stages of syphilis

* Primary Syphilis:

Chancre- Painless, indurated, usually single

Lymphadenopathy- Painless, unilateral or bilateral, shotty and rubbery inguinal nodes

Dory flop sign- As the chancre is too hard to fold, it will flip over once the prepuce is retracted back.

The chancre self heals in 1-4 months.

Secondary Syphilis:

A & B: Generalized rash(non-itchy, no vesicles, and palm and sole involvement).

This is the most common lesion.

C & D: Condyloma lata.

E: Moth-eaten alopecia (Non-scarring)

F: Mucous patches(Flat erosions on the tongue which can coalesce and form snail track ulcers).These are the most infectious lesions.

G: Pigmentary plaques

H: Psoriasiform syphilitic lesions

Generalized diffuse non-tender lymphadenopathy

Tertiary Syphilis:

Gummatous syphilis(deep punched-out ulcers, with gum-like secretions on the floor)

Pseudo-chancre redux is a gumma occurring at the site of a previously healed ulcer

CVS-Aortitis and aneurysm of the ascending aorta

CNS-General paresis of the insane and tabes dorsalis

Latent Syphilis-Period between secondary and tertiary syphilis, when the patient is asymptomatic clinically, and only serological evidence of infection is present.

* Early latent- Within 1 year of infection

* Late latent- After 1 year of infection
questions.learning: Secondary syphilis — This clinical scenario of maculopapular rash with flu-like symptoms and epitrochlear lymphadenopathy points to secondary syphilis. Secondary syphilis occurs within 6 weeks to 8 weeks of the onset of the primary chancre.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with hypertension, tachycardia, and early renal involvement is prescribed Telmisartan. What is the most likely mechanism by which this medication improves heart rate and blood pressure?
options: Increases sodium excretion via loop diuresis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Decreases peripheral vascular resistance

The most likely mechanism of action of telmisartan in this case is the decrease in peripheral vascular resistance.

Telmisartan, an angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB), has shown evidence of having PPARγ agonist action. It is very useful in hypertensive patients with diabetes. PPARγ agonists are the thiazolidinedione group of drugs that act by inducing several insulin-sensitising genes, thereby reducing overall insulin resistance. Common side effects of telmisartan are hypotension, hyperkalaemia, teratogenicity, headache, gastrointestinal upset, and dizziness.

By acting as an agonist on the PPARγ receptor, telmisartan regulates the downstream glucose and lipid metabolism. It increases basal and insulin-stimulated uptake of glucose into the adipocytes via GLUT-4. It also decreases the amount of reactive oxygen species and increases serum adiponectin. By these mechanisms, it improves oxidative stress and insulin resistance in patients with type II diabetes mellitus. Furthermore, it has been shown to reduce cardiac fibrosis and hypertrophy. Telmisartan can be given safely to a patient with chronic renal failure (CRF) because it is mainly cleared from the circulation by biliary excretion.

The drugs that reduce mortality in patients with HFrEF are

* Beta-blockers block β1 receptors and prevent ventricular remodelling promoted by the stimulated RAAS and sympathetic system. Metoprolol and bisoprolol are selective for the β1 receptor, whereas carvedilol also blocks the β2 and α1 receptors, resulting in vasodilation. Adverse effects include fluid retention, worsening HFrEF, fatigue, bradycardia or heart block, and hypotension.

* ACE inhibitors—enalapril and lisinopril—reduce mortality. ACE inhibitors decrease peripheral resistance and reduce the load on the failing myocardium by inhibiting the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II. Hereby, it prevents vasoconstriction and causes relaxation of the vasculature.

* Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) – They inhibit the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS) by blocking the binding of angiotensin II to its receptor, which in turn leads to vasodilation and prevents the release of aldosterone. They are found to reduce mortality and morbidity in HFrEF cases.

* Angiotensin receptor neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI) sacubitril/valsartan is a novel therapy that was approved in July 2015 to reduce the risk of cardiovascular death and hospitalisation for patients with HFrEF. Sacubitril/valsartan consists of the neprilysin inhibitor sacubitril and the ARB valsartan.

* Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists like spironolactone and eplerenone are also known to decrease the mortality risk.

Diuretics like furosemide and torsemide are not found to reduce mortality or hospital readmission. They are the only agents that can adequately control the fluid retention associated with HFrEF.

Prazosin, an alpha-1 adrenergic blocker, does not decrease mortality risk in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), unlike other neurohormonal antagonists such as beta-blockers and ACE inhibitors.

Pearl PF0729: Cardioselective beta blockers: Mnemonic

Cardioselective Beta blockers Act At Nothing But Myocardium Exclusively.

* C: Celiprolol ( III )

* B: Bisoprolol

* A: Acebutolol

* A: Atenolol

* N: Nebivolol ( III )

* B: Betaxolol ( III )

* M: Metoprolol

* E: Esmolol

( III ) - Third generation beta blockers. All the others are second generation beta blockers
questions.learning: Decreases peripheral vascular resistance — The most likely mechanism of action of telmisartan in this case is the decrease in peripheral vascular resistance.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 2-month-old infant presents with inspiratory stridor that worsens during crying and feeding. Which statement is true regarding the most likely diagnosis?
options: Omega sign, improves in prone position
Thumb sign, improves in tripod position
Thumb sign, improves in tripod position Steeple sign is seen
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Omega sign, improves in prone position

Recognize laryngomalacia as the most common cause of congenital inspiratory stridor. It typically presents within the first few weeks to months of life with inspiratory stridor that worsens during crying, feeding, or when supine and improves in the prone position. Laryngoscopy shows a characteristic omega-shaped, floppy epiglottis with collapse of supraglottic structures during inspiration.

Why not the other options?

• B. Thumb sign, improves in tripod position: Thumb sign indicates acute epiglottitis, which presents with high fever, drooling, dysphagia, and toxic appearance, not a chronic infantile stridor.
• C. Steeple sign is seen: Steeple sign is characteristic of croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) on AP neck X-ray, presenting with barking cough and stridor.
• D. Epiglottis is reddish and oedematous: Seen in acute epiglottitis, not laryngomalacia.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A patient shows flat affect. What does it indicate?
questions.explanation: In psychiatry, especially regarding schizophrenia, symptoms are categorized based on whether they reflect an excess or a loss of normal function. "Flat affect" refers to a significant reduction or complete lack of emotional expression, where the patient exhibits minimal facial expressions, vocal inflection, or gestures. This is classified as a negative symptom because it represents a "loss" of normal emotional responsiveness. Positive symptoms (Option A) include distortions like delusions or hallucinations. Cognitive symptoms (Option D) involve impairments in memory, attention, and executive function. "Affect symptom" (Option C) is not a standard psychiatric classification. Other negative symptoms include avolition (lack of motivation) and alogia (poverty of speech). Therefore, flat affect is a hallmark negative symptom that often contributes to poor social functioning in schizophrenic patients

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The ideal per capita space for students in a classroom should be
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. >10 sq. ft.

Per capita space for students in classroom should be >10 sq. ft.

Healthful school environment includes

* Location: Properly approachable roads and away from noisy surroundings

* Site: 5 acres for primary schools; 10 acres for higher elementary schools.

* Structure: Exterior walls 10 inch thick and heat resistant.

* Class room: 1 class room per 40 students maximum; Per capita space > 10 sq. feet

* Furniture: Minus type with proper back-rests.

* Doors and windows: Doors and windows area> 25% of floor area

* Color: Inside color of walls should be white.

* Lighting: Natural light,from sides and not from the front.

* Water supply: Safe and potable and continuous supply through taps.

* Lavatory: 1 urinal per 60 students and 1 latrine per 100 students.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A patient who underwent right limb amputation 2 years back, now presents with severe pain in the limb (Phantom limb pain). On radiological investigations, What is the finding seen?
options: Projection of adjacent fibres to overlap the right somatosensory cortex
Projection of adjacent fibres to overlap the left somatosensory cortex
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Projection of adjacent fibres to overlap the left somatosensory cortex

In the given scenario of phantom limb pain, on the radiological investigation of the brain projection of adjacent fibres to overlap the left somatosensory cortex can be seen. This pain is based on cortical plasticity.

Cortical structures are capable of reorganization after the loss of a body part. The cortical representation of the neighbouring parts spreads into the cortical area that was formerly occupied by the representation of the amputated part. This is called cortical plasticity leads to the phenomenon of phantom limb pain. The sensory cortical area occupied by the right limb is the left somatosensory cortex.

Cortical plasticity / Phantom limb: It is the sensation that an amputated or missing limb is still attached. Plasticity is the ability of the brain to adapt to such a condition by reorganization of thalamic and cortical structures.

The converse also holds true: if the cortical area representing a limb is removed, the somatosensory map of the limb moves to the surrounding cortex.

Diagnosis and Management :

• PET scan is used to document these plastic changes in cortex.
• Use of epidural analgesia during amputation surgery decreases incidence of phantom pain.
• Spinal cord stimulation also helps in reducing phantom pain. (interferes with ascending impulses to brain)
questions.learning: Projection of adjacent fibres to overlap the left somatosensory cortex In the given scenario of phantom limb pain, on the radiological investigation of the brain projection of adjacent fibres to overlap the left somatosensory cortex can be seen.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10-year-old boy has a history of spontaneous excessive bruising and hemarthrosis, with laboratory findings of a normal platelet count, prolonged partial thromboplastin time (PTT), and a normal prothrombin time (PT). What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of spontaneous bruising, hemarthrosis (bleeding into joints), and an isolated prolonged PTT in a young boy is highly characteristic of Hemophilia A. Hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by a deficiency of Factor VIII. Factors in the intrinsic pathway, such as Factor VIII, are measured by the PTT. Because the extrinsic and common pathways (measured by PT) and platelet function are normal, those tests remain within normal limits. Von Willebrand disease (Option A) could show a prolonged PTT but typically presents with mucosal bleeding (nosebleeds, gum bleeding) rather than deep joint bleeds. Bernard-Soulier (Option C) and Glanzmann thrombasthenia (Option D) are qualitative platelet disorders that would present with an increased bleeding time and abnormal platelet function tests, which are not described here . Therefore, the specific joint bleeding pattern and clotting profile definitively identify Hemophilia A
questions.learning: The clinical triad of spontaneous bruising, hemarthrosis (bleeding into joints), and an isolated prolonged PTT in a young boy is highly characteristic of Hemophilia A.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A male patient with a long-standing history of smoking presents with complaints of dysphagia. Based on this clinical scenario, which type of lung cancer is most commonly associated with such a presentation?
questions.explanation: In a male chronic smoker presenting with dysphagia, the clinical suspicion points toward a central lung tumor that is compressing the esophagus. Squamous cell carcinoma (Option A) is the type of lung cancer most strongly associated with smoking and is classically located in a central (hilar) position. Because of its central location, it is the most likely subtype to cause extrinsic compression of the esophagus, leading to the patient's difficulty swallowing. Adenocarcinoma (Option B) is the most common lung cancer overall but is typically located peripherally and is less specifically linked to heavy smoking compared to the squamous type. Large cell carcinoma (Option C) is also often peripheral. "Bronchogenic carcinoma" (Option D) is a general term for all primary lung cancers rather than a specific pathological subtype. Therefore, given the specific combination of smoking history and central compressive symptoms, Squamous cell carcinoma is the expected predominant diagnosis

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Identify the phenomenon shown below
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Complementation

The image shows a schematic of the blue-white assay used in the screening of recombinant vectors for inserted DNA fragments. It uses the phenomenon of complementation (α-complementation of the β-galactosidase gene).

Blue–white assay:

The DNA of interest is ligated into a vector. The vector is then inserted into a competent host cell viable for transformation, which is then grown in the presence of X-gal (X-gal detects active β-galactosidase). Cells transformed with vectors containing recombinant DNA will produce white colonies; cells transformed with non-recombinant plasmids (i.e., only the vector) grow into blue colonies.

The image below shows the result of a blue–white assay.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient with a known marginal placenta presents for follow-up evaluation. Ultrasonography reveals a 4 × 4 cm placental mass extending beyond the uterus and invading the urinary bladder. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Placenta percreta is the most severe grade of the placenta accreta spectrum. It occurs when chorionic villi penetrate through the entire thickness of the myometrium and the uterine serosa, often invading adjacent pelvic organs such as the urinary bladder. Placenta previa (Option A) refers only to the location of the placenta near or over the internal os without invasion. Placenta accreta (Option C) involves adherence to the myometrium without penetration. Placenta increta (Option D) involves invasion deep into the myometrium but not through the serosa. Because the ultrasound explicitly identifies invasion into the bladder, the condition has progressed beyond the myometrium, confirming the diagnosis of percreta. This requires complex surgical management, often including a hysterectomy and partial cystectomy
questions.learning: Placenta percreta is the most severe grade of the placenta accreta spectrum. It occurs when chorionic villi penetrate through the entire thickness of the myometrium and the uterine serosa, often invading adjacent pelvic organs such as the urinary bladder.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding the management of patients who have achieved return of spontaneous circulation following CPR?
options: Initiate targeted temperature management of <33°C, if the patient is confused
Perform emergent cardiac intervention if ST elevation is present in the ECG
Maintain a mean arterial pressure (MAP) above 65 mmHg
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Initiate targeted temperature management of <33°C, if the patient is confused

After successful CPR, the patient may develop Post–Cardiac Arrest Syndrome, which includes:

• Brain injury
• Myocardial dysfunction
• Systemic ischemia-reperfusion injury
• Persistent precipitating pathology (e.g., MI)

Immediate management focuses on oxygenation, circulation, neuroprotection, and treating the cause. Post–cardiac arrest care includes maintaining SpO₂ >94%, MAP ≥65 mmHg, and urgent coronary intervention if STEMI is present.

Current guidelines (AHA 2020 and the post-TTM2 trial era) recommend targeted temperature management between 32–36°C, with a strong shift toward simply maintaining normothermia and actively preventing fever (≤37.5°C). A target of "<33°C" is not the standard — aggressive hypothermia below 33°C showed no benefit over 36°C or fever prevention in major trials (TTM, TTM2). The underlying concept: after successful CPR, patients develop post-cardiac arrest syndrome — anoxic brain injury, myocardial stunning, systemic ischemia-reperfusion injury, plus the precipitating pathology. Management bundles target oxygenation (94%+), perfusion (MAP ≥65), temperature control (prevent fever; cool only if comatose), and treating the cause (e.g., PCI for STEMI).
questions.learning: Initiate targeted temperature management of 94%, MAP ≥65 mmHg, and urgent coronary intervention if STEMI is present. Current guidelines (AHA 2020 and the post-TTM2 trial era) recommend targeted temperature management between 32–36°C, with a strong shift…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 70-year-old man presented with back pain for the past 3 months. On examination, he has pallor, and gamma globulins are elevated. Liver function tests are normal. X-ray spine shows multiple lytic lesions. Which of the following cells are involved in the pathogenesis of this patient's condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Plasma cells

The given clinical scenario of a patient with backache for the past 3 months and multiple lytic lesions is suggestive of multiple myeloma, a malignant plasma cell dyscrasia with the proliferation of plasma cells derived from a single clone.

Bone pain is the most common symptom of multiple myeloma. Tumor cells release osteoclast activating factors (OAFs), which increase osteoclast activity and accelerated bone destruction. Furthermore, there is suppression of osteoblast activity to form new bone. Lysis of the bone leads to hypercalcemia. Patients with multiple myeloma also have an increased susceptibility to infections because of diffuse hypogammaglobulinemia (decreased production and increased destruction) of normal antibodies.

Other important features of multiple myeloma include:

* Renal failure

* Normocytic and normochromic anemia

* Hyperviscosity syndromes

* Elevated ESR

* Normal alkaline phosphatase due to suppression of osteoblast activity.

* Monoclonal protein in serum protein electrophoresis

* Urinalysis shows free kappa and lambda light chains (Bence-Jones proteins)

Diagnostic Criteria for Multiple Myeloma include:

Clonal bone marrow plasma cells ≥10% (or) biopsy-proven bony or extramedullary plasmacytoma

plus

Any one or more of the following myeloma-defining events:

* Evidence of end-organ damage attributable to the underlying plasma cell proliferative disorder, specifically: (CRAB features)

* Hypercalcemia: Serum calcium level >1 mg/dL higher than the upper limit of normal or >11 mg/dL

* Renal insufficiency: Serum creatinine >2 mg/dL

* Anemia: Hemoglobin level of >2 g/dL below the lowest limit of normal, or Hb <10 g/dL

* Bone lesions: One or more osteolytic lesions on radiography, computed tomography (CT), or positron emission tomography (PET).

* Any one or more of the following biomarkers of malignancy:

* Clonal bone marrow plasma cells ≥ 60%

* Serum involved / uninvolved free light-chain ratio of 100 or greater.

* >1 focal lesion on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Glycogen phosphorylase is activated by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Calcium

Glycogen phosphorylase is activated by calcium in the muscle.

Glycogen phosphorylase is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycogenolysis and is decreased in the fed state.

In the muscle, the increased cytosolic calcium ion concentration initiates both contraction and glycogenolysis. Muscle phosphorylase kinase has four different subunits, α, β, γ, and δ. The α and β subunits are phosphorylated by cAMP-dependent protein kinase. The δ subunit is identical to the calcium-binding protein calmodulin and binds four calcium ions. Calcium coordinates the activation of Glycogen Phosphorylase with the contraction of the muscle.

Glycogen phosphorylase catalyzes the cleavage of α1 → 4 linkages of glycogen to single units of glucose 1-phosphate. It uses pyridoxal phosphate as the coenzyme. Different isoenzymes of glycogen phosphorylase are seen in the liver, muscles, and brain.

Other options:

Option B: During glycogenolysis, glucose 6-phosphate allosterically inhibits glycogen phosphorylase.

Option C: Insulin entirely suppresses glycogenolysis in the skeletal muscle and liver.

Option D: In glycogenolysis protein phosphatase is inactivated by inhibitor proteins in response to cAMP, to maintain the glycogen phosphorylase in an active state.
questions.learning: Calcium Glycogen phosphorylase is activated by calcium in the muscle. Glycogen phosphorylase is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycogenolysis and is decreased in the fed state.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which term describes the exchange process in red blood cells in which bicarbonate ions are swapped for chloride ions to maintain electrical neutrality?
questions.explanation: The chloride shift, also known as the Hamburger phenomenon, is the process by which red blood cells (RBCs) maintain electrical neutrality during gas exchange. In peripheral tissues, enters RBCs and is converted into bicarbonate and hydrogen ions . The bicarbonate then exits the cell into the plasma in exchange for chloride ions entering the cell. This exchange ensures ionic balance and facilitates the transport of in the blood. The Haldane effect (Option A) describes how deoxygenated hemoglobin has a higher affinity for . The Root effect (Option B) refers to a reduction in oxygen-carrying capacity in acidic conditions, primarily seen in fish. The Bohr effect (Option C) explains how high and low pH decrease hemoglobin's oxygen affinity, promoting unloading in tissues. In the lungs, a "reverse chloride shift" occurs where exits the RBC to allow to re-enter for exhalation
questions.learning: The chloride shift, also known as the Hamburger phenomenon, is the process by which red blood cells (RBCs) maintain electrical neutrality during gas exchange.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 25-year-old man presents with pain and swelling of the right knee. Radiography reveals an eccentric, lytic “soap-bubble” lesion involving the epiphysis of the distal femur. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The X-ray shows a displaced patellar fracture in a 25-year-old presenting with pain and swelling of the right knee. The white arrow points to fragmentation and displacement of patellar fragments, confirming patellar fracture. Key Radiological Features visible: 1. Disrupted patellar continuity with visible fragment separation 2. Displaced bony fragments near the patella 3. Soft tissue swelling around the knee joint 4. Arrow specifically indicating the fracture site Why other options are wrong: (B) Tibial fracture is incorrect because the tibial cortex appears completely intact without any visible fracture line, periosteal reaction, or bony displacement in the tibial region. (C) Foreign body is incorrect because the radio-opaque opacity seen represents displaced bony patellar fragments — not an extrinsic foreign body. The density corresponds anatomically to the patella rather than an external object. (D) Femur fracture is incorrect because the distal femur appears structurally intact with no visible cortical break, fracture line, or displacement of femoral fragments anywhere in the image
questions.learning: The X-ray shows a displaced patellar fracture in a 25-year-old presenting with pain and swelling of the right knee. The white arrow points to fragmentation and displacement of patellar fragments, confirming patellar fracture.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Hormone responsible?
questions.explanation: Breastfeeding and lactation are regulated by two primary hormones: prolactin and oxytocin. Prolactin is responsible for milk production within the breast. Oxytocin, however, is the hormone responsible for the "milk ejection reflex" or "let-down reflex". When an infant suckles, it triggers the release of oxytocin from the posterior pituitary, which causes the myoepithelial cells surrounding the breast alveoli to contract, forcing milk into the ducts for the baby. TSH (Option B) regulates the thyroid gland and has no role in lactation. Growth Hormone (GH) (Option C) promotes general growth but does not influence milk release. FSH (Option D) regulates the development of ovarian follicles and is not involved in breastfeeding. Thus, oxytocin is the hormone directly responsible for facilitating the flow of milk during feeding
questions.learning: Breastfeeding and lactation are regulated by two primary hormones: prolactin and oxytocin. Prolactin is responsible for milk production within the breast.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A primigravida presents with labor pains, and per vaginal examination reveals that the cervix is 7 cm dilated and fully effaced. Which stage of labor is she currently in?
questions.explanation: The first stage of labor is divided into the latent and active phases . Friedman’s curve further subdivides the active phase into the acceleration phase, the phase of maximum slope, and the deceleration phase . The latent phase ends and the active phase begins around 4 cm of cervical dilation. Between 4 cm and 9 cm of dilation, particularly at 7 cm, the patient is in the phase of maximum slope. This is when cervical dilation occurs at its fastest rate. The acceleration phase (Option A) occurs just before this, usually between 3–4 cm. The deceleration phase (Option C) occurs after 9 cm, when dilation slows down before full dilation (10 cm). The latent phase (Option B) is the early part of labor with slow cervical change. Because the patient is 7 cm dilated and fully effaced, she has progressed well into the most rapid portion of the active stage, identifying this as the phase of maximum slope
questions.learning: The first stage of labor is divided into the latent and active phases . Friedman’s curve further subdivides the active phase into the acceleration phase, the phase of maximum slope, and the deceleration phase .

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A young patient develops oxygen desaturation and bilateral basal crepitations soon after surgery performed under general anesthesia using oxygen, nitrous oxide, and desflurane. What is the most likely cause of these postoperative symptoms?
questions.explanation: Negative Pressure Pulmonary Edema (NPPE), also known as post-obstructive pulmonary edema, is a classic post-anesthesia complication, especially in young, healthy patients. It typically occurs following an upper airway obstruction, such as "laryngospasm" during emergence from general anesthesia. As the patient makes forceful inspiratory efforts against a closed glottis, a high negative intrathoracic pressure is generated. This pressure draws fluid from the pulmonary capillaries into the alveoli, leading to rapid onset "desaturation and crepitations". ARDS (Option A) takes longer to develop and is associated with sepsis or major trauma. Pleural effusion (Option B) is a slower accumulation of fluid. Atelectasis (Option D) is common post-operatively but usually causes localized findings rather than diffuse acute pulmonary edema symptoms. NPPE is a medical emergency but usually resolves quickly with supplemental oxygen, CPAP, or brief mechanical ventilation once the airway obstruction is relieved. Clinicians must be vigilant for laryngospasm to prevent this sudden respiratory deterioration
questions.learning: Negative Pressure Pulmonary Edema (NPPE), also known as post-obstructive pulmonary edema, is a classic post-anesthesia complication, especially in young, healthy patients.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents with abdominal pain, hypotension, and a CT scan showing no abnormalities. On physical examination, there is blackish discoloration of the perineal skin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of severe abdominal pain, systemic hypotension (shock), and blackish discoloration of the perineal skin (specifically known as Turner's sign) is highly suggestive of severe, necrotizing Acute Pancreatitis. Turner's sign results from the retroperitoneal tracking of blood from the inflamed pancreas into the subcutaneous tissues of the flanks or perineum. While Necrotizing fasciitis (Option A) also presents with skin discoloration and shock, the primary symptom is typically excruciating local pain rather than general abdominal pain with a normal abdominal CT. Pancreatitis-related skin signs include Cullen's sign (periumbilical) and Turner's sign (flank). A "normal" CT scan very early in the disease course does not rule out pancreatitis, as radiographic signs of necrosis can take 48-72 hours to develop. Management involves intensive fluid resuscitation, analgesia, and monitoring for organ failure. These skin signs are ominous indicators of a poor prognosis and severe internal hemorrhage
questions.learning: The combination of severe abdominal pain, systemic hypotension (shock), and blackish discoloration of the perineal skin (specifically known as Turner's sign) is highly suggestive of severe, necrotizing Acute Pancreatitis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following medications is used for the management of tumor lysis syndrome?
questions.explanation: Tumor Lysis Syndrome (TLS) is a metabolic emergency occurring during cancer treatment when a large number of tumor cells are rapidly destroyed, releasing intracellular contents. This results in hyperuricemia, which can cause acute renal failure. Rasburicase is a recombinant urate oxidase enzyme that directly converts poorly soluble uric acid into highly soluble allantoin, which is easily excreted by the kidneys. Rituximab (Option B), Gemtuzumab (Option C), and Alemtuzumab (Option D) are all monoclonal antibodies used as chemotherapy agents to kill the cancer cells (potentially triggering TLS) rather than managing the metabolic byproduct. Rasburicase is specifically indicated for the prevention and treatment of hyperuricemia in patients receiving therapy for highly proliferative malignancies like leukemias and lymphomas. Therefore, among the choices provided, Rasburicase is the only medication utilized specifically for the biochemical management of TLS complications
